questions.q: Elastic cartilage is found in each of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.explain: (Repeat of Q67.) The intervertebral disc is fibrocartilage — the exception, C.

questions.q: Why is the outer layer of skin (epidermis) specifically keratinized, while the epithelium lining the esophagus — although also stratified squamous — is not?
options: The esophagus cannot regenerate, so keratin is unnecessary there
There is no functional reason; keratinization is random
Keratin only forms in tissues that lack a basement membrane

The epidermis needs a tough, water-resistant surface exposed to the external environment, while the esophagus needs a moist surface resistant to abrasion from swallowed food, without needing waterproofing
questions.explain: Keratinization equips the epidermis with a tough, waterproof surface suited to protecting against the external environment, whereas the esophagus needs a moist, abrasion-resistant lining for swallowed food but does not require waterproofing, so it remains non-keratinized.

questions.q: True or False: Taking folic acid during pregnancy can help minimise the likelihood of cleft palate.
questions.explain: True. The notes state that the likelihood of cleft palate is minimised by taking folic acid during pregnancy.

questions.q: A doctor opens the chest wall to access the heart for emergency surgery. This procedure is known as:
questions.explain: A thoracotomy is a surgical incision through the chest wall — D. (-stomy = opening/drain; -scopy = scope; -centesis = needle aspiration.)

questions.q: Which best distinguishes the perichondrium (covering cartilage) from the periosteum (covering bone) in terms of a key functional similarity, despite covering different tissues?
options: Only the periosteum contains any cells at all
The perichondrium supplies blood vessels directly into the cartilage matrix, unlike the periosteum
Both serve as nutrient-supplying, protective outer membranes for their respective connective tissue, and both contain cells capable of contributing to growth or repair
They serve entirely unrelated functions with no meaningful similarity
questions.explain: Despite covering different tissues, the perichondrium and periosteum share a key functional similarity: both act as protective, nutrient-supplying outer membranes containing cells (chondrogenic or osteogenic) capable of contributing to the growth or repair of the underlying tissue.

questions.q: Which muscle of the rotator cuff is described as the strongest?
questions.explain: Among the rotator cuff muscles (subscapularis, teres minor, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus), the supraspinatus is described as the strongest.

questions.q: A small foramen at the base of the frontal crest, used for passage of vessels during development, is called the:
questions.explain: The foramen caecum is located at the base of the frontal crest and is a small foramen for passage of vessels during embryonic development.

questions.q: Transitional epithelium is found in all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Urothelium lines the renal pelvis, ureter, bladder and prostatic urethra. The membranous urethra is stratified/pseudostratified columnar — the exception.

questions.q: A man puts his foot on a table while standing to lace his shoe. At this point the hip would be in which position?
questions.explain: Lifting the thigh up onto the table decreases the hip angle = flexion — B.

questions.q: In anatomical position, the scapula lies posterolateral to which ribs?
questions.explain: The scapula is a large, flattened triangular bone that lies posterolateral to the 2nd through 7th ribs in the normal anatomical position.

questions.q: MULTIAXIAL JOINT
options: Universal movement is allowed in all axis
Rotation is allowed in all axis
An example is the shoulder joint
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: Multiaxial (ball-and-socket) joints allow universal movement including rotation in all axes; the shoulder joint is a classic example.

questions.q: Which best captures why the thyroid gland, despite being made of epithelial tissue arranged in follicles, is classified functionally as endocrine rather than exocrine?
options: The thyroid actually has a duct that has simply never been observed
It secretes hormones directly into surrounding capillaries rather than through a duct system onto a surface
Endocrine glands must always be shaped like follicles
It has no epithelial cells at all
questions.explain: Despite being epithelial in origin, the thyroid is functionally endocrine because its follicular cells secrete hormones directly into the surrounding rich capillary network rather than through a duct system to an epithelial surface — duct presence or absence is the defining functional criterion.

questions.q: In this anterior/posterior view of the shoulder, the joint formed between the acromion and the clavicle is labelled as the:
questions.explain: The diagram labels the joint between the acromion of the scapula and the lateral end of the clavicle as the acromioclavicular joint, distinct from the glenohumeral joint (shoulder joint proper) and sternoclavicular joint (medial clavicle to sternum).

questions.q: How many cervical vertebrae are typically present in the body?
questions.explain: There are 7 cervical vertebrae (C1–C7) in virtually all humans (and most mammals).

questions.q: True or False: The two parts of the ischiopubic rami typically fuse by the 9th year of life.
questions.explain: The ischiopubic rami (the inferior ramus of the pubis and the ramus of the ischium) usually fuse together by around 9 years of age, earlier than the main triradiate fusion at the acetabulum.

questions.q: 'Nursemaid's elbow' refers to which condition?
options: Radial head subluxation pulled out of the annular ligament
questions.explain: Nursemaid's elbow (radial head subluxation) occurs when the radial head is traumatically pulled out of its normal position within the annular ligament, common in young children pulled by the arm.

questions.q: A weightlifter's shoulders visibly rise toward the ears when bracing under a heavy load. Which term describes this upward movement of the shoulder girdle?
questions.explain: Elevation is the upward movement of a body part, such as the shoulders rising, and is the opposite of depression.

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding the cells of connective tissue.
options: "Blast" cells are undifferentiated, actively dividing cells
Connective tissue does not contain cells
Chondroblasts are the main cell type of connective tissue proper
questions.explain: "-blast" cells (fibroblasts, osteoblasts, chondroblasts) are immature, actively dividing matrix-producing cells — D. (Fibroblasts, not chondroblasts, dominate CT proper.)

questions.q: All the following are bilateral organs EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Lungs, kidneys and testes are paired (bilateral). The paper's answer is the brain (a single midline organ) — A. Note: the spleen is also a single, unpaired organ, so this question is a bit ambiguous — but the exam key marks A.

questions.q: A patient experiences a sudden allergic reaction, with localized swelling and redness at the site of an insect sting. Which connective tissue cell type, releasing histamine and heparin from its granules, is most directly responsible for triggering this response?
questions.explain: Mast cells release histamine and heparin from their granules during allergic and inflammatory responses, directly producing the swelling and redness characteristic of a localized allergic reaction.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly reflects the relative abundance of interneurons compared to sensory and motor neurons combined?
options: Interneurons are extremely rare, making up less than 1% of neurons
Interneurons do not actually exist as a distinct category
Sensory, motor, and interneurons exist in exactly equal numbers
Interneurons vastly outnumber sensory and motor neurons combined, comprising roughly 99.98% of all neurons in the body
questions.explain: Interneurons, confined to the CNS and providing the integrative link between sensory and motor neurons, vastly outnumber the other two functional categories combined, comprising approximately 99.98% of all neurons in the body.

questions.q: Region B (small yellow patch, medial orbit) houses part of the tear drainage system. Name this bone.
questions.explain: Region B corresponds to the lacrimal bone, a small bone in the medial orbital wall that houses the lacrimal sac of the tear drainage system.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the femur?
options: Lateral condyle, medial condyle and adductor tubercle
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: The distal femur bears the condyles, adductor tubercle, intercondylar notch, and patellar surface. The gluteal tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest (C) belong to the proximal/shaft region, not the distal end.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the paranasal sinuses?
options: Paranasal sinuses enhance the resonance of the voice and lighten the skull.
Paranasal sinuses contain passages acting as one-way valves.
Paranasal sinuses are found in maxillary, frontal and lacrimal bones.
Paranasal sinuses open into the oral cavity.
Paranasal sinuses are found in maxillary, ethmoid, and lacrimal bones.
questions.explain: The paranasal sinuses (in frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary bones — not the lacrimal) reduce skull weight and add resonance to the voice.

questions.q: The pectoral girdle is composed of the
questions.explain: The pectoral (shoulder) girdle consists of the clavicle and scapula; the humerus is part of the free upper limb, not the girdle.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, explaining why hip disease can cause referred pain in the knee?
questions.explain: The obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, which explains why hip joint disease sometimes presents with referred pain felt in the knee.

questions.q: A structure needs to allow substances to diffuse in from surrounding tissue while also providing a physical framework — but must NOT contain blood vessels of its own. Which of the following tissues satisfies this description?
questions.explain: Cartilage uniquely fits this description among connective tissues generally, being avascular (no blood vessels of its own) yet still providing structural support, relying entirely on diffusion for nutrient exchange.

questions.q: True or False: In females, the sacrum and coccyx show greater curvature, arcing further into the pelvic outlet compared to males.
questions.explain: It is the male sacrum and coccyx that arc more sharply into the pelvic outlet; the female sacrum and coccyx show LESS curvature, helping to enlarge the pelvic outlet for childbirth.

questions.q: Given that regenerating peripheral axons grow toward their distal targets at roughly 1.5 mm per day, approximately how long would you predict it might take an axon to regrow across a 3 cm gap, assuming ideal conditions (intact neurolemma, small gap)?
options: Regrowth speed is unrelated to distance
questions.explain: At a rate of approximately 1.5 mm per day, regrowth across a 3 cm (30 mm) gap would be predicted to take roughly 20 days under otherwise ideal regenerative conditions.

questions.q: Rheumatism is best defined as:
options: A type of synovial fluid abnormality
A fracture of the epiphyseal plate
Any painful disorder of supporting structures not caused by infection or injury
questions.explain: Rheumatism is defined as any painful disorder of the body's supporting structures that is NOT due to infection or injury.

questions.q: "Stove-in-chest" is another name for which condition?
questions.explain: Flail chest, caused by multiple adjacent rib fractures in more than one place, is also called a stove-in-chest because the loose segment moves paradoxically with breathing.

questions.q: True or False: The lunate carpal bone is part of the distal row of carpal bones.
questions.explain: The lunate belongs to the proximal row of carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform), not the distal row.

questions.q: In this vertebra illustration, the large tan oval (A) is the weight-bearing portion that is joined to neighbouring vertebrae by intervertebral discs. What is this structure called?
questions.explain: Structure A is the vertebral body, the rounded weight-bearing part of the vertebra connected to adjacent vertebral bodies via intervertebral discs.

questions.q: How is hyaline cartilage DIFFERENT from elastic or fibrocartilage?
questions.explain: In hyaline cartilage the type II collagen is masked by ground substance, so fibres aren't visible under the light microscope — C. Elastic and fibrocartilage show visible fibres.

questions.q: A fibrous sheath that surrounds and protects individual fascicles of a muscle is called
questions.explain: The perimysium wraps individual fascicles (bundles of muscle fibers); endomysium wraps individual fibers, epimysium wraps the whole muscle.

questions.q: The supraorbital notch or foramen allows passage of which nerve and vessels?
questions.explain: The supraorbital notch or foramen allows passage of the supraorbital nerve and accompanying vessels, supplying the forehead and scalp.

questions.q: Cranial nerves VII and VIII pass through which structure?
questions.explain: The internal acoustic (auditory) meatus transmits cranial nerves VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear) into the petrous temporal bone.

questions.q: An area of the body exposed to the external environment would be composed of which tissue type?
questions.explain: External surfaces are covered by epithelium — A.

questions.q: A cervical rib, an accessory rib arising from C7, is most strongly associated with which clinical condition?
questions.explain: A cervical rib can compress the neurovascular bundle (brachial plexus and subclavian vessels) as they pass through the thoracic outlet, producing thoracic outlet syndrome. Flail chest results from multiple rib fractures, not an accessory rib.

questions.q: Most elbow dislocations occur in which direction, named by the position of the ulna and radius?
questions.explain: Elbow dislocations are mostly posterior, and are named according to the position of the ulna and radius relative to the humerus, not the humerus itself.

questions.q: The bone(s) of the leg which bears no weight is/are
questions.explain: The fibula bears essentially no body weight (its main roles are muscle attachment and ankle stability).

questions.q: Which characteristic of epithelial tissue would you expect in a duct subject to a high degree of pressure?
questions.explain: High pressure/abrasion demands multiple protective layers → stratified layering — D.

questions.q: Joints are classified functionally according to which criterion?
options: The embryological origin of the bones
The amount of movement permitted at the joint
The number of bones meeting at the joint
The blood supply to the joint
questions.explain: The functional classification of joints is based purely on the amount of movement allowed at the joint, giving the categories synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis, and diarthrosis.

questions.q: A typical (thoracic-pattern) vertebra consists of a body and which other major component?
questions.explain: A typical vertebra consists of a body and a vertebral (neural) arch, which together enclose the vertebral foramen housing the spinal cord.

questions.q: The elbow joint is composed of how many distinct articulations?
questions.explain: The elbow joint comprises three distinct articulations: humero-ulnar, humeroradial, and superior radio-ulnar.

questions.q: A small foramen on the zygomatic bone, generally visible and used for passage of a sensory nerve, is the:
questions.explain: The zygomaticofacial foramen is a small foramen typically visible on the anterior surface of the zygomatic bone.

questions.q: Muscle tone, important for maintaining posture, is best defined as:
options: Tension present in a relaxed muscle
The size of a muscle belly
questions.explain: Muscle tone refers to the baseline tension present in a relaxed muscle, which is important for joint stability and posture.

questions.q: Elastic cartilage is found in each of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.explain: The intervertebral disc is fibrocartilage, not elastic — the exception, C.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why cartilage, though technically part of the skeletal framework, is NOT typically visible on a standard X-ray the way bone is?
options: Cartilage is actually invisible to all forms of medical imaging
X-rays can only detect soft tissue, not hard tissue
Cartilage is less dense than bone and does not absorb X-rays as strongly, so it appears far less distinct on X-ray images
Cartilage contains no matrix at all
questions.explain: X-ray contrast depends on tissue density — dense bone absorbs more radiation and appears clearly white, while less dense cartilage absorbs far less, making it much less distinct on a standard X-ray compared to bone.

questions.q: T1, an atypical thoracic vertebra, has costal facets on its body that are described as:
questions.explain: T1 has circular upper costal facets on its body, along with smaller, semilunar inferior facets, distinguishing it from typical thoracic vertebrae.

questions.q: A researcher wants to identify the specific junction type responsible for mechanically binding epidermal cells together so the skin can resist friction and stretching without cells tearing apart. Which junction is most directly responsible?
questions.explain: Desmosomes are spot-like junctions that mechanically anchor adjacent cells together, giving epithelium (such as the epidermis) resistance to mechanical stress like friction and stretching.

questions.q: This illustration highlights a small H-shaped region on the lateral skull, marked A, where four bones meet. What is this clinically important region called?
questions.explain: The highlighted region is the pterion, where the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and parietal bones meet; it is clinically important because it overlies the middle meningeal artery.

questions.q: Most synchondroses are permanent structures that persist throughout adult life.
questions.explain: False. Most synchondroses are temporary structures that disappear during growth, such as the articulation between the diaphysis and epiphysis.

questions.q: Which best explains why bone tissue, despite being extremely hard, is not brittle and completely inflexible like a ceramic?
options: Bone contains organic collagen fibers alongside its mineral component, and this collagen provides some flexibility and tensile strength that pure mineral would lack
Bone's hardness comes entirely from water content
Bone is actually a type of cartilage with added calcium
Bone contains no minerals at all
questions.explain: Bone's composite structure — mineral salts (hydroxyapatite) providing hardness, combined with organic type I collagen fibers providing some flexibility and tensile strength — is what prevents it from being as brittle as a purely mineral (ceramic-like) material would be.

questions.q: A characteristic feature of T9 is that it:
options: Has costal facets on transverse processes only
Has the largest body of all vertebrae
Fails to form joints with the 10th rib and lacks inferior demifacets
questions.explain: T9 is atypical because it fails to form joints with the 10th rib and has no inferior demifacets on the body, unlike typical thoracic vertebrae.

questions.q: In standard anatomical position, which bone of the forearm lies laterally?
questions.explain: In anatomical position (forearm supinated, palm facing forward), the radius lies lateral and the ulna lies medial.

questions.q: A motor neuron specifically innervates skeletal muscle under voluntary control, as opposed to smooth muscle or glands. Which functional subtype of motor neuron is this?
options: Sensory motor neuron (not a real category)
questions.explain: A motor neuron innervating skeletal muscle specifically is classified as a somatic motor neuron, in contrast to visceral (autonomic) motor neurons, which innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.

questions.q: Which cranial bones are described as paired, rather than single unpaired bones?
questions.explain: Among the eight cranial bones, the temporal and parietal bones are paired, whereas the frontal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid bones are each single (unpaired).

questions.q: The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperflexion of the hip joint.
questions.explain: False. The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperextension of the hip joint when standing, not hyperflexion.

questions.q: The capitulum and the coronoid process in this illustration are marked as
questions.explain: In the elbow illustration, F marks the capitulum (articulating with the radial head) and A marks the coronoid process (of the ulna).

questions.q: In this illustration of a long bone in longitudinal section, structure A points to the rounded end of the bone, made mostly of spongy bone. What is this structure called?
questions.explain: Structure A is the epiphysis, the rounded end of a long bone, composed mostly of spongy bone and capped with articular cartilage where it forms a joint.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements about the mandibular and the mental foramina of the mandible.
options: The mandibular foramen is on the lateral surface of the ramus and is for injecting anaesthetic
The mandibular foramen is on the medial surface of the ramus
The mental foramen is on the anterior part of the mandibular body
The mental foramen is on the anterolateral side of the mandibular body and is for blood vessels and nerves to the lower lip
questions.explain: A and D correctly describe the two foramina: the mandibular foramen is on the ramus's MEDIAL surface (entry point for the inferior alveolar nerve block), and the mental foramen is anterolaterally on the body, transmitting vessels/nerves to the lower lip.

questions.q: The functional unit of skeletal muscle is the:
questions.explain: The sarcomere (Z-line to Z-line) is the contractile/functional unit — A.

questions.q: Multicellular exocrine glands can be classified:
options: Structurally into alveolar and acinar types
Structurally into proliferative and secretory types
Structurally into vascular and avascular types
Functionally into secreting or nonsecreting types
Functionally into merocrine, holocrine, and apocrine divisions
questions.explain: Functional (mode-of-secretion) classification into merocrine, apocrine and holocrine is a clean, correct statement — C. Note: The paper ticks A. But "acinar" and "alveolar" are synonyms, so "alveolar and acinar types" isn't a real two-way structural distinction (and it omits tubular). C is the unambiguously correct classification. Worth confirming with your lecturer — if they taught acinar ≠ alveolar, A is defensible.

questions.q: During a pudendal nerve block performed to relieve perineal pain in childbirth, the nerve wraps around which structure before giving its branches?
questions.explain: The pudendal nerve curves around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament before dividing into its terminal branches, making this region the target for a pudendal nerve block.

questions.q: Which PNS glial cell type forms the myelin sheath and neurolemma around a single axon at a time, in contrast to its CNS counterpart, which can myelinate multiple axon segments simultaneously?
questions.explain: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath and neurolemma in the PNS, and each Schwann cell myelinates only a single axon segment — in contrast to oligodendrocytes in the CNS, which can myelinate segments of multiple different axons.

questions.q: Which movement pair correctly represents true opposites at the same joint action?
questions.explain: Elevation (upward movement) and depression (downward movement) are true opposites of the same action category; the other listed pairs mix unrelated movement types rather than being direct opposites.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rupture of the ligament of the head of femur can result in avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Reason (R): The ligamentum teres encloses a branch of the obturator artery that supplies part of the femoral head.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are true, and the Reason directly explains the Assertion: damage to the artery enclosed within the ligamentum teres compromises blood supply to the femoral head, leading to avascular necrosis.

questions.q: On this surface anatomy image of the wrist, the small bone palpable on the medial side, embedded in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris, is labelled as the:
questions.explain: The image identifies the pisiform bone (with palmaris brevis) as a palpable landmark on the medial wrist, adjacent to the head of the ulna.

questions.q: A structural engineer studying biological materials notes that compact bone is organized into repeating cylindrical units, each centered on a canal carrying blood vessels. What is the name of this repeating structural unit?
questions.explain: Compact bone is organized into repeating cylindrical units called osteons (Haversian systems), each built around a central canal that carries blood vessels supplying the surrounding bone tissue.

questions.q: Which statement correctly relates gross anatomy and histology as subdivisions of anatomical study?
options: Gross anatomy is a subdivision of histology
Histology can only be performed on living patients, never on preserved tissue
Histology and gross anatomy study entirely unrelated organisms
Gross anatomy studies structures visible without magnification; histology studies tissue at the microscopic level — they examine different scales of the same body
questions.explain: Gross anatomy and histology examine the same body at different scales — gross anatomy at the level visible to the naked eye, and histology at the microscopic tissue level — making them complementary subdivisions of anatomical study.

questions.q: Which of the following structures serves as a "seat" of the endocrine system by supporting the pituitary gland?
options: Greater wings of the sphenoid bone
Lesser wings of the sphenoid bone
questions.explain: The sella turcica, a saddle-shaped depression on the sphenoid bone, cradles and supports the pituitary gland.

questions.q: The oblique groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus, which transmits the radial nerve, is also called the:
questions.explain: The radial groove (spiral groove) runs obliquely across the posterior surface of the humeral shaft and houses the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels.

questions.q: Which hormone produced by bone tissue helps regulate bone formation?
questions.explain: Bones produce osteocalcin, which helps regulate bone formation. Insulin, cortisol, and prolactin are produced by other endocrine tissues and are not specific bone-derived regulators of ossification mentioned here.

questions.q: Which labelled structure on this clavicle diagram corresponds to the costal tuberosity?
options: The midpoint of the shaft anteriorly
The structure near the medial/sternal extremity, on the posterior aspect
The structure near the lateral/acromial extremity
There is no costal tuberosity on the clavicle
questions.explain: The costal tuberosity sits near the medial (sternal) end on the posterior/inferior aspect of the clavicle and serves as the attachment for the costoclavicular ligament, anchoring the clavicle to the first rib.

questions.q: Which neck of the humerus joins the proximal end to the shaft, and is clinically significant because fractures here can injure the axillary nerve?
questions.explain: The surgical neck joins the proximal end of the humerus to the shaft. It is clinically important because the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels wrap around it closely and are vulnerable in fractures here.

questions.q: Body weight is transferred from the vertebral column to the femurs via which sequence of joints?
options: Directly from sacrum to femur with no joints
questions.explain: Weight passes from the vertebral column through the sacroiliac joints to the hip bones, and then through the hip joints to the femurs.

questions.q: Which articulation of the elbow is classified as a hinge joint?
questions.explain: The humero-ulnar articulation, between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna, is a hinge joint.

questions.q: The lacrimal bone can be identified within which structure when viewing the lateral aspect of the skull?
questions.explain: The lacrimal bone, housing the lacrimal sac, can be identified within the orbit on the lateral aspect of the skull.

questions.q: A structure lies closer to the trunk than the elbow but farther from the trunk than the shoulder joint. Which single directional term best captures its position relative to the elbow?
questions.explain: Being nearer the point of attachment to the trunk than the elbow is means it is proximal relative to the elbow — proximal/distal describe relative nearness to the trunk along a limb.

questions.q: Which bone contains diaphysis and epiphysis areas and is proportionally more compact than spongy bone?
questions.explain: As a typical long bone, the humerus has a diaphysis (shaft, mostly compact bone) and epiphyses, and is proportionally more compact than spongy.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements concerning the radius:
options: The proximal end consists of a head, neck and tuberosity
The distal end is expanded and bears a pointed process known as the styloid process
It articulates with the carpus proximally and the ulna medially
It is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm
questions.explain: C and D correctly describe the radius. A is wrong (the ulna is longer), and B mixes up proximal/distal relations (the radius articulates with the carpus distally, not proximally).

questions.q: Which of the following are associated with the ethmoid bone?
options: Styloid process, inferior nasal conchae, jugular foramen and carotid canal
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, hypoglossal canal and foramen ovale
Crista galli, cribriform plates, perpendicular plate and superior nasal conchae
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: The ethmoid bone bears the crista galli, cribriform plates, perpendicular plate, and superior/middle nasal conchae.

questions.q: Excretory glands are classified as "simple branched tubular and merocrine" by the:
options: Mechanism of secretion and shape of secretory units
Presence or absence of ducts and mechanism of secretion
Types of secretory products and mechanism of secretion
Shape of secretory units and types of ducts only
Nature of the ducts, shape of secretory unit and mechanism of secretion
questions.explain: "Simple/branched" = nature of the duct; "tubular" = shape of the secretory unit; "merocrine" = mechanism of secretion. All three axes are used — E.

questions.q: If the distal fragment in a distal radius fracture is displaced anteriorly instead of posteriorly, the injury is termed:
questions.explain: Anterior displacement of the distal fragment, opposite to the classic Colles' pattern, is termed a reverse Colles' fracture, also known as a Smith's fracture.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about epithelia?
options: Stratified epithelia are associated with filtration
Simple epithelia are commonly found in areas of high abrasion
Endothelium provides a slick surface lining all hollow cardiovascular organs
questions.explain: Endothelium gives a smooth low-friction lining to the heart and vessels — C. (High abrasion needs stratified; filtration needs simple squamous.)

questions.q: Striated borders:
options: Consist of tightly packed stereocilia and microvilli and usually line male reproductive tract
Consist of tightly packed cilia and usually line the respiratory tract
Consist of tightly packed microvilli and usually line intestinal absorptive cells
Consist of tightly packed stereocilia and usually line the proximal segment of the nephron
Consist of tightly packed microvilli and usually line blood vessels
questions.explain: A striated/brush border = tightly packed microvilli on absorptive cells (small intestine, PCT). E is the only option that pairs microvilli with an absorptive site.

questions.q: Which best explains why blood, despite being fluid, is still classified as a connective tissue rather than forming its own separate category?
options: Blood contains no cells, matching the definition of connective tissue matrix alone
Blood follows the general connective tissue pattern of cells suspended within an extracellular matrix — in blood's case, the fluid matrix is plasma
Blood is actually classified as a type of epithelial tissue
Connective tissue must always be solid, so blood does not truly qualify
questions.explain: Blood fits the defining connective tissue pattern — cells suspended within an extracellular matrix — even though its matrix (plasma) is fluid rather than solid or gel-like, which is why it is classified as a specialized connective tissue.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements about aponeuroses.
options: Flattened sheets of dense connective tissue
Composed of collagenous bundles and fibroblasts
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: Aponeuroses are flat, tendon-like sheets of dense regular CT (collagen bundles + fibroblasts) that attach to muscle sheets — all three true, E.

questions.q: An epithelium has microvilli and cilia. This epithelium:
options: Was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses
Is from a chamber that changes its volume continually
Was involved with secretion or absorption
Is from a surface where both absorption and motility are required
questions.explain: Microvilli (absorption) + cilia (motility) → a surface needing absorption and motility — D.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Synchondroses are typically permanent joints that persist unchanged throughout life.
Reason (R): The epiphyseal plate, a synchondrosis, eventually ossifies and disappears once skeletal growth is complete.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: The Reason is true — the epiphyseal plate does ossify and disappear after growth — but this fact disproves the Assertion, since it shows synchondroses are typically temporary, not permanent.

questions.q: The following are characteristics of the vertebral column EXCEPT
options: It has a chain of 33 individual vertebrae with 23 intervertebral discs of fibrocartilage
Only the thoracic and sacral curvatures are well developed at birth and are termed as primary curvatures
About 1/4 of the length is contributed by the 23 intervertebral discs
In the adult there are 29 vertebrae; 27 mobile, 2 immobile, and 20 intervertebral discs
The sacral curvature positions the weight of the upper part of the body over the lower limbs, providing optimal balance during standing
questions.explain: The adult vertebral column has 26 bones (24 individual vertebrae + fused sacrum + fused coccyx) with 23 intervertebral discs — not 29 vertebrae with 20 discs, making E the false/incorrect statement.

questions.q: The prominent bump on the lateral aspect of the leg at the ankle joint is the
options: A lateral extension of the tibia
questions.explain: The lateral malleolus, a distal projection of the fibula, forms the bony prominence on the lateral ankle.

questions.q: Which factor does NOT directly influence the stability of a synovial joint, according to the lecture?
questions.explain: Stability depends on articular surface shape, ligament number/position, and muscle tone — blood type has no role in joint stability.

questions.q: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) passes through which foramen?
questions.explain: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, V2, passes through the foramen rotundum of the sphenoid bone.

questions.q: Which of the following tarsal bones are shown in figure 11?
questions.explain: Figure 11 shows the calcaneus & talus (i), navicular & medial cuneiform (ii), and navicular & intermediate cuneiform (iv) — combination i, ii, iv.

questions.q: A pathology slide shows an epithelium that is one cell layer thick, with cube-shaped cells, lining small ducts of a gland. Which classification correctly names this tissue?
options: Pseudostratified cuboidal epithelium (not a real category)
questions.explain: A single layer (simple) of cube-shaped (cuboidal) cells lining small ducts describes simple cuboidal epithelium, commonly found in gland ducts and kidney tubules.

questions.q: The pubis is divided into a body and two rami. Which two rami are these?
questions.explain: The pubis is composed of a body plus a superior ramus and an inferior ramus, which together help form the obturator foramen and pubic arch.

questions.q: Which PNS glial cell type performs a supportive, protective role around neuron cell bodies within ganglia, functionally comparable to astrocytes in the CNS?
questions.explain: Satellite cells (amphicytes), located in the PNS, surround and protect neuron cell bodies within ganglia, performing a role functionally comparable to astrocytes in the CNS.

questions.q: In an adult X-ray, the thin radiopaque line marking the former site of the epiphyseal plate is called the:
questions.explain: Once growth is complete, the epiphyseal plate ossifies and is seen radiographically as a thin epiphyseal line.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a cranial bone?
questions.explain: The maxilla is a facial bone, not one of the 8 cranial bones (frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid).

questions.q: The xiphoid process of the sternum is composed of which tissue in youth, before ossifying around age 40?
questions.explain: The xiphoid process is composed of hyaline cartilage in youth and typically ossifies around age 40, occasionally remaining bifid or perforated.

questions.q: Cartilage is different from bone in that:
options: Cartilage regenerates faster than bone when damaged in the adult skeleton
Cartilage contains about 80% water and is more resilient
questions.explain: Cartilage is ~70–80% water, avascular and more resilient/flexible — A. (It CAN calcify, and it regenerates poorly, so D and E are false.)

questions.q: Which best explains why a biopsy of transitional epithelium taken from a fully distended (stretched) bladder would look noticeably different from one taken from an empty bladder?
options: Transitional epithelium is destroyed each time the bladder empties and regenerates from scratch
Transitional epithelium's cells flatten and the tissue appears thinner when stretched, compared to the more rounded, dome-shaped, thicker appearance when relaxed
There is no visible difference regardless of bladder fullness
The cell type completely changes from squamous to columnar upon stretching
questions.explain: Transitional epithelium's distinctive feature is that its surface cells flatten and the whole layer thins out when stretched (as in a full bladder), compared to the thicker, more rounded, dome-shaped appearance seen when the tissue is relaxed (as in an empty bladder).

questions.q: The rotator cuff muscles surround and provide muscular support to the glenohumeral joint. One of the rotator cuff muscles is called the supraspinatus muscle. The origin of this muscle in figure 1 is
questions.explain: The supraspinatus originates from the supraspinous fossa — the region above the scapular spine, labelled A in Figure 1.

questions.q: A synarthrosis is best described as which type of joint?
options: A joint with a synovial cavity
questions.explain: Synarthrosis literally means 'joined together' and refers to an immovable joint, such as a suture, gomphosis, or synchondrosis.

questions.q: An electrophysiologist notes that a myelinated axon conducts impulses considerably faster than a comparable unmyelinated axon of similar diameter. Which property of myelin best explains this speed advantage?
options: Myelin has no effect on conduction speed; the difference must be due to axon length alone
Myelin contains its own independent nervous system
Myelin insulates the axon and prevents leakage of electrical current, increasing conduction speed
Myelin actively pumps ions across the membrane
questions.explain: Myelin acts as an insulating layer around the axon, preventing leakage of electrical current and thereby increasing the speed of impulse conduction compared to an unmyelinated axon of similar diameter.

questions.q: Which bursa of the elbow is implicated in 'student's elbow' or 'miner's elbow'?
questions.explain: The subcutaneous (olecranon) bursa, located between the olecranon and overlying connective tissue, is implicated in olecranon bursitis, also called student's or miner's elbow.

questions.q: True or False: The hyoid bone articulates directly with the mandible above it.
questions.explain: False. The hyoid bone is unique in that it does not articulate with any other bone; it is suspended in the neck by muscles and ligaments.

questions.q: Acquired hip dislocation is most commonly seen in which direction, and is associated with risk to which nerve?
questions.explain: Posterior dislocation accounts for about 90% of acquired hip dislocations, since the joint is least stable when flexed and adducted, and this may injure the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: The presence of microvilli and cilia on a cell usually indicates that the cell functions in:
questions.explain: Microvilli → absorption; cilia → surface motility. Together = absorption and motility — C.

questions.q: Prepatellar bursitis is also commonly known as:
questions.explain: Prepatellar bursitis, caused by inflammation and swelling of the prepatellar bursa, is commonly called housemaid's knee.

questions.q: True or False: The medial tibial condyle is more prominent than the lateral condyle.
questions.explain: It is the lateral condyle that is more prominent than the medial condyle, the opposite of this statement.

questions.q: Which of the following facial bones contains a sinus?
questions.explain: The maxilla contains the large maxillary sinus, one of the paranasal sinuses.

questions.q: Arthritis is best described as:
options: A muscle disorder unrelated to joints
A form of rheumatism with joint swelling, stiffness, and pain
questions.explain: Arthritis is a form of rheumatism characterized by swollen, stiff, and painful joints, with causes including infection, metabolic disorders, trauma, and immune disorders.

questions.q: Which bone cell type is the exception that does NOT originate from mesenchymal cells?
questions.explain: Osteoclasts are derived from hematopoietic (blood-forming) precursor cells, unlike osteogenic cells, osteoblasts, osteocytes, and bone lining cells, which all arise from mesenchymal cells.

questions.q: According to the labels shown, how many cuneiform bones are present, and what are they called?
questions.explain: The diagram labels three cuneiform bones: the first (medial) cuneiform, second (intermediate) cuneiform, and third (lateral) cuneiform, sitting between the navicular and the metatarsals.

questions.q: The type of epithelium which appears to have two or three layers of cells, although all the cells are in contact with the basement membrane, is:
questions.explain: Looks layered but every cell touches the membrane = pseudostratified columnar — D.

questions.q: The classification of bony pelvis shapes (gynecoid, android, anthropoid, platypelloid) is attributed to which classification system?
questions.explain: The Caldwell and Moloy classification describes the four basic types of bony pelvis: gynecoid, android, anthropoid, and platypelloid.

questions.q: A joint injury involving tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule is termed a/an:
questions.explain: A sprain is a joint injury involving tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule, whereas a strain involves muscle or tendon injury.

questions.q: This illustration of the piriform aperture shows a vertical midline plate, labelled A, dividing the nasal cavity in two. Together with the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, which bone forms this septum?
questions.explain: Structure A represents the vomer, which together with the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the bony nasal septum.
