questions.q: A Colles' fracture of the distal radius classically produces which deformity?
questions.explain: In a Colles' fracture, the distal fragment of the radius is displaced and tilted posteriorly, producing the characteristic dinner fork (or silver fork) deformity of the wrist.

questions.q: Which of the following ribs is a true rib?
questions.explain: True ribs (1–7) attach directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilage; rib 7 is the last true rib.

questions.q: True or False: Both the clavicle and the femur can be used to estimate a person's stature because their length correlates with overall body height.
questions.explain: While the femur is most classically used for stature estimation (1/4 to 1/3 of body height), long bone length generally correlates with stature, and forensic methods may also use other long bones including the humerus or, in some methods, account for the clavicle, though the femur remains the gold standard.

questions.q: In adults, new surface epithelial cells and the epithelial cells lining the intestine are derived from:
options: Mitotic division of existing epithelial cells
questions.explain: Intestinal/epithelial turnover comes from stem cells (in the crypts) that divide and differentiate — B.

questions.q: Compared to the radius, the ulna is described as the:
options: Equal in length but more lateral
Shorter and more lateral bone of the forearm
Longer and more medial bone of the forearm
questions.explain: The ulna is the longer of the two forearm bones and lies on the medial side, in contrast to the shorter, laterally placed radius.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of bone's dry weight is made up of organic components such as collagen fibres and cells?
questions.explain: Organic components make up about 35% of the dry weight of bone, including cells, mostly type I collagen fibres, and ground substance.

questions.q: All the following body cavities are components of the ventral body cavity EXCEPT:
questions.explain: The ventral cavity = thoracic (pleural + pericardial) + abdominopelvic. The vertebral cavity is part of the DORSAL cavity — the exception, B.

questions.q: Extracellular matrix is composed of:
questions.explain: The ECM = fibres + ground substance. Cells are NOT part of the matrix — B.

questions.q: The 'unhappy (terrible) triad' of knee injuries involves the ACL, medial meniscus, and which other structure?
questions.explain: The unhappy triad involves the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial meniscus, and the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, common in contact sports with lateral knee blows.

questions.q: A single mucus-secreting cell is found scattered among absorptive columnar cells lining the intestine. What is this cell called, and how is it classified as a gland?
options: An endocrine follicular cell; ductless gland
A sweat gland cell; a multicellular exocrine gland
An osteoblast; a connective tissue cell, not a gland
A goblet cell; a unicellular exocrine gland
questions.explain: This scattered, mucus-secreting single cell is a goblet cell, classified as a unicellular exocrine gland since it is a single specialized secretory cell embedded within an epithelial layer.

questions.q: The muscular system:
options: Is responsible for locomotion and facial expression
questions.explain: Manipulation, locomotion & expression, posture and heat production are all muscular functions — E.

questions.q: True or False: The patella is a classic example of a sesamoid bone.
questions.explain: True. The patella forms within the quadriceps tendon and is the textbook example of a sesamoid bone, protecting the tendon from compressive forces at the knee.

questions.q: The greater and lesser palatine foramina, located posterolaterally on the hard palate, transmit:
options: Nerves and vessels of the same name
questions.explain: The greater and lesser palatine foramina transmit the greater and lesser palatine nerves and vessels respectively, supplying the palate.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a plane joint?
questions.explain: The acromioclavicular joint is listed as a plane joint, alongside intertarsal, intercarpal, and 2nd–7th sternocostal joints.

questions.q: Which part of the vertebral column receives the most stress by bearing most of the weight of the body?
questions.explain: The lumbar region bears the most body weight of the mobile spine, which is why its vertebral bodies are the largest/most massive.

questions.q: An action potential arrives at a muscle fiber's surface and must be conducted rapidly into the cell's interior, near the sarcoplasmic reticulum, to trigger contraction throughout the whole fiber almost simultaneously. Which structure specifically enables this rapid deep conduction?
options: The sarcolemma alone, without any specialized invagination
Transverse tubules, invaginations of the sarcolemma carrying the impulse into the fiber's interior
Terminal cisternae alone, without any surface connection
questions.explain: T tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that extend into the fiber's interior, allowing the action potential to be conducted rapidly and deeply into the cell, close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, ensuring near-simultaneous activation throughout the fiber.

questions.q: How many bones make up the entire upper limb (one side), according to the standard count of arm, forearm, and hand bones?
questions.explain: The upper limb has 30 bones: humerus (1), radius and ulna (2), and the hand with carpals (8), metacarpals (5), and phalanges (14) = 1+2+8+5+14 = 30.

questions.q: Which bone tissue is adapted to support weight and withstand tension stress?
questions.explain: Compact (cortical) bone bears weight and resists bending/tension along the shaft — C.

questions.q: Unlike the other bone cell types, one type is not derived from mesenchymal cells but instead arises from blood-forming (hematopoietic) precursors related to monocytes, and its function is to break down (resorb) bone matrix. Which cell is this?
questions.explain: Osteoclasts are the exception among bone cells, arising from hematopoietic precursors (related to monocytes) rather than mesenchymal cells, and their specific function is to resorb (break down) bone matrix, unlike the matrix-forming osteoblasts and osteocytes.

questions.q: Which of the following would you expect to find lining the ducts of a sweat gland, given that this location needs slightly more durability than a single-layer epithelium but is a relatively minor structural demand?
questions.explain: Stratified cuboidal epithelium, though relatively uncommon, is found lining structures like sweat gland ducts, providing a sturdier lining than a simple epithelium would, appropriate for this modest structural demand.

questions.q: True or False: The fibula is a major weight-bearing bone of the lower limb.
questions.explain: Despite forming synovial joints with the tibia above and the talus below, the fibula is NOT a weight-bearing bone; weight transmission occurs primarily through the tibia.

questions.q: Which historical discovery established that the heart pumps blood around the body in a single, continuous circuit rather than the blood being newly produced and consumed?
options: The invention of the compound microscope
questions.explain: William Harvey demonstrated that blood circulates continuously, pumped by the heart, overturning the earlier belief that blood was continuously produced and consumed by the tissues.

questions.q: Which two types of arthritis are described as the most common?
questions.explain: The lecture identifies rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis as the most common types of arthritis.

questions.q: The functions of the nervous system include:
options: Transport of hormones and regulation of water content of the body
Regulates processes such as growth and reproduction
Maintenance of the extracellular fluid volume
Responds to internal and external changes
questions.explain: The nervous system detects and responds to internal and external stimuli — A. The others (growth, hormone transport, nutrient use, ECF volume) are endocrine/CV/renal roles.

questions.q: Comparing merocrine and holocrine secretion: a gland whose cells periodically rupture entirely, becoming the secreted product themselves, uses which mechanism — and what would you predict about that gland's need for cell replacement?
options: Merocrine secretion; no replacement is needed since cells remain intact
Holocrine secretion; the gland requires ongoing replacement of destroyed secretory cells
Apocrine secretion; only the nucleus is lost each cycle
None of the mechanisms involve cell loss
questions.explain: Holocrine secretion involves complete destruction of the secretory cell as part of the secretion itself (as in the sebaceous gland), meaning such glands must continuously replace their secretory cells to sustain output.

questions.q: An imaging report describes a cut that passes through the body offset from the midline, producing a smaller anterior segment and a larger posterior segment. Which plane was used?
questions.explain: A parasagittal plane is any sagittal cut that does not pass through the exact midline, so it necessarily produces unequal right and left portions — here shown by unequal anterior/posterior mass on either side, which only makes sense for an off-center sagittal cut.

questions.q: The side to which a scapula belongs can be determined from the following:
options: Supraspinous and infraspinous fossae are located on the anterior surface
The acromion and glenoid cavity belong to the lower and lateral part of the scapula
The large concave surface is posterior
Coracoid process is located on the posterior surface
The spine projects from the posterior surface and extends laterally as the acromion
questions.explain: The scapular spine projects from the posterior surface, extending laterally to become the acromion — a reliable landmark for determining side/orientation.

questions.q: Structurally, joints are classified based on what feature?
options: The shape of the surrounding muscles
What separates or binds the articulating bones
questions.explain: Structural classification of joints depends on what separates or binds the articulating bones — fibers, cartilage, or a joint cavity — giving fibrous, cartilaginous, and synovial categories.

questions.q: Which relationship between a tissue and its general function is NOT correct?
questions.explain: The general role of epithelium is protection/absorption/secretion/lining — not "digestion" as such (that's a system-level function). The mismatched pair is A.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of cartilage?
options: Provision of an embryonic model prior to development of long bones
Allowing long bones to increase in length
Provision of a smooth surface for epiphyses of articulating joints
Provision of rigidity to soft tissues requiring support
Maintenance of a tubular shape of structures in the digestive tract
questions.explain: Cartilage keeps the respiratory tract (trachea/bronchi) patent — not the digestive tract. So E is NOT a cartilage function.

questions.q: An epithelial membrane:
options: Contains simple or stratified epithelia and a basement membrane
Is formed of epithelium and smooth muscle
questions.explain: An epithelial membrane = a sheet of epithelium (simple or stratified) resting on a basement membrane over connective tissue — C.

questions.q: Using figure 10 the letter(s) that represents the maxilla is
questions.explain: The maxilla (upper jaw, bearing the upper teeth) is labelled E in the lateral skull diagram.

questions.q: Two students disagree about how a joint's shape relates to the movements it permits. Which anatomical principle are they discussing?
questions.explain: The principle of complementarity of structure and function holds that a structure's form directly suits the function it performs — here, joint shape dictating the range of motion available.

questions.q: A middle-aged woman presents with chronic fatigue, disrupted sleep, and widespread musculoskeletal pain involving muscle, its connective tissue coverings, and nearby joint capsules, with no clear infectious cause. Which condition does this presentation most closely match?
questions.explain: This presentation — chronic fatigue, disrupted sleep, and widespread pain involving muscle, its connective tissue coverings, and nearby joint capsules, predominantly affecting women — matches fibromyositis (fibromyalgia).

questions.q: Using figure 10, the letters that represent the maxillary, temporal and zygomatic bones are
questions.explain: On the lateral skull view: E = maxilla, B = temporal (squamous part/parietal region shown), C = zygomatic.

questions.q: When the trunk of the body is subjected to physical trauma as happens in automobile accidents the most vulnerable organs are those within:
options: The abdominal cavity because the walls of the abdominal cavity are formed only by muscles without bone reinforcement
The thoracic cavity because they are well protected within the bony rib cage
The bony abdominal cavity because they have little protection
The thoracic cavity because they have little protection
The pelvic cavity because the walls of the pelvic cavity are formed only by muscles
questions.explain: Unlike the thoracic cavity (protected by the rib cage) or pelvic cavity (protected by the bony pelvis), the abdominal cavity's walls are formed only by muscle, leaving its organs comparatively vulnerable to blunt trauma.

questions.q: Intervertebral discs exhibit a large amount of tensile strength to absorb shock because they possess:
questions.explain: IV discs are fibrocartilage, packed with type I collagen fibres that give tensile strength — B.

questions.q: Which nasal concha(e) is a facial bone?
questions.explain: Only the inferior nasal concha is an independent facial bone; the superior and middle conchae are projections of the ethmoid bone (a cranial bone).

questions.q: Which of the following would be the LEAST likely finding in a healthy sample of loose areolar connective tissue?
options: A tightly packed, parallel arrangement of collagen fibers with very little ground substance
Blood vessels running through the tissue
Scattered fibroblasts, macrophages, and mast cells within abundant ground substance
A sparse, loosely arranged network of collagen and elastic fibers
questions.explain: A tightly packed, parallel fiber arrangement with minimal ground substance describes dense regular connective tissue (as in tendons), not the loosely arranged, ground-substance-rich structure characteristic of areolar connective tissue.

questions.q: Thoracic vertebrae are described as having costal facets mainly for articulation with which structures?
questions.explain: Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets on the body (and most also on transverse processes) for articulation with the heads and tubercles of the ribs.

questions.q: The superior portion of the sternum is the
questions.explain: The sternum has three parts from superior to inferior: manubrium, body, and xiphoid process.

questions.q: Which scapular angle is formed at the junction of the lateral and superior borders?
questions.explain: The lateral angle is the junction of the lateral and superior borders, and is thickened to form the head of the scapula bearing the glenoid cavity.

questions.q: The roughened anterior border of the pubis is named the:
questions.explain: The pubic crest is the roughened ridge forming the anterior border of the pubic body, an attachment site for abdominal muscles.

questions.q: A physiologist compares the contraction speed of skeletal muscle (used for a sprinter's rapid stride) with that of the smooth muscle propelling food through the intestine. What functional difference would be predicted?
options: Skeletal muscle contracts rapidly for quick, powerful movements, while smooth muscle contracts slowly and sustains contraction over a longer period, suited to gradual propulsion
Neither tissue can sustain contraction for more than a fraction of a second
Smooth muscle contracts faster than skeletal muscle in all cases
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle is adapted for rapid, powerful contractions suited to voluntary movements like sprinting, whereas smooth muscle is specialized for slow, sustained contraction, appropriate for the gradual, prolonged propulsion of substances through hollow organs like the intestine.

questions.q: A researcher identifies a lighter band within a sarcomere that contains only thin filaments, with no thick filament overlap. Which band is this, and what accounts for its lighter appearance?
options: The I band, appearing lighter because it contains only thin filaments without the additional density of overlapping thick filaments
The Z disc, which is defined by its complete absence of any protein
The A band, because it lacks any filaments at all
The H zone, which always appears darker than the A band
questions.explain: The I band contains only thin (actin) filaments, without overlapping thick filaments, which is why it appears lighter under the microscope compared to the denser A band, where thick and thin filaments overlap.

questions.q: A physiotherapist instructs a patient to decrease the angle between the forearm and upper arm at the elbow. Which movement is being requested?
questions.explain: Decreasing the angle between two body parts at a joint is, by definition, flexion — extension is the opposite, increasing that angle.

questions.q: Which ligaments of the shoulder joint stabilise the anterior aspect of the joint?
questions.explain: The superior, middle, and inferior glenohumeral ligaments specifically stabilise the anterior aspect of the shoulder joint.

questions.q: Which type of epithelium is normally found in glands?
questions.explain: Secretory (glandular) epithelium is typically simple cuboidal — D.

questions.q: The knee joint is best classified as a:
questions.explain: The knee is described as a modified hinge joint and is the largest and most complicated joint in the body.

questions.q: On the border separating epithelial cells and connective tissue can be found:
options: Tight junctions, adhering junctions and hemidesmosomes
Zonula occludens and zonula adherens only
Zonula adherens and macula adherens only
questions.explain: The epithelium–CT (basal) border is anchored by hemidesmosomes. Among the options only A leads with hemidesmosomes as the border structure — A. (Strictly, hemidesmosomes are the true basal anchor; desmosomes are lateral.)

questions.q: Which of the following structures is the most difficult to observe on an X-Ray film?
questions.explain: Tracheal (hyaline) cartilage is poorly mineralized/radiolucent, so it is far harder to visualize on X-ray than the dense bony structures listed.

questions.q: Bones united by hyaline cartilage, such as the epiphyseal plate, describe which type of joint?
questions.explain: Synchondroses are primary cartilaginous joints in which bones are united by hyaline cartilage, with the epiphyseal plate as a key example.

questions.q: Children are often told to keep this process off the table while eating.
questions.explain: The olecranon process of the ulna is the bony point of the elbow — the process children are told to keep off the table.

questions.q: The symphysis pubis:
options: Contains alternating layers of collagen fibers and chondrocytes
Contains hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes that occur singly
Contains a large amount of ground substance
Has numerous chondroblasts and few collagen fibers
questions.explain: The symphysis pubis is fibrocartilage — alternating layers of type I collagen and rows of chondrocytes — A.

questions.q: Which cruciate ligament of the knee is described as weaker and more commonly injured?
questions.explain: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is weaker and more commonly injured than the posterior cruciate ligament, and it blends with the medial meniscus.

questions.q: The vertebra which has no body is the
questions.explain: The atlas (C1) is a ring of bone lacking a body, allowing the dens of the axis to occupy its anterior arch space.

questions.q: True or False: Infant skull bones are described as thin but somewhat flexible, making them less easily fractured than adult skull bones.
questions.explain: True. The notes describe infant skull bones as thin but flexible, which makes them less easily fractured compared to the more rigid adult skull bones.

questions.q: Inflammation of the bursa covering the ischial tuberosity is termed:
questions.explain: The ischial tuberosity is covered by a bursa that, when inflamed (often from prolonged sitting), causes ischial bursitis.

questions.q: Which of the following makes up the axial skeleton?
options: The skull, vertebral column and rib cage
The skull, vertebral column and pelvis
The skull, shoulder girdles and rib cage
questions.explain: The axial skeleton comprises the skull, vertebral column, and rib cage/sternum — the body's central axis.

questions.q: True or False: Spina bifida is associated with folic acid deficiency in genetically susceptible individuals.
questions.explain: True. Spina bifida is associated with folic acid deficiency in certain genetically susceptible individuals, which is why folic acid supplementation is recommended during pregnancy.

questions.q: Which combination of features would you expect in an epithelium specialized to both protect against significant abrasion and allow for a modest degree of secretion, as seen in parts of the oral cavity?
options: Simple squamous epithelium with abundant goblet cells
Stratified squamous epithelium, which still permits underlying glands to secrete through it via ducts
questions.explain: Stratified squamous epithelium, particularly the non-keratinized moist variety lining much of the oral cavity, provides abrasion resistance from swallowed food or chewing while still allowing underlying glands to deliver secretions to the surface via ducts that penetrate the epithelium.

questions.q: Which four bones meet at the pterion, forming an H-shaped suture pattern?
questions.explain: The pterion is the region where the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and parietal bones meet, forming an H-shaped suture roughly 3-4 cm superior to the midpoint of the zygomatic arch.

questions.q: On this anterior and posterior view of the patella, the pointed inferior tip where the medial and lateral borders converge is the:
questions.explain: The apex of the patella is the pointed distal tip where the medial and lateral borders converge, located opposite the broader superior base.

questions.q: What are the three main components of connective tissue?
options: Alveoli, fibrous capsule, and secretory cells
questions.explain: Connective tissue = cells + fibres + ground substance — A. (Fibres + ground substance together make the extracellular matrix.)

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares tight junctions and desmosomes in terms of their primary function?
options: Tight junctions provide mechanical anchorage, while desmosomes control paracellular passage
Both function identically, providing only mechanical strength
Neither junction type has any functional role in epithelium
Tight junctions primarily control what can pass between cells, while desmosomes primarily provide mechanical anchorage between cells
questions.explain: Tight junctions are primarily barrier-forming, sealing the intercellular space to control paracellular passage, while desmosomes are primarily anchoring structures, providing mechanical strength between adjacent cells — distinct but complementary roles.

questions.q: Approximately how long is the adult vertebral column?
questions.explain: The adult vertebral column is approximately 70 cm (28 inches) long, extending from the skull to the coccyx.

questions.q: The foramen magnum is a large hole in the base of the occipital bone that transmits the spinal cord. The homologous structure in an individual vertebra is the:
questions.explain: The vertebral foramen of each vertebra (through which the spinal cord passes) is developmentally/functionally analogous to the foramen magnum of the skull.

questions.q: A pathologist examines a tumor biopsy under a microscope to determine the tissue of origin. Which subdivision of anatomy is she practicing?
questions.explain: Examining tissue under magnification is histology, the microscopic study of tissue architecture, distinct from gross (naked-eye) anatomy.

questions.q: On the inferior surface of the clavicle's shaft, the conoid tubercle forms a synovial joint with which part of the scapula?
questions.explain: The conoid tubercle, on the inferior surface of the clavicle, anchors the conoid ligament and corresponds to a synovial-type connection with the coracoid process of the scapula.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A 'sprain' and a 'strain' refer to the exact same type of soft-tissue injury.
Reason (R): A sprain involves tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule, whereas a strain involves injury to muscle or tendon.
options: Both A and R are false
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: The Reason correctly distinguishes the two terms, which is precisely why the Assertion (claiming they are the same) is false.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly lists features associated with the PROXIMAL end of the humerus?
options: Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle, intertrochanteric crest
Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, intertubercular groove
Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter, bicipital groove
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa, olecranon fossa
questions.explain: The proximal humerus bears the head, anatomical and surgical necks, and the greater and lesser tubercles separated by the intertubercular groove. Trochanters belong to the femur, not the humerus.

questions.q: An imaging study identifies a bundle of neuron processes running within the spinal cord itself, connecting different regions of the CNS. What is this type of bundle called, as opposed to the equivalent structure in the PNS?
questions.explain: Within the CNS, a bundle of neuron processes is called a tract; the equivalent bundle located in the PNS is instead called a nerve.

questions.q: Which carpal bone is most frequently fractured, with tenderness elicited at the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explain: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand raises strong suspicion for a scaphoid fracture.

questions.q: Which of the following phrases best describes the function of the vertebral curves?
options: To improve cervical center of gravity
To accommodate the weight of the pelvic girdle
questions.explain: The spine's alternating curves act like a coiled spring, giving it resilience and flexibility to absorb shock during movement.

questions.q: A body in anatomical position has the following characteristics EXCEPT:
options: Arms adjacent to sides with palms facing backward
Lower limbs close together with feet parallel and toes forward
questions.explain: In anatomical position the palms face forward (supinated), not backward — so B is the incorrect (EXCEPT) statement.

questions.q: The scapula articulates with the humerus at which structure?
questions.explain: The scapula articulates with the head of the humerus at the glenoid fossa, forming the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint.

questions.q: Comparing the terms 'superior' and 'cephalic': what is their relationship?
options: Superior applies only to the trunk, cephalic only to the limbs
They are essentially synonymous, both meaning toward the head end
questions.explain: Superior and cephalic are essentially synonymous directional terms, both indicating a position toward the head end of the body.

questions.q: The following functions are performed by the skeletal system:
options: Mineral storage and attachment of muscles
Protection, production of blood cells and filtration of blood
Only A and B are correct
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: A and B are true. C fails because "filtration of blood" is a spleen/kidney job, not a skeletal one — so only A and B (D).

questions.q: The enlargement of existing muscle fibres due to increasing diameters of cell but not increasing the number of new muscle fibres is known as
questions.explain: Hypertrophy is growth in fiber SIZE (diameter) without an increase in fiber NUMBER; hyperplasia would involve more fibers.

questions.q: A ball-and-socket joint, formed when a spherical head fits into a concave socket, is classified functionally as:
questions.explain: Ball-and-socket (spheroid) joints are multiaxial, permitting flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, and circumduction — exemplified by the shoulder and hip.

questions.q: Cervical vertebrae can be uniquely identified by the presence of
questions.explain: Transverse foramina are unique to cervical vertebrae (all vertebrae have transverse/spinous/vertebral foramina/processes in general, but only cervical vertebrae have the foraminal openings in the transverse processes).

questions.q: The hip joint articulates between the head of the femur and which structure?
questions.explain: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the hip bone.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Synovial fluid contributes to the nutrition of articular cartilage.
Reason (R): Articular cartilage is avascular and relies on diffusion from synovial fluid for nourishment.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are true. Because articular cartilage lacks its own blood supply, it depends on diffusion of nutrients from the surrounding synovial fluid, directly explaining the Assertion.

questions.q: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), being stronger, shorter, and broader than the ACL, primarily limits which movement?
options: Knee hyperflexion and posterior tibial dislocation
questions.explain: The PCL limits knee hyperflexion and prevents posterior dislocation of the tibia relative to the femur.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the best real-world illustration of an axodendritic synapse specifically, as opposed to other synapse types?
options: An axon terminal of one neuron forming a synapse onto a dendrite of a second neuron, the most statistically common arrangement in the nervous system
Two axons synapsing directly onto each other with no dendrite involved
A motor neuron synapsing directly onto a skeletal muscle fiber
A dendrite synapsing directly onto another dendrite
questions.explain: An axon terminal from one neuron synapsing onto the dendrite of a second neuron is the defining pattern of an axodendritic synapse, and this is also the most statistically common synapse type in the nervous system — distinguishing it from axoaxonic, dendrodendritic, or neuromuscular junction examples.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the femur?
options: Lateral condyle, medial condyle and adductor tubercle
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: The proximal femur/shaft region bears the gluteal tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest, along with the head, neck, and trochanters. Condyles (A, B) are distal features.

questions.q: The shaft of the radius has anterior, posterior, and lateral surfaces, along with anterior, posterior, and which other border?
questions.explain: The radial shaft has three borders: anterior, posterior, and an interosseous border, the last of which gives attachment to the interosseous membrane (except near its proximal-most part).

questions.q: A physiologist stimulates an isolated tissue sample with a nerve impulse and observes it shorten. Which functional property of muscle tissue is being demonstrated?
questions.explain: The tissue's response to a nerve impulse by contracting demonstrates excitability — its ability to respond to electrical stimulation with contraction.

questions.q: Which of the following is the largest of the paranasal sinuses?
questions.explain: The maxillary sinuses are the largest of the paranasal sinuses, located within the maxillary bones.

questions.q: A patient with a suspected fracture but with a known dye/contrast allergy and no urgent need for cross-sectional detail is scheduled for baseline imaging. Which of the following would be the simplest, most direct first-line choice?
questions.explain: For a straightforward suspected fracture, plain X-ray remains the simplest first-line imaging choice, using differences in tissue density to visualize bone, without requiring contrast dye.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The deltoid (medial) ligament of the ankle is more frequently torn than the lateral ligament.
Reason (R): The deltoid ligament is anatomically larger and stronger than the lateral ligament.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are false. The lateral ligament, not the deltoid, is more frequently torn, precisely because the deltoid ligament is the stronger of the two — the opposite of what is asserted.

questions.q: Which one of these bones is not found in the pelvis?
questions.explain: The hyoid is located in the neck, entirely unrelated to the pelvis.

questions.q: A comparison of skin (dense irregular connective tissue) and tendon (dense regular connective tissue) both under significant, but differently directed, mechanical stress would predict which outcome?
options: The tendon would tolerate multidirectional stress better than the skin
The skin would tolerate multidirectional stress well due to its randomly oriented fibers, while a tendon subjected to stress from an unexpected angle would be more vulnerable to injury
Both tissues perform identically regardless of stress direction
Neither tissue type is affected by the direction of applied stress
questions.explain: Because dense irregular tissue (skin) has randomly oriented fibers suited to multidirectional stress, while dense regular tissue (tendon) has fibers aligned to resist force along one specific direction, a tendon subjected to stress from an unexpected angle would be comparatively more vulnerable to injury than skin facing the same off-axis stress.

questions.q: A biopsy shows tissue with cells packed tightly together and almost no space between them for extracellular material. Which basic tissue type does this most likely represent?
questions.explain: Epithelial tissue is defined by cells packed closely with minimal extracellular matrix, the opposite arrangement to connective tissue, which has abundant matrix and sparse cells.

questions.q: Which digit does not have a middle phalanx?
questions.explain: Digit I (the thumb/pollex) has only a proximal and distal phalanx — no middle phalanx.

questions.q: True or False: The lesser trochanter of the femur is larger and more laterally placed than the greater trochanter.
questions.explain: This is reversed: the greater trochanter is the larger, laterally placed prominence, while the lesser trochanter is smaller and located medially/posteriorly.

questions.q: The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is best described functionally as:
options: The least movable but most stable joint
questions.explain: The shoulder joint is highly movable but is also the least stable major joint of the body, owing to its shallow socket.

questions.q: True or False: To correctly orient an isolated hip bone, the obturator foramen should be positioned posteriorly and pointing upward.
questions.explain: To orient a hip bone correctly, the obturator foramen should face anteriorly and is positioned inferiorly (below and in front), not posteriorly or upward.

questions.q: A zygapophyseal joint is a synovial joint between the superior and inferior articular processes (facets) of adjacent vertebrae. The inferior articular process in figure 9 is
questions.explain: In the vertebra diagram, letter E marks the inferior articular process (which points downward to meet the superior articular process of the vertebra below).

questions.q: The thumb and the great toe are known as
questions.explain: In anatomical terminology, the thumb is the pollex and the great toe is the hallux.

questions.q: Goblet cells are found in each of the following organs EXCEPT the:
questions.explain: The stomach lining is simple columnar mucous epithelium WITHOUT discrete goblet cells. Intestine and bronchus have them — so the exception is A.

questions.q: The sternum:
options: Is a bony plate anterior to the heart
Is an irregular bone that is divided into 3 regions: manubrium, body and xiphoid process
Is also known as the "breastbone" and its xiphoid process is a plate of hyaline cartilage until about age 40
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: All three statements correctly describe the sternum.

questions.q: Specimen A: surface under severe mechanical stress. Specimen B: surface where filtration/diffusion occurs. Specimen C: internal chamber needing absorption AND motility. A, B, C are from:
options: Skin, alveoli of lungs, efferent ductules
Hard palate, respiratory bronchioles and oesophagus
Filiform papillae of tongue, endothelium of blood vessels and skin
Filiform papillae of tongue, parietal layer of renal corpuscle and vagina
Soles of feet, visceral layer of renal corpuscle and oesophagus
questions.explain: A = mechanical stress → keratinised stratified squamous → skin. B = diffusion → simple squamous → alveoli. C = absorption + motility → the efferent ductules (absorptive cells + ciliated cells that move sperm). Oesophagus (option D) does neither, so C wins.

questions.q: The primary centre of ossification in endochondral bone formation typically appears in which part of the developing bone?
questions.explain: The primary centre of ossification appears around the 7th to 12th week, in the middle of the diaphysis, where mesenchymal tissue, osteoblasts, and blood vessels initiate bone formation.

questions.q: The superior orbital fissure is formed in the sphenoid bone, whereas the inferior orbital fissure is formed between the sphenoid and
questions.explain: The inferior orbital fissure lies between the greater wing of the sphenoid and the zygomatic (and maxilla), with the zygomatic bone as the key second contributor here.

questions.q: The annular ligament of the elbow attaches the radius firmly so it cannot rotate within it during pronation and supination.
questions.explain: False. The annular ligament holds the head of the radius in place against the radial notch of the ulna while still permitting the radial head to rotate within it, enabling pronation and supination.

questions.q: SYNOVIAL JOINTS possess
options: Hyaline cartilage that absorbs compressive forces
Hyaline cartilage at the ends of the opposing bones
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: Synovial joints have articular (hyaline) cartilage on opposing bone ends that absorbs compressive loads, plus a fluid-filled joint cavity.

questions.q: The floor of the anatomical snuffbox is formed by which two carpal bones?
questions.explain: The anatomical snuffbox, a triangular depression on the radial side of the wrist, has the scaphoid and trapezium forming its floor.

questions.q: The upper end of the femur consists of the head, neck, and two trochanters. Which trochanters are these?
questions.explain: The proximal femur bears the head and neck plus the greater trochanter (lateral, larger) and lesser trochanter (medial, smaller), both serving as muscle attachment sites.

questions.q: Which type of epithelium is best suited for areas where diffusion or filtration occurs?
questions.explain: A single thin layer minimises the diffusion distance → simple squamous (alveoli, glomerulus, endothelium) — C.

questions.q: Which structure forms the coracoacromial arch that prevents superior (upward) displacement of the humeral head?
options: Coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament
questions.explain: The coracoacromial arch is formed by the coracoid process, the acromion, and the coracoacromial ligament, and it blocks superior displacement of the humeral head.

questions.q: Estrogen replacement therapy in postmenopausal women, while reducing bone loss risk, is associated with an increased risk of which of the following?
options: Heart attack, stroke, and breast cancer
questions.explain: Although estrogen decline increases postmenopausal bone loss risk, estrogen replacement therapy itself is associated with an increased risk of heart attack, stroke, and breast cancer.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bursae located near a joint can sometimes become distended when the joint itself produces excess synovial fluid.
Reason (R): Some bursae, such as the suprapatellar bursa at the knee, directly communicate with the synovial cavity of the adjacent joint.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion: because certain bursae like the suprapatellar bursa communicate directly with the joint cavity, excess synovial fluid in the joint can flow into and distend the bursa.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an example of a synchondrosis?
questions.explain: The first sternocostal joint (between the first rib and the sternum) is cited as a synchondrosis, alongside epiphyseal plates and the costochondral joint.

questions.q: True or False: Clubfoot is described as a congenital defect in which the soles of the foot face medially and the talus points inferiorly.
questions.explain: Clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) is a congenital condition in which the soles face medially (inward) and the talus points inferiorly, consistent with the inverted, adducted, plantar-flexed positioning.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the humerus?
options: Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove
Greater tubercle, Lesser tubercle and intertubercular groove
Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa and olecranon fossa
Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest
questions.explain: The proximal humerus bears the greater and lesser tubercles separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove. Trochanters belong to the femur, not the humerus.

questions.q: Disc herniation classically occurs posterolaterally rather than directly posteriorly because of the protective action of the:
questions.explain: The posterior longitudinal ligament prevents herniation from proceeding directly posteriorly, so herniation usually occurs posterolaterally instead.

questions.q: A patient suffers a period of cardiac arrest lasting several minutes before resuscitation. Given what is known about neurons' tolerance for oxygen deprivation, what would be the most likely neurological consequence?
options: Only glial cells would be affected, sparing all neurons
No neurological effect, since neurons can survive indefinitely without oxygen
Significant neuronal death, since neurons typically die after about 5 minutes without oxygen due to their high metabolic demand
Neurons would simply pause activity and resume normally with no damage after any duration
questions.explain: Because neurons have a high metabolic rate and typically die after about 5 minutes without oxygen, a period of cardiac arrest lasting several minutes would be expected to cause significant neuronal death, an important basis for the urgency of resuscitation.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the best real-world example of dense irregular connective tissue in action, based on its multidirectional fiber arrangement?
options: A tendon transmitting force from a single muscle in one direction
The wall of a large elastic artery stretching with each heartbeat
Hyaline cartilage at the end of a long bone
The dermis of the skin, resisting pulling and stretching forces from many directions during movement
questions.explain: The dermis, composed of dense irregular connective tissue with randomly oriented collagen fibers, is well suited to resisting mechanical stress from multiple directions, unlike the single-direction force resisted by dense regular tissue in a tendon.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is/are not weight bearing?
questions.explain: The fibula bears minimal body weight; it mainly serves as a muscle attachment site and stabilizer of the ankle.

questions.q: On the inferior aspect of the skull cap (calvaria), pits formed by arachnoid granulations, marking sites of CSF transfer, are called:
questions.explain: Granular foveolae are pits on the inner skull cap formed by arachnoid granulations, which are sites of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) transfer into the venous system.

questions.q: Body cavities and Membranes
options: The serous pericardium is associated with the pericardial cavity and the lungs
The thoracic cavity contains two pleural cavities and a thick band of organs called the mediastinum
The abdominal cavity contains the stomach, urinary bladder, uterus and the prostate gland
Synovial cavities are enclosed within fibrous capsules that fill the sutures of the skull
The ventral body cavity is subdivided into a cranial cavity and a vertebral cavity
questions.explain: The thoracic cavity correctly contains two pleural cavities flanking the mediastinum (which houses the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus). The other options misplace structures (bladder/uterus/prostate are pelvic, not abdominal; pericardium relates to the heart not lungs; synovial cavities are at joints not sutures).

questions.q: Point B marks the peg-like projection rising from the lower vertebra into the ring above. Name this projection.
questions.explain: Point B marks the dens (odontoid process) of the axis, which projects upward into the atlas and allows rotation of the head.

questions.q: An increased Q-angle is considered a risk factor for several knee disorders. Which group typically has a greater Q-angle, owing to wider pelves?
questions.explain: The Q-angle is greater in adult females than males, owing to females generally having wider pelves.

questions.q: In this labelled diagram of the hand, the carpal bone bearing a hook-shaped process (used as a landmark for Guyon's canal) is the:
questions.explain: The hamate, shown with its characteristic hook in the diagram, is the carpal bone whose hook of hamate forms a key landmark for structures passing through Guyon's canal.

questions.q: A student claims that all three muscle types are voluntary. Which single fact most directly disproves this claim?
options: Smooth and cardiac muscle are both classified as involuntary, unlike skeletal muscle
questions.explain: Since both smooth and cardiac muscle are functionally classified as involuntary — not under conscious control — the claim that all three muscle types are voluntary is directly disproved by this fact.

questions.q: In which anatomic region of the abdomen would you expect to locate the gall bladder?
questions.explain: The gallbladder lies beneath the liver in the right hypochondriac region of the abdomen.

questions.q: The canal that runs through the core of each osteon is the principal site of:
questions.explain: The central (Haversian) canal at the core of each osteon contains blood vessels and nerve fibres that nourish and innervate the surrounding bone tissue.

questions.q: Given that hormone signaling in the endocrine system generally has a slower onset but longer duration than nervous signaling, which of the following body functions would be better suited to endocrine rather than nervous control?
options: Millisecond-scale coordination of a sprinter's muscles
Long-term regulation of growth over months to years
Rapid withdrawal of a hand from a hot surface
questions.explain: Long-term processes like growth regulation benefit from the slower-onset, longer-lasting nature of hormonal control, whereas split-second actions like reflexes or sprinting require the nervous system's rapid signaling.

questions.q: Articular cartilage at the very surface of a joint lacks a perichondrium. Given cartilage's usual reliance on this membrane for nutrition, how does articular cartilage obtain nutrients instead?
options: By diffusion from the surrounding synovial fluid
It does not require nutrients since it is composed of dead cells
It receives nutrients directly from the bone marrow through the matrix
It has its own direct blood supply, unlike other cartilage
questions.explain: Lacking a perichondrium at the joint surface, articular cartilage instead relies on diffusion of nutrients from the surrounding synovial fluid within the joint cavity.

questions.q: Osteomyelitis is best described as:
options: Inflammation of bone caused by pus-forming bacteria
Caused by altered vitamin D metabolism only
Caused purely by hyperactivity of osteoclasts
questions.explain: Osteomyelitis is inflammation of bone caused by pus-forming bacteria, distinguishing it from metabolic bone diseases like rickets or osteomalacia.

questions.q: True or False: A fractured femoral neck can interrupt the blood supply to the head of the femur, risking avascular necrosis.
questions.explain: The blood supply to the femoral head largely depends on retinacular vessels running along the neck; a femoral neck fracture can disrupt this supply, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.q: Comparing myelin formation in the CNS versus the PNS: which pairing of glial cell and location is correct?
options: Astrocytes myelinate both CNS and PNS axons
Microglia myelinate CNS axons; ependymal cells myelinate PNS axons
Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons
Schwann cells myelinate CNS axons; oligodendrocytes myelinate PNS axons
questions.explain: The correct pairing is oligodendrocytes forming myelin in the CNS, and Schwann cells forming myelin in the PNS — the reverse or other pairings listed are incorrect.

questions.q: What does the acronym RICE, used in management of soft tissue joint injuries, stand for?
questions.explain: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation — the standard immediate management for soft tissue joint injuries.

questions.q: A stroke damages CNS tissue, and astrocytes at the injury site respond by proliferating and forming dense scar tissue. What consequence does this astrocyte-driven scarring have for axon regrowth at the injury site?
options: It has no effect on axon regrowth whatsoever
It blocks axon regrowth and, along with released inhibitory chemicals, contributes to the CNS's generally poor capacity for repair after injury
It converts damaged axons directly into new, functional oligodendrocytes
It actively promotes and accelerates axon regrowth across the injury
questions.explain: Astrocyte-produced scar tissue physically blocks axon regrowth across the injury site, and astrocytes also release chemicals that further inhibit regrowth — together contributing to the CNS's generally poor capacity for repair after significant injury.

questions.q: An exocrine gland's cells remain completely intact throughout secretion, releasing their product purely through vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane. Which mode of secretion is this, and which of the three modes is most common among exocrine glands?
options: None of the three modes describes intact-cell secretion
Holocrine secretion; the least damaging mode
Merocrine secretion; and yes, it is the most common mode among exocrine glands
Apocrine secretion; also the most common mode
questions.explain: Merocrine secretion releases the product by exocytosis with the cell remaining fully intact, and it is indeed the most common secretory mechanism among exocrine glands generally.

questions.q: The most abundant cartilage type is:
questions.explain: Hyaline cartilage is by far the most abundant type — A.

questions.q: True or False: The shaft of the tibia is the most frequent site of an open fracture, commonly resulting from motorcycle accidents.
questions.explain: Because the tibial shaft lies just beneath the skin with little soft tissue covering anteriorly, it is the most common site for open (compound) fractures, frequently from motorcycle accidents.

questions.q: What fibrocartilaginous structure deepens the acetabulum in the hip joint?
questions.explain: The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous collar that deepens the acetabulum, improving congruency with the femoral head.

questions.q: The tuberosity of the ulna serves as an attachment site for which muscle?
questions.explain: The ulnar tuberosity is a roughened area distal to the coronoid process that receives the insertion of the brachialis muscle.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the LEAST consistent finding with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, given that this disease specifically demyelinates CNS axons?
options: Slowed conduction velocity in affected CNS pathways
Variable neurological symptoms depending on which CNS tracts are affected
Progressive damage to myelin produced by oligodendrocytes
Damage strictly limited to Schwann-cell-produced myelin in peripheral nerves, sparing the CNS entirely
questions.explain: Because multiple sclerosis is specifically a CNS demyelinating disease targeting oligodendrocyte-produced myelin, a presentation strictly limited to peripheral (Schwann-cell) myelin damage while sparing the CNS entirely would be the least consistent finding with this diagnosis.

questions.q: Intramembranous ossification occurs in the
options: A, B, C are all correct
questions.explain: Per the marked answer key, intramembranous (direct) ossification is credited here for the clavicle, sternum and scapula.

questions.q: Rupture of the ligament of the head of femur can damage its accompanying artery and lead to which complication?
questions.explain: The ligamentum teres encloses a branch of the obturator artery, and rupture of the ligament can damage this artery, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.q: Which of the following bones does not articulate directly with any other bone in the skeleton?
questions.explain: As established earlier, the hyoid bone articulates with no other bone in the skeleton.

questions.q: Which best summarizes the overall functional division of labor between neurons and neuroglia in the nervous system?
options: Neurons are the excitable, signal-transmitting cells; neuroglia are nonexcitable cells that support, protect, nourish, and insulate neurons, among other roles
Neurons and neuroglia perform identical functions with complete redundancy
Neither cell type has any specialized function
Neuroglia transmit all electrical signals, while neurons provide only structural support
questions.explain: The fundamental division of labor is that neurons are the excitable cells specialized for transmitting electrical signals, while neuroglia are nonexcitable supporting cells that nourish, protect, insulate, and otherwise support neurons in their signaling role.

questions.q: In a pseudostratified columnar epithelium, which is characteristic of ALL cells?
options: Location of nuclei at the same horizontal level
Direct contact with the basement membrane
Possession of highly folded basal membranes
questions.explain: The defining feature is that every cell touches the basement membrane (even though not all reach the free surface) — C.

questions.q: True or False: A lumbar rib is sometimes referred to as a gorilla rib because gorillas typically possess an extra rib at this vertebral level.
questions.explain: A lumbar rib (an extra rib articulating with a lumbar vertebra) is nicknamed the gorilla rib because gorillas normally have 13 pairs of ribs, including one attached to the first lumbar vertebra.

questions.q: The lower end of the femur has two spirally curved condyles separated by which structure?
questions.explain: The two distal femoral condyles (medial and lateral) are separated posteriorly by the intercondylar fossa (notch), which provides attachment for the cruciate ligaments of the knee.

questions.q: A textbook diagram labels a neuron's telodendria at the very tip of its longest process. Which process is being illustrated, and what do the telodendria lead to?
options: A dendrite; the telodendria are branches leading back to the cell body
The axon hillock; telodendria mark where the axon originates
A node of Ranvier; telodendria are gaps in the myelin sheath
The axon; the telodendria are its terminal branches, ending in axon terminals
questions.explain: Telodendria are the terminal branches found at the very end of an axon (not a dendrite), and these branches lead to the axon terminals (synaptic boutons), where synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitter.

questions.q: How many bones comprise the skull?
questions.explain: The skull consists of 22 bones: 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones.

questions.q: Compression of the median nerve as it passes deep to the flexor retinaculum at the wrist produces which condition?
questions.explain: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, the space bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: Given that roughly 99% of neurons have numerous dendrites and a single axon, which structural type accounts for the vast majority of neurons in the nervous system?
options: None of these; most neurons have no processes at all
questions.explain: Multipolar neurons, with numerous dendrites and a single axon, make up approximately 99% of neurons — the dominant structural type in the nervous system.

questions.q: True or False: The spaces between trabeculae in spongy bone are typically filled with red bone marrow.
questions.explain: True. The spaces between trabeculae in spongy bone are filled with red bone marrow, which is involved in blood cell formation.

questions.q: Osteocytes are housed in:
questions.explain: Osteocytes sit in small spaces called lacunae — A. (Howship's lacunae hold osteoclasts.)

questions.q: Membranous gaps between cranial bones that make up the calvaria of a foetus are called:
questions.explain: Fontanelles are the membranous gaps between cranial bones in the developing foetal/infant calvaria, before they fuse into rigid sutures.

questions.q: The bone in figure 7 is
questions.explain: The costal (anterior) surface orientation and position of the glenoid cavity/spine in Figure 7 identify this as a right scapula.

questions.q: In this cross-section of an intervertebral disc, the pale central region (A) is a soft, gel-like core. What is it called?
questions.explain: Region A is the nucleus pulposus, the soft, gel-like centre of the intervertebral disc that helps absorb compressive forces.

questions.q: During an autopsy the pathologist may perform a laminectomy to expose the spinal cord. Using the diagram of a vertebra, the letter that best represents where the bone saw will cut during this procedure is
questions.explain: A laminectomy involves cutting through the lamina (the flattened part of the vertebral arch between the transverse and spinous processes), marked D in the diagram.

questions.q: In the same illustration, structure C points to the hollow space running through the centre of the shaft, shown here containing a small blood vessel. Name this space.
questions.explain: Structure C is the medullary cavity, the hollow central space of the diaphysis that houses bone marrow and is lined by the endosteum.

questions.q: Which of the following abnormal curve(s) is often seen in obese men with "potbellies" as they attempt to preserve their center of gravity?
questions.explain: An anterior abdominal weight shift (as with a "potbelly") is often compensated by an exaggerated lumbar curvature — lordosis.

questions.q: The side of the intervertebral disc where herniation most commonly occurs is the:
questions.explain: The posterolateral part of the intervertebral disc is where herniation most commonly occurs, due to the protective effect of the posterior longitudinal ligament centrally.

questions.q: In this infant skull illustration, the large yellow diamond (A) sits at the crossing of the sagittal and coronal sutures. Which fontanelle is this?
questions.explain: Structure A is the anterior fontanelle, the largest fontanelle, located at the bregma where the sagittal and coronal sutures meet; it is the last to close, around 12-18 months.

questions.q: The bulk of the sternum, whose sides are notched for articulation with costal cartilages of ribs 2-7, is called the:
questions.explain: The body forms the bulk of the sternum, with notched sides for articulation with the costal cartilages of ribs 2 through 7.

questions.q: Small spaces between lamellae that house mature bone cells are called:
questions.explain: Lacunae are small spaces between lamellae that contain mature bone cells, the osteocytes. Canaliculi are the tiny channels that radiate from lacunae.

questions.q: Figure 5 shows the bones of the forearm in a superior view. Identify the radius bone.
questions.explain: In this cross-sectional superior view of the forearm, the radius is labelled A (typically the more lateral/rounded bone in this view).

questions.q: True or False: Elderly individuals are prone to fracturing the neck of the femur even after only a minor fall.
questions.explain: Due to age-related osteoporosis, elderly individuals are particularly susceptible to femoral neck fractures even from relatively minor falls.

questions.q: A slightly movable joint is functionally termed:
questions.explain: Amphiarthrosis describes a slightly movable joint, with the symphysis and syndesmosis given as examples in the lecture.

questions.q: Which canal and three foramina are found going through the sphenoid bone?
options: Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen magnum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, jugular foramen and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, jugular foramen and foramen magnum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
questions.explain: The sphenoid bone contains the optic canal plus foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum (the stylomastoid, jugular foramina and foramen magnum belong to the temporal/occipital bones).

questions.q: A tissue sample shows a single layer of cells, all of which touch the basement membrane, yet the nuclei are staggered at different heights, giving a false impression of multiple layers. Which epithelial type is this?
questions.explain: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is actually a single layer (simple), but because all the cells vary in height and their nuclei sit at staggered levels, it gives a false appearance of stratification.

questions.q: Which of these joints is classified as a condyloid (ellipsoid) joint?
questions.explain: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is a condyloid joint, along with metacarpophalangeal, metatarsophalangeal, and temporomandibular joints.

questions.q: Which connective tissue is described as hard, dense, and forms most of the adult skeleton?
questions.explain: Bone, or osseous tissue, is the hard, dense connective tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton. Cartilage is more flexible and is found at joints and a few other sites, not throughout most of the skeleton.

questions.q: The shape of the external ear is maintained by:
questions.explain: The auricle keeps its springy shape thanks to elastic cartilage — B.

questions.q: The smooth, slightly depressed area located just superior to the nasion, on the frontal bone, is called the:
questions.explain: The glabella is a smooth, slightly depressed area on the frontal bone located just superior to the nasion, between the eyebrows.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why a transverse plane through the abdomen and a transverse plane through the head both use the same term, despite being at very different heights on the body?
options: Transverse planes can only occur at the level of the abdomen
Transverse planes are actually a type of sagittal plane
The term changes name depending on which body region is cut
'Transverse' refers to the orientation of the cut at any level, not to a single fixed height
questions.explain: The term 'transverse' describes the plane's orientation — perpendicular to the body's long axis — which can occur at any level of the body, from head to feet, not a single fixed location.

questions.q: The functions of the respiratory system:
options: Transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide
Responsible for the sense of smell
A, B, C and D are all functions of the respiratory system
questions.explain: Gas exchange, phonation (larynx), olfaction and air filtration (nasal hairs/mucus) are all respiratory roles — E.

questions.q: True or False: The lesser tubercle of the humerus is located posteriorly, while the greater tubercle is anterior.
questions.explain: This is reversed: the greater tubercle is lateral/posterior in position while the lesser tubercle is anterior, with the intertubercular groove lying between them.

questions.q: Articular facets on vertebrae form joints between adjacent vertebrae, also known as:
questions.explain: Articular facets form the zygapophyseal (facet) joints between adjacent vertebrae, guiding and limiting spinal movement.

questions.q: True or False: The inferior angle of the scapula is formed at the junction of the medial and lateral borders.
questions.explain: The inferior angle marks the meeting point of the medial and lateral borders of the scapular body at the lowest point of the bone.

questions.q: Why are endocrine glands described as 'ductless,' and how does their secretion actually reach its target?
options: They lack ducts and instead release their secretions directly into a rich network of surrounding blood capillaries
They release secretions only onto the skin surface
They rely entirely on nerve fibers to transport hormones
They are not ductless; all glands have ducts
questions.explain: Endocrine glands lack a duct system; instead, their hormonal secretions are released directly into the dense network of blood capillaries surrounding the gland, allowing distribution throughout the body via the bloodstream.

questions.q: Damage to the epiphyseal plate following a long bone fracture in a child may lead to:
questions.explain: Because the epiphyseal plate is responsible for longitudinal bone growth, damage to it in a child can disrupt growth and lead to shortening of the affected limb.

questions.q: A protein fiber in connective tissue allows a stretched structure, like the wall of a large elastic artery, to spring back to its original length. Which type of fiber is primarily responsible for this recoil property?
questions.explain: Elastic fibers, rich in the protein elastin, give tissue the capacity to stretch and then recoil back to its original shape — the property responsible for the resilience of structures like elastic artery walls.

questions.q: Mesenchymal cells are most commonly found in which type of connective tissue?
questions.explain: Mesenchyme IS embryonic connective tissue, where mesenchymal cells predominate — C.

questions.q: The posterior drawer sign, classically caused by a 'dashboard injury,' assesses tearing of which ligament?
questions.explain: The posterior drawer sign tests for PCL tear, occurring when a large force is applied to the shins of a flexed knee, pushing the tibia posteriorly — classically in dashboard injuries.

questions.q: The pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs both experience substantial compressive load and must resist shearing forces, particularly during activities like childbirth or heavy lifting. Which cartilage type, reinforced with thick collagen bundles, is adapted to these structural demands?
questions.explain: Fibrocartilage, reinforced by thick bundles of collagen fibers, provides the strength needed to withstand compressive load and resist shearing forces at sites like the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs.

questions.q: The posterior fontanelle ossifies how soon after birth, and its point of fusion is called what?
questions.explain: The posterior fontanelle ossifies 2-3 months after birth, with its point of fusion being the lambda.

questions.q: The mucus-secreting cells prevalent in simple columnar epithelium are known as:
questions.explain: Goblet cells are the mucus-secreting cells wedged among columnar cells — A.

questions.q: How many distinct curvatures give the adult vertebral column its characteristic S-shape?
questions.explain: Four distinct curvatures give the vertebral column its S-shape: the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral curvatures.

questions.q: Which canal and three foramina, all passing through the sphenoid bone, are correctly grouped together?
options: Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, foramen spinosum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, foramen ovale, foramen spinosum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, foramen magnum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, jugular foramen, foramen spinosum
questions.explain: The sphenoid bone transmits structures through the optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, and foramen spinosum, all associated with branches of the trigeminal nerve and middle meningeal vessels.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the 'ankle ring' concept described in the lecture?
options: The ankle mortise behaves like a flexible band that never fractures
The talus can dislocate without bony injury
A ring, when broken, usually breaks in two places
The ankle joint has no ligamentous support
questions.explain: The 'ankle ring' analogy describes how the bony-ligamentous ring of the ankle, like any ring, usually breaks (fractures) in two places when subjected to significant force, as seen in Pott's fracture.

questions.q: An epithelium: cells taller than wide, appearing >1 layer thick, but ALL cells attached to the basement membrane; some had cilia; goblet cells present. Most likely located in the:
options: Penile urethra, primary bronchi and respiratory bronchioles
Trachea, membranous urethra and vas deferens
Nasal cavity, larynx and secondary bronchi
Primary bronchi, terminal bronchioles and the epiglottis
questions.explain: All cells touching the membrane + cilia + goblet cells = pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium. Terminal & respiratory bronchioles lose goblet cells and become simple, so A (nasal cavity, larynx, secondary bronchi) is the clean fit.

questions.q: A basal epithelial cell is torn away from the underlying basement membrane during a biopsy, seemingly detaching more easily than its neighboring cells detach from each other. Which junction type, connecting cells specifically to the basement membrane rather than to each other, was most likely compromised?
questions.explain: Hemidesmosomes specifically anchor the basal surface of an epithelial cell to the underlying basement membrane, distinct from desmosomes, which link adjacent cells to one another.

questions.q: Which nerve can be stretched and damaged by downward displacement of the humerus in shoulder dislocation, in addition to the axillary nerve?
questions.explain: The lecture notes that downward displacement of the humerus can stretch and damage the radial nerve, in addition to the axillary nerve.

questions.q: Pott's fracture of the ankle, caused by forced eversion of the foot, typically involves which malleoli?
questions.explain: Pott's fracture involves a bimalleolar (medial and lateral malleoli) or trimalleolar (medial and lateral malleoli plus distal tibia) fracture pattern, resulting from forced eversion of the foot.

questions.q: True or False: Intramembranous ossification forms most of the long bones of the limbs.
questions.explain: False. Intramembranous ossification forms most of the flat bones of the skull, the mandible, the sternum, and the clavicle, whereas long bones form mainly via endochondral ossification.

questions.q: Which cells, located in the periosteum and endosteum, persist as stem cells throughout life and can be activated for fracture repair?
questions.explain: Osteoprogenitor (osteogenic) cells reside in the periosteum and endosteum, persisting as stem cells that can later differentiate to aid in bone repair, such as after a fracture.

questions.q: A patient presents with skeletal-muscle spasms that progress to muscle weakness, accompanied by an abnormal heart rhythm. Which muscular dystrophy variant does this combination most specifically suggest?
questions.explain: Myotonic dystrophy is specifically characterized by skeletal-muscle spasms progressing to weakness, together with abnormal heart rhythm — this combination of features distinguishes it from Duchenne muscular dystrophy and the other listed conditions.

questions.q: Specimens A & B: secretory cells, branched ducts, dense irregular CT dividing them into compartments; dark serous units. Specimen B ALSO has ductless cell clusters near blood vessels. The best description:
options: Specimens A and B are both exocrine with serous secretory units
Specimen A is solely serous-secreting whereas B is both exocrine and endocrine
Specimens A and B are the parotid and pancreas respectively
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: Ductless clusters near blood vessels in B = endocrine islets. So A = pure serous compound gland (parotid) and B = exocrine + endocrine (pancreas). Statements B and C are correct → D. (A is rejected because it ignores B's endocrine part.)

questions.q: At the knee, lateral and medial rotation can only occur when the knee is in which position?
questions.explain: Medial and lateral rotation at the knee can only occur when the knee is flexed; if the knee is extended, such rotation occurs instead at the hip joint.

questions.q: Which observation about a tissue sample would most clearly indicate specialized rather than connective tissue proper — cartilage, bone, or blood — rather than one of the connective tissue proper subtypes?
options: The presence of fibroblasts within a loose fiber network
Randomly oriented collagen fibers, as in the dermis
Parallel collagen fibers, as in a tendon
A mineralized matrix, a firm non-mineralized avascular matrix with chondrocytes, or a fluid matrix with suspended cells
questions.explain: The specialized connective tissues — bone, cartilage, and blood — are distinguished by matrix properties not seen in connective tissue proper: bone's mineralization, cartilage's firm avascular non-mineralized matrix with chondrocytes, and blood's fluid plasma matrix, versus the fibrous, cellular connective tissue proper subtypes.

questions.q: A researcher examines two muscle samples: one is striated and involuntary, the other is striated and voluntary. Which two muscle types does this pair most likely represent?
options: Cardiac muscle and skeletal muscle, respectively
Both samples must be skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle and cardiac muscle, respectively
Skeletal muscle and smooth muscle, respectively
questions.explain: Cardiac muscle is striated yet involuntary, while skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary — matching the described pair; smooth muscle, in contrast, is non-striated.

questions.q: Movements of inversion and eversion of the foot take place primarily at which joints, NOT at the ankle joint itself?
questions.explain: The lecture specifically notes that inversion and eversion occur at the tarsal joints, not at the ankle (talocrural) joint, which itself permits dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.

questions.q: A patient with four lumbar vertebrae and 6 fused sacral vertebrae, but an otherwise normal spine, most likely shows which condition?
questions.explain: Sacralisation occurs when the lowest lumbar vertebra fuses with the sacrum, effectively reducing lumbar vertebrae to four and increasing fused sacral vertebrae to six.

questions.q: This illustration shows a rib cage with a region of adjacent ribs highlighted in red on the right side, representing multiple rib fractures creating a free-floating chest wall segment. What is this clinical condition called?
questions.explain: Multiple adjacent rib fractures creating a free-floating segment of chest wall, as highlighted in red, is known as flail chest or 'stove-in-chest', which causes paradoxical chest wall movement during breathing.
