questions.q: A peripheral nerve is dissected in layers, from the innermost connective tissue wrapping a single axon, outward to a wrapping around a bundle of axons, and finally to the tough outer sheath around the whole nerve. In order from innermost to outermost, what are these three layers called?
questions.explain: From innermost to outermost, a peripheral nerve's connective tissue layers are: the endoneurium (around a single axon), the perineurium (around a fascicle/bundle of axons), and the epineurium (the tough outer sheath around the whole nerve).

questions.q: Perforating (Volkmann's) canals are oriented in what direction relative to the central (Haversian) canals?
questions.explain: Perforating (Volkmann's) canals lie at right angles to the central canals, connecting blood vessels and nerves from the periosteal and endosteal surfaces to the central canals and marrow cavity.

questions.q: True or False: A pudendal nerve block reliably abolishes the pain of uterine contractions during labour.
questions.explain: Pudendal nerve blocks relieve perineal pain (useful for the second stage of labour and episiotomy) but do NOT relieve the pain of uterine contractions, nor do they completely abolish sensation from the anterior perineum.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is TRUE of connective tissue?
options: When connective tissue is stretched, collagen gives it the ability to snap back
Collagen fibers provide high tensile strength
Ground substance is thick and semi-rigid
Reticular fibers form thick, ropelike structures
Elastin fibers are sometimes called white fibers
questions.explain: Collagen gives high tensile strength — C. (Collagen = white fibres; ELASTIN gives recoil; reticular fibres are thin/fine.)

questions.q: Which is the best explanation for why fibroblasts, despite being the most numerous cell in connective tissue proper, are rarely the focus when discussing a tissue's immune or defensive function?
options: Fibroblasts are primarily biosynthetic cells, producing fibers and ground substance, whereas defensive roles belong to other resident cells such as macrophages, mast cells, and plasma cells
Fibroblasts destroy all immune cells in the tissue
Fibroblasts are not actually part of connective tissue
Connective tissue has no defensive function at all
questions.explain: Fibroblasts are primarily biosynthetic, responsible for producing the fibers and ground substance of the extracellular matrix, while the defensive functions of connective tissue are carried out by other resident cell types — macrophages (phagocytosis), mast cells (inflammatory mediators), and plasma cells (antibody production).

questions.q: Which region of a long bone is the growing area where the diaphysis and epiphysis meet, containing the epiphyseal (growth) plate?
questions.explain: The metaphysis is the growing region between diaphysis and epiphysis, containing the cartilaginous epiphyseal growth plate responsible for longitudinal bone growth.

questions.q: Lumbar vertebrae are characterised by a body that is described as:
questions.explain: Lumbar vertebrae have a large, kidney-shaped body, reflecting their role in bearing significant load in the lower back.

questions.q: An 80-year-old patient shows measurably reduced muscular strength compared to earlier decades, along with a biopsy showing increased connective tissue relative to the number of muscle fibers. Which age-related process best explains these combined findings?
options: Sarcopenia, the age-related decline in muscle fibers and mass, accompanied by a relative increase in connective tissue
Fibromyositis, which requires an inflammatory trigger
Muscular dystrophy, which is not age-related
questions.explain: Sarcopenia refers to age-related muscle wasting, characterized by a decline in the number of muscle fibers and overall muscle mass, with a corresponding relative increase in connective tissue — matching this patient's findings.

questions.q: Albers-Schonberg disease (osteopetrosis) is characterised by:
options: Normal bone marrow function in all cases
Increased bone density due to defective resorption of immature bone
questions.explain: Osteopetrosis (Albers-Schonberg disease) is an inherited disorder causing increased bone density due to defective resorption of immature bone; in severe forms the marrow cavity may be obliterated.

questions.q: Which of these joint pairs are BOTH classic examples of ball-and-socket joints?
questions.explain: The shoulder (glenohumeral) and hip joints are the two principal ball-and-socket joints highlighted in the lecture.

questions.q: The cervical curvature of the spine develops as an infant begins to:
questions.explain: As an infant lifts his or her head, around 3 months of age, the cervical (neck) curve and its supporting muscles begin to develop.

questions.q: A researcher observes that damaged mature neurons in the brain, unlike epithelial cells in the skin, generally do not get replaced by new cell division after injury. Which property of neurons explains this?
options: Neurons regenerate faster than any other cell type
questions.explain: Neurons are largely amitotic, meaning most cannot divide to replace themselves if destroyed — a key contrast with tissues like epithelium, which regenerate readily through ongoing cell division.

questions.q: The point where the sagittal and coronal sutures meet is called the:
questions.explain: Bregma is the point where the sagittal and coronal sutures intersect, an important craniometric landmark.

questions.q: Charactristics of the ulna include:
options: The distal end includes the head and the styloid process
The proximal end includes the olecranon, the trochlear notch and the radial notch
The ulna is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm
It articulates with the humerus proximally and the radius laterally
B, C and D are correct
questions.explain: B, C, D correctly describe the ulna. A is wrong — the ulna is the more MEDIAL bone of the forearm (the radius is lateral).

questions.q: Which bone marking term refers to a hard framework that anchors soft organs of the body, allowing the skeleton to bear weight?
questions.explain: Support describes the skeleton acting as a hard framework that supports and anchors the soft organs of the body. Protection instead refers to shielding organs like the brain and spinal cord.

questions.q: Cartilage classified as elastic cartilage would be obtained from the:
options: Intervertebral discs and the epiglottis only
Thyroid cartilage of the larynx and the pinna of ear
Corniculate and cuneiform cartilages of the larynx and the pinna of ear
Arytenoid cartilage and corniculate cartilage of the larynx
Symphysis pubis and cricoid cartilage of the larynx
questions.explain: Elastic cartilage = pinna, auditory tube, epiglottis, corniculate and cuneiform laryngeal cartilages. Option E lists three genuinely elastic sites; D's arytenoid is mostly hyaline. So E.

questions.q: Removing the fine, branching fiber network that forms the structural framework (stroma) of the spleen would primarily disrupt which fiber-dependent function?
options: Allowing the organ to stretch and recoil like an artery wall
Supporting free cells such as lymphocytes and macrophages within a soft organ's framework
Providing tensile strength to resist stretching, like a tendon
questions.explain: This fine, branching network is formed by reticular fibers, whose primary role in organs like the spleen and lymph nodes is to provide a supportive framework (stroma) that houses free cells such as lymphocytes and macrophages — not tensile strength or elasticity.

questions.q: An epithelium: several layers, only basal cells attached; superficial cells covered by an anucleate eosinophilic (keratin) band and fibrillar structures; no goblet/cilia/microvilli. Most likely located:
options: In an internal environment subject to abrasion or the external environment
In the oesophagus, cornea, vagina and tongue
Tongue, soft palate, oral surface of lips and anal canal
questions.explain: The anucleate eosinophilic surface = keratin → keratinised stratified squamous. It occurs on skin (external) and on abraded internal surfaces (hard palate, gingiva). The specific lists (A, C, E) include non-keratinised sites, so the general answer D is correct.

questions.q: An epithelium showed 3 layers of cells taller than wide, lacking surface specialization. This epithelium is most likely located in the:
options: Membranous urethra and fossa navicularis of the penis
Ureter, spongy urethra and prostatic urethra
Prostatic urethra, membranous urethra and ureter
questions.explain: "Taller than wide" = columnar; several layers = stratified columnar. That lines the membranous and (parts of the) spongy urethra. Ureter/prostatic urethra are transitional; fossa navicularis is stratified squamous — so E.

questions.q: A pathologist examines a tumor biopsy under a microscope to determine the tissue of origin. Which subdivision of anatomy is she practicing?
questions.explain: Examining tissue under magnification is histology, the microscopic study of tissue architecture, distinct from gross (naked-eye) anatomy.

questions.q: A first-year student dissects the entire contents of the axilla in one sitting — nerves, vessels, muscles, and lymph nodes together. Which approach to studying anatomy is this?
questions.explain: Studying all structures within one bounded area together, regardless of which organ system they belong to, is the regional approach — as opposed to systemic anatomy, which tracks one system (e.g. the cardiovascular system) across the whole body.

questions.q: Two students disagree about how a joint's shape relates to the movements it permits. Which anatomical principle are they discussing?
questions.explain: The principle of complementarity of structure and function holds that a structure's form directly suits the function it performs — here, joint shape dictating the range of motion available.

questions.q: A 16th-century anatomist corrected many long-standing errors in anatomical texts by insisting on direct human dissection rather than relying on older, unverified sources. Who is most closely associated with this shift?
questions.explain: Andreas Vesalius produced a landmark, meticulously illustrated anatomical text based on direct human dissection, correcting many inherited errors from earlier authorities.

questions.q: Which historical discovery established that the heart pumps blood around the body in a single, continuous circuit rather than the blood being newly produced and consumed?
options: The invention of the compound microscope
questions.explain: William Harvey demonstrated that blood circulates continuously, pumped by the heart, overturning the earlier belief that blood was continuously produced and consumed by the tissues.

questions.q: A body in anatomical position has the following characteristics EXCEPT?
options: Arms adjacent to sides with palms facing backward
Lower limbs close together with feet parallel and toes directed forward
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a parasagittal plane?
options: A transverse section just above the knees
Two sections dividing the body into left and right halves
Any sagittal plane except the median
Any section dividing the body into anterior and posterior
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Assume the body is sectioned along a median sagittal, a frontal or a transverse plane at the level of each organ. Which organs would not be visible in all three cases?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which single plane, and only that plane, guarantees mirror-image right and left halves of the body?
questions.explain: Only the midsagittal (median) plane, passing through the exact midline, produces truly equal (mirror-image) right and left halves; any other sagittal cut is parasagittal and gives unequal portions.

questions.q: Which term refers to the region of the body between the elbow and the shoulder?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A radiology report notes a mass 'nearer the body surface than the underlying rib, but still deep to the skin.' Which best matches this description overall relative to the skin?
options: Deep to the skin but superficial to the rib
questions.explain: The mass is deep relative to the skin (it lies beneath it) but superficial relative to the rib (it lies closer to the surface than the rib does) — superficial/deep are always relative comparisons between two structures, not absolute positions.

questions.q: Which pair of terms would correctly describe the little toe's position relative to the big toe, and the heel's position relative to the toes, respectively?
questions.explain: The little toe sits farther from the body's midline than the big toe (lateral), while the heel is nearer the point where the foot attaches to the leg than the toes are (proximal).

questions.q: A physiotherapist instructs a patient to decrease the angle between the forearm and upper arm at the elbow. Which movement is being requested?
questions.explain: Decreasing the angle between two body parts at a joint is, by definition, flexion — extension is the opposite, increasing that angle.

questions.q: During a shoulder exam, a patient moves the arm in a sequence: out to the side, forward, back to the side, and down — tracing a cone shape with the hand while the shoulder stays fixed. Which single term describes this whole sequence?
questions.explain: Circumduction combines flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction in continuous sequence, so the distal end of the limb traces a cone while the proximal joint stays relatively fixed — exactly the pattern described.

questions.q: A patient with a forearm injury cannot turn the palm to face upward without pain, though turning it to face downward is unaffected. Which specific movement is impaired?
questions.explain: Supination is the movement that rotates the forearm so the palm faces upward (or forward); pronation is the opposite, turning the palm downward — so pain specifically on the upward-facing rotation points to impaired supination.

questions.q: An athlete rolls her ankle so that the sole of the foot turns to face inward, toward the other foot. Which movement occurred, and which ligaments on the ankle's outer side are typically stressed by this motion?
questions.explain: Turning the sole inward (toward the midline) is inversion; because the foot rolls outward at the ankle joint during this motion, it characteristically stresses the ligaments on the lateral (outer) side of the ankle — the mechanism behind the common 'rolled ankle' sprain.

questions.q: Which single movement allows the thumb to touch the tip of the little finger, a motion essential for gripping small objects, and is unique to the thumb among the digits?
questions.explain: Opposition is the specialized movement of the thumb across the palm to meet the fingertips, and it is unique to the thumb's saddle joint — no other digit performs true opposition.

questions.q: The mandible:
options: It has a horizontal body that forms the inferior jawline
The superior margin of each ramus bears the coronoid and condylar processes
A, B and C are correct
Only A and B are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct pairing of a body region with the broader division (axial vs appendicular) it belongs to?
questions.explain: The humerus, as a limb bone, belongs to the appendicular region; the femur, sternum, and vertebral column are all part of the axial region (head, neck, trunk).

questions.q: All the following body cavities are components of the ventral body cavity EXCEPT?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which abdominopelvic region is located directly beneath the umbilical region?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Body cavities and Membranes
options: The ventral body cavity is subdivided into a cranial cavity and a vertebral cavity
The thoracic cavity contains two pleural cavities and a thick band of organs called the mediastinum
Synovial cavities are enclosed within fibrous capsules that fill the sutures of the skull
The serous pericardium is associated with the pericardial cavity and the lungs
The abdominal cavity contains the stomach, urinary bladder, uterus and the prostate gland
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A patient's endocrine gland is surgically removed, and afterward her stress response becomes sluggish and slow to develop, though it still eventually occurs. Which general property of endocrine (versus nervous) signaling does this best illustrate?
options: Endocrine signaling tends to have a slower onset than nervous signaling
Hormones cannot travel through the bloodstream
Endocrine signals are always faster than nervous signals
Only the nervous system can influence the stress response
questions.explain: This scenario reflects the general contrast that endocrine signaling, relying on hormones traveling through the blood, has a slower onset than the nervous system's rapid electrical signaling, though its effects can be longer lasting.

questions.q: Which body system provides the structural framework that both protects internal organs and, by offering attachment sites for muscles, makes coordinated movement possible?
questions.explain: The skeletal system provides the body's rigid framework, protecting organs (e.g. the ribs shielding the lungs) and serving as the attachment scaffold that muscles pull against to produce movement.

questions.q: A dermatologist explains that a patient's condition affects not just the outer skin but also the hair follicles and sweat glands. Which body system does this condition primarily involve?
questions.explain: The integumentary system comprises the skin together with its associated structures — hair, nails, and glands — so a condition spanning skin, follicles, and sweat glands sits within this system.

questions.q: Barbara is 3 months pregnant and her doctor wants to measure the foetal head. Newton is suspected of a brain tumour. The imaging techniques used are:
options: Transabdominal ultrasonography and Positron emission tomography respectively
Computed tomography and Transabdominal ultrasonography respectively
Positron emission tomography and Transvaginal ultrasonography respectively
Transabdominal ultrasonography and Magnetic resonance imaging respectively
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A neurologist wants to visualize soft tissue contrast in the brain in fine detail, without exposing the patient to radiation, and is willing to accept a longer scan time. Which modality best fits this need?
questions.explain: MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves rather than ionizing radiation, and is particularly valued for its excellent soft-tissue contrast, making it well suited to detailed brain imaging despite typically longer scan times than CT.

questions.q: An oncologist wants to know not just where a suspicious mass is located, but whether it is metabolically active (a marker of malignancy). Which imaging technique specifically targets this functional information, rather than structure alone?
questions.explain: PET scanning uses a radioactive tracer to visualize metabolic activity in tissue, providing functional information (such as abnormal metabolic activity in a tumor) rather than just structural detail.

questions.q: Comparing CT and plain X-ray: what is the key technical difference that allows CT to generate cross-sectional 'slices' of the body rather than a single flat image?
options: CT requires no radiation at all
CT can only image bone, unlike plain X-ray
CT uses sound waves instead of X-rays entirely
CT combines many X-ray images taken from different angles and reconstructs them by computer into slices
questions.explain: CT scanning takes a series of X-ray images from multiple angles around the body and uses computer processing to reconstruct detailed cross-sectional slices, unlike a conventional X-ray, which produces a single two-dimensional projection.

questions.q: Which of the following imaging devices would best localize a tumour in a person's brain?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A man a puts his foot on a table while standing to enable him lace his shoe, based on your knowledge of anatomical movement, the hip at this point in time would be in which position?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A weightlifter's shoulders visibly rise toward the ears when bracing under a heavy load. Which term describes this upward movement of the shoulder girdle?
questions.explain: Elevation is the upward movement of a body part, such as the shoulders rising, and is the opposite of depression.

questions.q: Regarding regenerative capacity: why is epithelial tissue often described as recovering quickly from surface injuries such as abrasions?
options: Because epithelial tissue is highly vascular, unlike other tissues
Because epithelial tissue does not actually contain living cells
Because epithelial tissue is mineralized and self-sealing
Because epithelial cells have a notably high capacity for regeneration
questions.explain: Epithelial tissue is characterized by a high regenerative capacity, allowing rapid replacement of damaged or worn cells — the underlying reason superficial abrasions of skin or mucosa heal relatively quickly.

questions.q: A first-year anatomy course covers the digestive, respiratory, and urinary systems one after another as separate units across the semester, rather than dissecting one region of the body at a time. Which overall approach is this course following?
questions.explain: Organizing study of the body by organ system (digestive system, then respiratory system, and so on) rather than by bodily region is the systemic approach to anatomy.

questions.q: Two of the fingers on Theresa's right hand are fused by a web of skin. Ten-year-old Joseph has a small streak of white hair on top of his head although the rest is black. Both Theresa and Joseph exhibit:
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: In the anatomical position the:
options: Arms are extended away from the body
Body is erect and palms face anterior
Palms of the hands face posteriorly
The thumb is medial to the little finger
Body is in a foetal position.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A structure is described in a report as lying 'medial to the ulna, at the wrist.' Which bone of the forearm is most likely being referenced as the medial structure at that level?
options: The radius, since it lies medial to the ulna at the wrist
The ulna itself, describing its own position
The scaphoid, since carpal bones cannot be described as medial or lateral
questions.explain: At the wrist, the anatomical relationship reverses compared to the elbow: the ulna lies laterally and the radius lies medially at this level (in anatomical position), so a structure medial to the ulna at the wrist is on the radial side.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes proximal/distal from superior/inferior as directional terms?
options: Proximal/distal only apply to the head and neck
Superior/inferior only apply to the trunk, never the limbs
Proximal/distal apply specifically to limbs relative to their point of attachment, while superior/inferior apply to the body as a whole relative to the head and feet
They are simply synonyms and can always be used interchangeably
questions.explain: Proximal and distal are used specifically for positions along a limb relative to its point of attachment to the trunk, whereas superior and inferior describe position relative to the head (up) and feet (down) across the whole body, including the trunk.

questions.q: A clinician documents 'eversion and dorsiflexion' as the mechanism of a foot injury. Based on these two terms together, what combined motion likely occurred?
options: The sole rolled inward while the toes pointed downward
The whole foot moved toward the body's midline only
The sole rolled outward while the foot lifted toward the shin
The toes rotated around their own axis with no other motion
questions.explain: Eversion turns the sole outward (away from the midline) and dorsiflexion lifts the foot's dorsum toward the shin; combined, these describe the foot rolling outward while flexing upward at the ankle.

questions.q: Which functional distinction correctly separates flexion/extension from abduction/adduction as categories of movement?
options: Flexion/extension typically change the angle between parts in a mainly sagittal-plane motion, while abduction/adduction move a limb toward or away from the midline, typically in a coronal-plane motion
There is no meaningful distinction; all four terms describe identical motions
Abduction and adduction always occur only at the ankle
Flexion and extension can only occur at the shoulder
questions.explain: Flexion and extension generally describe angle-changing movements occurring roughly within the sagittal plane, while abduction and adduction describe movement of a limb toward or away from the body's midline, generally within the coronal plane — distinct movement categories with distinct reference planes.

questions.q: Suppose an organ lies within the abdominopelvic cavity but is not covered by the peritoneum, sitting instead against the posterior body wall. Which broad ventral cavity subdivision does it still belong to, despite this positioning?
options: The abdominopelvic cavity, since retroperitoneal structures are still part of this division
questions.explain: Even structures positioned behind the peritoneum (retroperitoneal) still lie within the abdominopelvic cavity, one of the two subdivisions of the ventral body cavity — peritoneal covering is a separate concept from cavity membership.

questions.q: Which of the following structures is the most difficult to observe on an X-Ray film?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Given that hormone signaling in the endocrine system generally has a slower onset but longer duration than nervous signaling, which of the following body functions would be better suited to endocrine rather than nervous control?
options: Rapid withdrawal of a hand from a hot surface
Millisecond-scale coordination of a sprinter's muscles
Long-term regulation of growth over months to years
questions.explain: Long-term processes like growth regulation benefit from the slower-onset, longer-lasting nature of hormonal control, whereas split-second actions like reflexes or sprinting require the nervous system's rapid signaling.

questions.q: A researcher wants to study how the heart's structure changes from the embryonic stage through to old age. Which subdivision of anatomy does this best represent?
options: Gross anatomy only, with no reference to time
questions.explain: Tracing structural change across an individual's entire lifetime — from embryo to old age — is the domain of developmental anatomy, of which embryology (prenatal development specifically) is one part.

questions.q: Which of the following scenarios describes physiology rather than anatomy?
options: Describing the layers of the epidermis
Explaining how insulin lowers blood glucose levels
Mapping the branches of the femoral artery
Measuring the length of the femur in cadavers
questions.explain: Explaining how a hormone functions to produce an effect (insulin lowering blood glucose) is a question of physiology — the study of function — rather than anatomy, which concerns structure.

questions.q: A student says 'the wrist is proximal to the elbow.' Is this statement correct?
options: No, because proximal and distal cannot be used to compare two joints
Yes, because the wrist is farther from the trunk than the elbow
Yes, but only when the arm is fully extended
No — the wrist is distal to the elbow, since it is farther from the trunk's point of attachment than the elbow is
questions.explain: This statement has proximal and distal reversed: since the wrist is farther from the trunk's attachment point than the elbow, the wrist is distal to the elbow, not proximal.

questions.q: Which phrase best describes the function of the vertebral curves?
options: To accommodate the weight of the pelvic girdle
To improve cervical center of gravity
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following organs or structures would be found in the left iliac region?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following body systems is primarily responsible for filtering blood and eliminating nitrogenous waste as urine?
questions.explain: The urinary system filters blood and removes nitrogenous waste products, excreting them as urine — distinct from the digestive system, which processes food.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why cartilage, though technically part of the skeletal framework, is NOT typically visible on a standard X-ray the way bone is?
options: X-rays can only detect soft tissue, not hard tissue
Cartilage is actually invisible to all forms of medical imaging
Cartilage contains no matrix at all
Cartilage is less dense than bone and does not absorb X-rays as strongly, so it appears far less distinct on X-ray images
questions.explain: X-ray contrast depends on tissue density — dense bone absorbs more radiation and appears clearly white, while less dense cartilage absorbs far less, making it much less distinct on a standard X-ray compared to bone.

questions.q: A trauma patient needs rapid bedside imaging of possible internal bleeding, without moving them to a scanner suite. Which modality is best suited to this point-of-care scenario?
options: Ultrasound, since portable units allow real-time bedside imaging
Plain X-ray exclusively, since it is the only portable modality
questions.explain: Ultrasound units are commonly portable and provide real-time images at the bedside, making it well suited to rapid trauma assessment (as in the FAST exam for internal bleeding) without needing to transport the patient.

questions.q: Place the following from darkest (black) to lightest (white) as they appear on X-ray film: 1. Soft tissue  2. Femur  3. Air in the lungs  4. Gold metal filling
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which movement pair correctly represents true opposites at the same joint action?
questions.explain: Elevation (upward movement) and depression (downward movement) are true opposites of the same action category; the other listed pairs mix unrelated movement types rather than being direct opposites.

questions.q: If a joint permits only flexion and extension, but not abduction, adduction, or rotation, would circumduction be possible at that joint?
options: Yes, because circumduction is unrelated to any of these movements
Yes, circumduction only requires flexion and extension
It depends only on whether the joint can rotate
No, circumduction requires flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction in combination, so a joint lacking abduction/adduction cannot circumduct
questions.explain: Because circumduction is defined as flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction performed in sequence, a joint that cannot abduct or adduct (such as a typical hinge joint) cannot perform true circumduction.

questions.q: A patient had pain in an infected kidney in his lumbar region, a hernia in his inguinal region, haemorrhoids in his perineal region. These regions are the:
options: Loin, Groin, between the anus and external genitalia respectively
Abdomen, loin and genital region respectively
Loin, groin and genital region respectively
Genital region, loin and groin respectively
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A student states: 'Since MRI does not use ionizing radiation, it must always be the safest and best choice for every type of scan.' What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
options: MRI actually uses more radiation than CT
Safety from ionizing radiation is only one factor; MRI is not always ideal because of cost, scan time, and unsuitability for patients with certain metal implants
There is no flaw; the statement is entirely correct
MRI cannot be used on any patient under any circumstance
questions.explain: While avoiding ionizing radiation is an advantage of MRI, choice of imaging modality depends on multiple factors — cost, scan duration, and safety with metal implants or pacemakers — so MRI is not universally 'best' despite this one advantage.

questions.q: The body cavity found medial to the pleural cavities with the pericardial cavity placed beneath it, is the
options: All of the above are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Comparing the terms 'superior' and 'cephalic': what is their relationship?
options: They are essentially synonymous, both meaning toward the head end
Superior applies only to the trunk, cephalic only to the limbs
questions.explain: Superior and cephalic are essentially synonymous directional terms, both indicating a position toward the head end of the body.

questions.q: A muscle contracts and, as a direct byproduct, warms the surrounding tissue during cold exposure (shivering). Which general function of muscle tissue does this illustrate?
questions.explain: Shivering illustrates thermogenesis, the generation of body heat as a byproduct of muscle contraction — one of the general functions of muscle tissue beyond producing visible motion.

questions.q: Which body plane cuts across the long axis of the body?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The ‘true wrist’ or carpus consists of
options: A group of eight short bones united by ligaments
A group of eight short bones and the metacarpals
The styloid processes of the radius and ulna
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The patella is a classic example of a sesamoid bone.
questions.explain: True. The patella forms within the quadriceps tendon and is the textbook example of a sesamoid bone, protecting the tendon from compressive forces at the knee.

questions.q: The sternum:
options: Is also known as the ‘breastbone’ and its xiphoid process is a plate of hyaline cartilage until about age 40
Is a bony plate anterior to the heart
Is an irregular bone divided into 3 regions: manubrium, body and xiphoid process
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a cranial bone?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The spaces between trabeculae in spongy bone are typically filled with red bone marrow.
questions.explain: True. The spaces between trabeculae in spongy bone are filled with red bone marrow, which is involved in blood cell formation.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is capable of bearing the greatest physical stress?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: Hard callus persists for about 3-4 months before being remodeled into compact bone.
questions.explain: True. During bone remodeling, hard callus persists for 3-4 months while osteoclasts dissolve broken bone fragments and osteoblasts bridge the gap with spongy bone, eventually remodeled into compact bone.

questions.q: True or False: Osteoporosis increases susceptibility to fractures of the hip and wrist, and may cause kyphosis.
questions.explain: True. Increased susceptibility to fractures of the hip and wrist, vertebral compression, loss of body height, and development of kyphosis are all features of osteoporosis.

questions.q: Children are often told to keep this process off the table while eating.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: Taking folic acid during pregnancy can help minimise the likelihood of cleft palate.
questions.explain: True. The notes state that the likelihood of cleft palate is minimised by taking folic acid during pregnancy.

questions.q: True or False: Infant skull bones are described as thin but somewhat flexible, making them less easily fractured than adult skull bones.
questions.explain: True. The notes describe infant skull bones as thin but flexible, which makes them less easily fractured compared to the more rigid adult skull bones.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is not an integral bone of the skull and is not attached by sutures to the remainder of the skull bones
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following abnormal curve(s) is often seen in obese men with ‘potbellies’ as they attempt to preserve their center of gravity?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: Spina bifida is associated with folic acid deficiency in genetically susceptible individuals.
questions.explain: True. Spina bifida is associated with folic acid deficiency in certain genetically susceptible individuals, which is why folic acid supplementation is recommended during pregnancy.

questions.q: Which connective tissue is described as hard, dense, and forms most of the adult skeleton?
questions.explain: Bone, or osseous tissue, is the hard, dense connective tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton. Cartilage is more flexible and is found at joints and a few other sites, not throughout most of the skeleton.

questions.q: The skeleton with the highest number of bones is that of:
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: What is the major function of the axial skeleton?
options: Provide an attachment point for muscles that allow movement
Provide a space for the major digestive organs
Provide central support for the body and protect internal organs
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which hormone produced by bone tissue helps regulate bone formation?
questions.explain: Bones produce osteocalcin, which helps regulate bone formation. Insulin, cortisol, and prolactin are produced by other endocrine tissues and are not specific bone-derived regulators of ossification mentioned here.

questions.q: Which category of bone is typically longer than wide, has a shaft with heads at both ends, and functions mainly as a lever?
questions.explain: Long bones are tubular, longer than wide, contain mostly compact bone, and act as levers for movement when muscles contract, e.g. the femur and humerus.

questions.q: The term diploë refers to the:
options: Double-layered nature of the connective tissue covering the bone
Two types of marrow found within most bones
Internal layer of spongy bone in flat bones
Fact that most bones are formed of two types of bone tissue
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A sesamoid bone is best described as shaped like which object, and forms within tendons under high pressure?
questions.explain: Sesamoid bones are small and round, shaped like a sesame seed, and form within tendons where considerable pressure is generated at a joint, such as the patella.

questions.q: Which region of a long bone is the growing area where the diaphysis and epiphysis meet, containing the epiphyseal (growth) plate?
questions.explain: The metaphysis is the growing region between diaphysis and epiphysis, containing the cartilaginous epiphyseal growth plate responsible for longitudinal bone growth.

questions.q: Which thin layer of hyaline cartilage covers each epiphysis of a long bone, reducing friction at joints?
questions.explain: Articular cartilage is a thin layer of hyaline cartilage covering each epiphysis where the bone forms a joint, allowing smooth, low-friction movement.

questions.q: The endosteum is best described as:
options: An avascular membrane found only in flat bones
A single-layered, osteogenic membrane lining inner bone surfaces
A double-layered membrane covering the outer bone surface
A non-cellular fibrous capsule around joints
questions.explain: The endosteum is single-layered, lines the inner bone surfaces, is osteogenic, and contributes to new bone formation, unlike the periosteum which covers outer surfaces.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of bone's dry weight is made up of organic components such as collagen fibres and cells?
questions.explain: Organic components make up about 35% of the dry weight of bone, including cells, mostly type I collagen fibres, and ground substance.

questions.q: Bone and cartilage tissues share several extracellular matrix components in common. Which of the following is generally NOT a feature shared between the two?
questions.explain: Hydroxyapatite crystals are characteristic of calcified bone matrix, not cartilage, which remains uncalcified under normal conditions. Collagen fibres, hyaluronic acid, and sulphated GAGs are shared ground substance/fibre components.

questions.q: The fibula:
options: Is a thin bone with two expanded ends
Its malleolus forms the medial bulge of the ankle and articulates with the talus
Several muscles originate from the fibula but it does not bear weight
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Mature bone cells housed within lacunae that maintain the bone matrix and connect to each other via canaliculi are called:
questions.explain: Osteocytes are mature bone cells residing in lacunae, maintaining the surrounding matrix, with cytoplasmic processes running through canaliculi to connect with neighbouring osteocytes.

questions.q: Which cells, located in the periosteum and endosteum, persist as stem cells throughout life and can be activated for fracture repair?
questions.explain: Osteoprogenitor (osteogenic) cells reside in the periosteum and endosteum, persisting as stem cells that can later differentiate to aid in bone repair, such as after a fracture.

questions.q: Osteocytes are housed within which structure?
questions.explain: Osteocytes occupy small spaces called lacunae within the bone matrix, from which canaliculi extend to allow communication and nutrient exchange between cells.

questions.q: Which bone contains diaphysis and epiphysis areas and is proportionally more compact than spongy bone?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Small spaces between lamellae that house mature bone cells are called:
questions.explain: Lacunae are small spaces between lamellae that contain mature bone cells, the osteocytes. Canaliculi are the tiny channels that radiate from lacunae.

questions.q: Perforating (Volkmann's) canals are oriented in what direction relative to the central (Haversian) canals?
questions.explain: Perforating (Volkmann's) canals lie at right angles to the central canals, connecting blood vessels and nerves from the periosteal and endosteal surfaces to the central canals and marrow cavity.

questions.q: The canal that runs through the core of each osteon is the principal site of:
questions.explain: The central (Haversian) canal at the core of each osteon contains blood vessels and nerve fibres that nourish and innervate the surrounding bone tissue.

questions.q: Endochondral ossification occurs in the
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The primary centre of ossification in endochondral bone formation typically appears in which part of the developing bone?
questions.explain: The primary centre of ossification appears around the 7th to 12th week, in the middle of the diaphysis, where mesenchymal tissue, osteoblasts, and blood vessels initiate bone formation.

questions.q: Damage to the epiphyseal plate following a long bone fracture in a child may lead to:
questions.explain: Because the epiphyseal plate is responsible for longitudinal bone growth, damage to it in a child can disrupt growth and lead to shortening of the affected limb.

questions.q: In an adult X-ray, the thin radiopaque line marking the former site of the epiphyseal plate is called the:
questions.explain: Once growth is complete, the epiphyseal plate ossifies and is seen radiographically as a thin epiphyseal line.

questions.q: Granular tissue formed after a fracture is infiltrated by which cells, according to the notes?
questions.explain: Granular tissue at the fracture site is infiltrated by blood capillaries and fibroblasts, along with macrophages, osteoclasts, and osteogenic cells, which together prepare the site for callus formation.

questions.q: Which hormone, produced by the parathyroid gland, increases blood calcium by stimulating osteoclast activity?
questions.explain: Parathyroid hormone increases blood calcium levels by stimulating osteoclasts to resorb bone, releasing calcium into the bloodstream.

questions.q: Estrogen replacement therapy in postmenopausal women, while reducing bone loss risk, is associated with an increased risk of which of the following?
options: Heart attack, stroke, and breast cancer
questions.explain: Although estrogen decline increases postmenopausal bone loss risk, estrogen replacement therapy itself is associated with an increased risk of heart attack, stroke, and breast cancer.

questions.q: Which of the following glands/organs produce hormones that tend to decrease blood calcium levels?
questions.explain: The thyroid gland produces calcitonin, which decreases blood calcium levels. The pineal gland, spleen, and ovary are not primary regulators of calcium homeostasis in this context.

questions.q: Rickets, caused by inadequate dietary calcium or vitamin D in children, primarily causes:
questions.explain: Rickets results from insufficient calcium or vitamin D in children, causing inadequate mineralisation of bone and characteristic bowing of the skeleton (bowed legs).

questions.q: The adult equivalent of rickets, caused by inadequate mineralisation of bone, is called:
questions.explain: Osteomalacia is the adult condition resulting from inadequate bone mineralisation due to vitamin D or calcium deficiency, analogous to rickets in children.

questions.q: In osteoporosis, what happens to the balance between bone resorption and bone formation?
options: Resorption and formation remain perfectly balanced
questions.explain: In osteoporosis, bone cells become less active due to oestrogen loss, and bone resorption outpaces bone formation, leading to net bone loss and fragility.

questions.q: Albers-Schonberg disease (osteopetrosis) is characterised by:
options: Increased bone density due to defective resorption of immature bone
Normal bone marrow function in all cases
questions.explain: Osteopetrosis (Albers-Schonberg disease) is an inherited disorder causing increased bone density due to defective resorption of immature bone; in severe forms the marrow cavity may be obliterated.

questions.q: Osteomyelitis is best described as:
options: Caused by altered vitamin D metabolism only
Inflammation of bone caused by pus-forming bacteria
Caused purely by hyperactivity of osteoclasts
questions.explain: Osteomyelitis is inflammation of bone caused by pus-forming bacteria, distinguishing it from metabolic bone diseases like rickets or osteomalacia.

questions.q: Inadequate growth hormone production in childhood leads to a condition characterised by:
options: Reduced epiphyseal cartilage activity and shorter stature
questions.explain: Pituitary growth failure from inadequate growth hormone in childhood reduces epiphyseal cartilage activity, leading to abnormally short bones and shorter stature.

questions.q: Acromegaly differs from gigantism mainly because the excess growth hormone occurs:
options: After the epiphyseal cartilages have closed
questions.explain: Acromegaly occurs when growth hormone is overproduced after the epiphyseal cartilages have closed, causing bones to thicken rather than lengthen, particularly affecting the face, jaw, and hands.

questions.q: Marfan's syndrome is an inherited condition resulting in excessive cartilage formation at the epiphyseal plate, leading to:
options: Premature suture closure of the skull
A very tall person with long, slender limbs and cardiovascular problems
questions.explain: Marfan's syndrome causes excessive cartilage formation at the epiphyseal plate, resulting in very tall stature, long slender limbs, and associated cardiovascular problems.

questions.q: At birth, an infant has roughly how many separate bony elements before later fusion reduces the number?
questions.explain: At birth, infants have about 270 separate bones; this number decreases over time due to gradual fusion of separate bony elements into the adult total of 206.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs indicate cranial sutures and the bones between which these sutures are found?
options: A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Internally, prominent bony ridges divide the cranial base into how many distinct fossae?
questions.explain: The cranial base is divided internally into three distinct fossae: the anterior, middle, and posterior cranial fossae.

questions.q: A small foramen at the base of the frontal crest, used for passage of vessels during development, is called the:
questions.explain: The foramen caecum is located at the base of the frontal crest and is a small foramen for passage of vessels during embryonic development.

questions.q: The saddle-shaped bony formation that houses and guards the pituitary gland, located on the body of the sphenoid, is the:
questions.explain: The sella turcica is a saddle-like formation on the sphenoid that houses and guards the pituitary gland, flanked by anterior and posterior clinoid processes.

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy fell off his bicycle and X-rays revealed damage to the sella turcica. This most likely indicates a fracture of which bone?
questions.explain: The sella turcica is a feature of the sphenoid bone, so damage to this structure on imaging indicates a likely fracture involving the sphenoid bone.

questions.q: The foramen magnum is a large hole in the base of the occipital bone that transmits the spinal cord. The homologous structure in an individual vertebra is the:
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following organs lies directly posterior to the sternum?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Cranial nerve II passes through which opening identified in the orbital/cranial base region?
questions.explain: The optic canal transmits cranial nerve II (the optic nerve), along with the ophthalmic artery, from the orbit into the middle cranial fossa.

questions.q: The skull
options: The opening that connects the cranial cavity to the spinal column is the foramen magnum
The bone surrounding the foramen magnum is the occipital bone
The lambdoid suture separates the two parietal bones from the frontal bone
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Cranial nerves VII and VIII pass through which structure?
questions.explain: The internal acoustic (auditory) meatus transmits cranial nerves VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear) into the petrous temporal bone.

questions.q: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) passes through which foramen?
questions.explain: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, V2, passes through the foramen rotundum of the sphenoid bone.

questions.q: Which canal and three foramina are found going through the sphenoid bone?
options: Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen magnum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, jugular foramen and foramen magnum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, jugular foramen and foramen spinosum
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which four bones meet at the pterion, forming an H-shaped suture pattern?
questions.explain: The pterion is the region where the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and parietal bones meet, forming an H-shaped suture roughly 3-4 cm superior to the midpoint of the zygomatic arch.

questions.q: The point where the sagittal and coronal sutures meet is called the:
questions.explain: Bregma is the point where the sagittal and coronal sutures intersect, an important craniometric landmark.

questions.q: The calvaria
options: Consists of the occipital, parietal and frontal bones
Consists of the occipital, parietal, maxillary, temporal and frontal bones
Bears fibrous areas known as fontanelles in the infant
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Grooves on the inner skull cap for branches of the middle meningeal artery are an example of which calvarial feature?
questions.explain: Vascular grooves on the inner aspect of the skull cap accommodate branches of the middle meningeal artery as they run along the inner table.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is not a facial bone?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following are associated with the frontal bone?
options: Supraorbital foramen, glabella, floor of anterior cranial fossa and superior part of the orbit
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The ridge just superior to the supraorbital margin, more pronounced in males, is the:
questions.explain: The superciliary arch is a prominent ridge just above the supraorbital margin, typically more pronounced in males, corresponding to the brow ridge.

questions.q: The supraorbital notch or foramen allows passage of which nerve and vessels?
questions.explain: The supraorbital notch or foramen allows passage of the supraorbital nerve and accompanying vessels, supplying the forehead and scalp.

questions.q: The maxillae:
options: Form the upper jaw and the central part of the facial skeleton
Do not articulate with the mandible
Form the bony roof of the oral cavity/mouth
A, C and D are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The skull bone that is connected to the rest of the cranium posteriorly via the coronal suture is the
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A small foramen on the zygomatic bone, generally visible and used for passage of a sensory nerve, is the:
questions.explain: The zygomaticofacial foramen is a small foramen typically visible on the anterior surface of the zygomatic bone.

questions.q: Evaluate the statements about the mandibular and mental foramina of the mandible.
options: The mandibular foramen is on the medial surface of the ramus
The mandibular foramen is on the lateral surface of the ramus and is for injecting anaesthetic
The mental foramen is on the anterior part of the mandibular body
The mental foramen is on the anterolateral side of the mandibular body and is for blood vessels and nerves to the lower lip
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following are associated with the temporal bone?
options: Squamous suture, zygomatic process, mandibular fossa and stylomastoid foramen
External acoustic meatus, styloid process, jugular foramen and carotid canal
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, hypoglossal canal and foramen ovale
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The superior orbital fissure is formed in the sphenoid bone, whereas the inferior orbital fissure is formed between the sphenoid and
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The posterior aspect of the maxilla, behind the upper molar teeth, is referred to as the:
questions.explain: The tuberosity of the maxilla is the rounded posterior aspect of the maxilla, located behind the upper molar teeth, containing small alveolar foramina.

questions.q: Which of the following facial bones is/are part of the hard palate?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Posterior to the central incisors, a small depression with paired canals for the nasopalatine nerves is the:
questions.explain: The incisive fossa, located posterior to the central incisors, contains the incisive canals which transmit the nasopalatine nerves.

questions.q: The greater and lesser palatine foramina, located posterolaterally on the hard palate, transmit:
options: Nerves and vessels of the same name
questions.explain: The greater and lesser palatine foramina transmit the greater and lesser palatine nerves and vessels respectively, supplying the palate.

questions.q: On the inferior aspect of the skull, three parts of the sphenoid bone can be appreciated. Which structure lies between the medial and lateral pterygoid plates?
questions.explain: The pterygoid fossa is located between the medial and lateral pterygoid plates of the sphenoid bone, visible on the inferior skull view.

questions.q: Which of the following facial bones contains a sinus?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the paranasal sinuses?
options: Paranasal sinuses open into the oral cavity.
Paranasal sinuses contain passages acting as one-way valves.
Paranasal sinuses enhance the resonance of the voice and lighten the skull.
Paranasal sinuses are found in maxillary, ethmoid, and lacrimal bones.
Paranasal sinuses are found in maxillary, frontal and lacrimal bones.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: How many bones comprise the skull?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The posterior fontanelle ossifies how soon after birth, and its point of fusion is called what?
questions.explain: The posterior fontanelle ossifies 2-3 months after birth, with its point of fusion being the lambda.

questions.q: A bulging fontanelle in an infant is typically a sign of:
questions.explain: A bulging fontanelle indicates increased pressure on the brain (raised intracranial pressure), whereas a depressed fontanelle indicates dehydration.

questions.q: The membranous area between the occipital and parietal bones of the foetal skull is called
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of homicides by strangulation result in a fractured hyoid bone, according to the notes?
questions.explain: According to the lecture notes, the hyoid bone is fractured in one-third of all homicides by strangulation.

questions.q: Which three small bones make up the auditory ossicles in each middle ear cavity?
questions.explain: The auditory ossicles consist of three small bones in each middle ear: the malleus, incus, and stapes, which transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear.

questions.q: How many bones make up the adult vertebral column?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Cervical vertebrae differ from the other vertebrae in that they have
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: If Robert's left kidney was deep to his last two left lower ribs, these ribs will be
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: How many cervical vertebrae are typically present in the body?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A 40-year old man has lordosis. This is
options: An exaggerated inward curvature of the lumbar region of the spine just above the sacrum
An abnormal lateral curvature of the vertebral column, common in obese men and pregnant women
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A 14-year old girl has Scoliosis. This is
options: An abnormal lateral curvature of the vertebral column
An exaggerated inward curvature of the lumbar region of the spine just above the sacrum
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Cervical and lumbar curvatures are classified as secondary (compensation) curvatures because they:
options: Develop after birth as the baby begins to walk
questions.explain: Cervical and lumbar curvatures are secondary curvatures that develop after birth as a baby begins to walk, redistributing the weight of the upper body over the lower limbs.

questions.q: The skull bone that provides the major passageway for the brain to communicate with the rest of the body is the
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The primary functions of the vertebral column include
options: Conducting nervous impulses from the brain.
Transmission of weight from the trunk to the lower limbs.
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Articular facets on vertebrae form joints between adjacent vertebrae, also known as:
questions.explain: Articular facets form the zygapophyseal (facet) joints between adjacent vertebrae, guiding and limiting spinal movement.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the sacrum is false?
options: Consists of six sacral vertebrae and four anterior foramina
Articulates with L5 superiorly and the coccyx inferiorly
Is located on the posterior aspect of the pelvis
Its alae articulate with the two hip bones
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following makes up the axial skeleton?
options: The skull, vertebral column and pelvis
The skull, shoulder girdles and rib cage
The skull, vertebral column and rib cage
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The intervertebral disc consists of an outer rim of fibrocartilage called annulus fibrosus and a central gelatinous core called:
questions.explain: The intervertebral disc has an outer annulus fibrosus and an inner gelatinous core called the nucleus pulposus, which together act as shock absorbers.

questions.q: Disc herniation classically occurs posterolaterally rather than directly posteriorly because of the protective action of the:
questions.explain: The posterior longitudinal ligament prevents herniation from proceeding directly posteriorly, so herniation usually occurs posterolaterally instead.

questions.q: Intramembranous ossification occurs in the
options: A, B, C are all correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The following are characteristics of the vertebral column EXCEPT
options: About ¼ of the length is contributed by the 23 intervertebral discs
It has a chain of 33 individual vertebrae with 23 intervertebral discs of fibrocartilage
The sacral curvature positions the weight of the upper part of the body over the lower limbs, providing optimal balance during standing
Only the thoracic and sacral curvatures are well developed at birth and are termed primary curvatures
In the adult there are 29 vertebrae; 27 mobile, 2 immobile, and 20 intervertebral discs
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A patient with four lumbar vertebrae and 6 fused sacral vertebrae, but an otherwise normal spine, most likely shows which condition?
questions.explain: Sacralisation occurs when the lowest lumbar vertebra fuses with the sacrum, effectively reducing lumbar vertebrae to four and increasing fused sacral vertebrae to six.

questions.q: The atlanto-occipital joint, formed between the atlas and occipital condyles, is a condyloid joint that primarily permits which movement?
questions.explain: The atlanto-occipital joint is a condyloid joint permitting nodding ('yes') movements of the head, as the occipital condyles articulate with the superior articular facets of the atlas.

questions.q: The axis (C2) has a peg-like projection called the dens, which articulates with the atlas to allow which movement?
questions.explain: The dens of the axis articulates with the atlas at a pivot joint, helping rotate the head, as in shaking the head to say 'no'. The transverse ligament secures the dens in place.

questions.q: Thoracic vertebrae differ from the other vertebrae in that they have
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Demifacets are a characteristic of which type of vertebrae?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The vertebra which has no body is the
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Lumbar vertebrae differ from the other vertebrae in that they have
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Cervical vertebrae can be uniquely identified by the presence of
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Compared to the male sacrum, the female sacrum is generally:
questions.explain: The female sacrum is generally wider and shorter than the male sacrum, with a shallower concavity, adapted for the wider female pelvis.

questions.q: The coccyx is composed of how many rudimentary fused bones, oriented downward and ventrally?
questions.explain: The coccyx has 4 rudimentary bones fused together according to the notes, directed downwards and ventrally, with laterally projecting rudimentary transverse processes. (Note: while commonly cited as 3-5 segments, this deck specifies 4 fused bones for the coccyx structure described.)

questions.q: The bulk of the sternum, whose sides are notched for articulation with costal cartilages of ribs 2-7, is called the:
questions.explain: The body forms the bulk of the sternum, with notched sides for articulation with the costal cartilages of ribs 2 through 7.

questions.q: The xiphoid process of the sternum is composed of which tissue in youth, before ossifying around age 40?
questions.explain: The xiphoid process is composed of hyaline cartilage in youth and typically ossifies around age 40, occasionally remaining bifid or perforated.

questions.q: How many pairs of false ribs are present in the skeleton?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The costal groove, found at the inferior border of the inner rib surface, contains which neurovascular structures, in order from superior to inferior?
questions.explain: The costal groove contains the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve arranged from superior to inferior, remembered by the mnemonic VAN.

questions.q: The constricted portion of a typical rib located between the head and tubercle is called the:
questions.explain: The neck of a typical rib is the constricted portion located between the head and the tubercle.

questions.q: The only group of vertebrae that articulates with the ribs is
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which ribs are described as having only one facet and articulating with a single vertebra, with no neck or tubercle?
questions.explain: The 10th and 12th ribs have only one facet and articulate with a single vertebra, and the 11th and 12th ribs are short with no neck or tubercle.

questions.q: The appendicular skeleton includes the bones of the upper and lower limbs, plus their attachments to the axial skeleton at the:
questions.explain: The appendicular skeleton includes limb bones along with their attachment points to the axial skeleton at the pectoral girdle (upper limb) and pelvic girdle (lower limb).

questions.q: The common names for the scapula, clavicle, sternum, calvaria and patella are the:
options: Shoulder blade, breast bone, skullcap, hip bone and knee cap respectively
Shoulder blade, knee cap, collar bone, breast bone and skull cap respectively
Shoulder blade, hip bone, collar bone, knee cap and skull cap respectively
Shoulder blade, collar bone, breast bone, skull cap and knee cap respectively
Shoulder blade, breast bone, skullcap, collar bone and knee cap respectively
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The scapula articulates with the humerus at which structure?
questions.explain: The scapula articulates with the head of the humerus at the glenoid fossa, forming the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint.

questions.q: This schematic radiograph of a child's long bone shows a dark (radiolucent) band near each end, marked by arrows. What does this band represent?
questions.explain: In a child, the radiolucent band seen between epiphysis and metaphysis is the still-active, cartilaginous epiphyseal (growth) plate, which has not yet ossified.

questions.q: Compression of the median nerve as it passes deep to the flexor retinaculum at the wrist produces which condition?
questions.explain: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, the space bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: The following are features of the humerus EXCEPT:
options: It articulates with the scapula at the shoulder
The distal end consists of the two condyles, a medial trochlea and a lateral capitulum
It consists of a shaft and two ends
The proximal end consists of the head, anatomical neck, and two tubercles
The proximal end consists of the condyle, the medial epicondyle and the lateral epicondyle
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The shaft of the tibia is the most frequent site of an open fracture, commonly resulting from motorcycle accidents.
questions.explain: Because the tibial shaft lies just beneath the skin with little soft tissue covering anteriorly, it is the most common site for open (compound) fractures, frequently from motorcycle accidents.

questions.q: Which tarsal bone is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which carpal bone is most frequently fractured, with tenderness elicited at the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explain: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand raises strong suspicion for a scaphoid fracture.

questions.q: On the shaft of the humerus, the deltoid tuberosity is located:
options: Laterally, for attachment of the deltoid muscle
questions.explain: The deltoid tuberosity is a roughened prominence on the lateral aspect of the humeral shaft that serves as the insertion site for the deltoid muscle.

questions.q: The appendicular skeleton includes the bones of the limbs together with the structures that attach them to the axial skeleton. Which pair correctly matches limb to its girdle?
options: Upper limb - pelvic girdle; Lower limb - pectoral girdle
Upper limb - pectoral girdle; Lower limb - pelvic girdle
Upper limb has no girdle attachment
Both limbs attach via the pectoral girdle
Both limbs attach via the pelvic girdle
questions.explain: The upper limb attaches to the axial skeleton at the pectoral (shoulder) girdle, while the lower limb attaches at the pelvic girdle.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about facial bones is FALSE?
options: The zygomatic bones are commonly called the cheekbones
The mandible is the largest and strongest bone of the face
The lacrimal bones contribute to the orbit's medial wall
The vomer is located in the orbit forming the inferior part of the orbit
The maxillae are considered as the keystone bones of the skeleton
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The medial epicondyle of the humerus has the ulnar nerve passing immediately behind it, making it vulnerable to injury (the 'funny bone' phenomenon).
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve runs in a groove just posterior to the medial epicondyle, which is why striking this area produces the tingling sensation commonly called hitting the 'funny bone'.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements concerning the radius:
options: It is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm
It articulates with the carpus proximally and the ulna medially
The proximal end consists of a head, neck and tuberosity
The distal end is expanded and bears a pointed process known as the styloid process
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the humerus?
options: Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa and olecranon fossa
Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove
Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and intertubercular groove
Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: In standard anatomical position, which bone of the forearm lies laterally?
questions.explain: In anatomical position (forearm supinated, palm facing forward), the radius lies lateral and the ulna lies medial.

questions.q: Which bone is not part of the pelvic girdle?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: What kind of tissue serves as a model for long bones in the embryo?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The bony pelvis:
options: All the above are features of the bony pelvis
Consists of the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx
In the female it is generally wider, shallower and lighter and adapted for childbearing
The outlet is bounded anteriorly by the pubic arch, laterally by the ischial tuberosities, posteriorly by the sacrum and coccyx
Has a pelvic inlet and pelvic outlet
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which carpal bone bears a hook-like projection (the hook of hamate)?
questions.explain: The hamate carpal bone is named for and characterized by its hook (hamulus), a projection on its palmar surface that anchors part of the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: True or False: Clubfoot is described as a congenital defect in which the soles of the foot face medially and the talus points inferiorly.
questions.explain: Clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) is a congenital condition in which the soles face medially (inward) and the talus points inferiorly, consistent with the inverted, adducted, plantar-flexed positioning.

questions.q: True or False: The supraspinous fossa is found on the costal (anterior) surface of the scapula.
questions.explain: The supraspinous fossa is on the dorsal (posterior) surface of the scapula, above the spine. The costal surface instead bears the subscapular fossa.

questions.q: The lesser trochanter, intertrochanteric crest and gluteal tuberosity are found on the
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: By approximately what age does fusion of the three hip bone components become complete?
questions.explain: Fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis begins between 15 and 17 years of age and is generally complete between 20 and 25 years of age.

questions.q: True or False: A lumbar rib is sometimes referred to as a gorilla rib because gorillas typically possess an extra rib at this vertebral level.
questions.explain: A lumbar rib (an extra rib articulating with a lumbar vertebra) is nicknamed the gorilla rib because gorillas normally have 13 pairs of ribs, including one attached to the first lumbar vertebra.

questions.q: On this labelled bony pelvis diagram, the structure marked C, a deep socket on the lateral hip bone, is the:
questions.explain: The structure labelled C sits laterally on the hip bone as a cup-shaped socket — this is the acetabulum, which receives the head of the femur.

questions.q: The thumb (pollex) corresponds to which numbered metacarpal?
questions.explain: Metacarpals are numbered 1 to 5 from lateral (thumb side) to medial; the thumb (pollex) corresponds to metacarpal I.

questions.q: A Colles' fracture of the distal radius classically produces which deformity?
questions.explain: In a Colles' fracture, the distal fragment of the radius is displaced and tilted posteriorly, producing the characteristic dinner fork (or silver fork) deformity of the wrist.

questions.q: Which of the following forms the largest portion of the hip bone?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The fibrous sheet connecting the radius and ulna along the middle of their shafts, visible between the two bones in this image, is the:
questions.explain: The interosseous membrane is the fibrous connective tissue sheet spanning between the radius and ulna along their shafts, providing stability and an attachment surface for forearm muscles.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not correct anatomically?
options: The Axis is inferior to the Atlas
The eye brow is superior to the eye lid
The index finger is medial to the pollex
The distal end of the radius lies lateral in a pronated antebrachium
The carpal bones are arranged into a proximal and distal rows of four bones each
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which digit does not have a middle phalanx?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The femur is described as the longest and heaviest bone of the body, with its length ranging approximately what fraction of total body height?
