questions.explain: The femur's length typically ranges from about one-quarter to one-third of total body height/stature, which is why stature can be estimated from femur length in forensic contexts.

questions.q: Which portion of the fibula articulates with the talus?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The roughened anterior border of the pubis is named the:
questions.explain: The pubic crest is the roughened ridge forming the anterior border of the pubic body, an attachment site for abdominal muscles.

questions.q: How many epiphyseal centres typically develop in the clavicle, and at which end?
options: Three, at the shaft and both ends
None — it ossifies entirely from a single primary centre
questions.explain: Only one epiphyseal centre develops in the clavicle, located at the sternal (medial) end, appearing during adolescent years.

questions.q: True or False: The lesser tubercle of the humerus is located posteriorly, while the greater tubercle is anterior.
questions.explain: This is reversed: the greater tubercle is lateral/posterior in position while the lesser tubercle is anterior, with the intertubercular groove lying between them.

questions.q: True or False: When examining a wet footprint, the medial margin from the heel to the first metatarsal head normally leaves no print because the medial longitudinal arch curves above the ground.
questions.explain: In a person with a normal medial longitudinal arch, the wet footprint shows no impression along the medial margin between heel and first metatarsal head, since that part of the foot is elevated off the ground by the arch.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the humerus?
options: Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and intertubercular groove
Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa and olecranon fossa
Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest
Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: On the inferior surface of the clavicle's shaft, the conoid tubercle forms a synovial joint with which part of the scapula?
questions.explain: The conoid tubercle, on the inferior surface of the clavicle, anchors the conoid ligament and corresponds to a synovial-type connection with the coracoid process of the scapula.

questions.q: In anatomical position, the scapula lies posterolateral to which ribs?
questions.explain: The scapula is a large, flattened triangular bone that lies posterolateral to the 2nd through 7th ribs in the normal anatomical position.

questions.q: The major function(s) of the thoracic cage is (are)
options: To help expand the thoracic cavity during breathing
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: In the image shown, what skeletal anomaly is illustrated arising near the C7 vertebra?
questions.explain: The image labels an accessory rib projecting from the C7 (cervical) level as a cervical rib, distinct from the normal first rib arising at T1.

questions.q: Characteristics of the ulna include:
options: The ulna is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm
It articulates with the humerus proximally and the radius laterally
The proximal end includes the olecranon, the trochlear notch and the radial notch
The distal end includes the head and the styloid process
B, C and D are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The greater tubercle of the humerus is palpable laterally and contributes to the rounded contour of the shoulder.
questions.explain: The greater tubercle, situated laterally on the proximal humerus, is a palpable bony landmark that contributes to the lateral contour of the shoulder.

questions.q: The ilium contributes what fraction of the acetabulum?
questions.explain: The ilium, the largest and uppermost of the three hip bone components, contributes about two-fifths (2/5th) of the acetabulum.

questions.q: The side to which an ulna belongs can be determined from the following:
options: On the lateral side of the olecranon process is the radial notch
The styloid process is proximal and lateral to the olecranon process
The olecranon process and coronoid process are located at the proximal end
The head and the styloid process are separated by a deep concavity known as the trochlear notch
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which neck of the humerus joins the proximal end to the shaft, and is clinically significant because fractures here can injure the axillary nerve?
questions.explain: The surgical neck joins the proximal end of the humerus to the shaft. It is clinically important because the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels wrap around it closely and are vulnerable in fractures here.

questions.q: On which bone is the head found at the distal end?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The wing-like flared portion of the ilium is called the:
questions.explain: The flared, wing-shaped portion of the ilium is called the ala (Latin for 'wing'), which provides broad surface area for gluteal muscle attachment.

questions.q: Just below the head of the femur lies a small pit. What is this pit called and what attaches there?
options: The trochanteric fossa, for obturator externus
The fovea, for the ligament of the head of femur
The intertrochanteric crest, for quadratus femoris
The linea aspera, for adductor muscles
questions.explain: The fovea is a small pit just below and slightly posterior to the femoral head, marking the attachment of the ligament of the head of the femur (ligamentum teres).

questions.q: Which of the following bones is/are not weight bearing?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: During a pudendal nerve block performed to relieve perineal pain in childbirth, the nerve wraps around which structure before giving its branches?
questions.explain: The pudendal nerve curves around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament before dividing into its terminal branches, making this region the target for a pudendal nerve block.

questions.q: In the same mnemonic, which carpal bone is represented by the word "Peter"?
questions.explain: The proximal row from lateral to medial is Scaphoid (So), Lunate (Luke), Triquetrum (Took), Pisiform (Peter) — "Peter" corresponds to the pisiform.

questions.q: The proximal row of carpal bones includes which of the following?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: A fractured femoral neck can interrupt the blood supply to the head of the femur, risking avascular necrosis.
questions.explain: The blood supply to the femoral head largely depends on retinacular vessels running along the neck; a femoral neck fracture can disrupt this supply, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.q: The pubis is divided into a body and two rami. Which two rami are these?
questions.explain: The pubis is composed of a body plus a superior ramus and an inferior ramus, which together help form the obturator foramen and pubic arch.

questions.q: Which of these bones would bear a ring?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: According to the labels shown, how many cuneiform bones are present, and what are they called?
questions.explain: The diagram labels three cuneiform bones: the first (medial) cuneiform, second (intermediate) cuneiform, and third (lateral) cuneiform, sitting between the navicular and the metatarsals.

questions.q: Which two tubercles of the proximal humerus are separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove?
questions.explain: The greater tubercle (laterally) and lesser tubercle (anteriorly) are separated by the intertubercular groove (sulcus), through which the long head of biceps tendon runs.

questions.q: The ischium consists of a body and a ramus, and the free lower end of the body forms which prominent landmark?
questions.explain: The free lower end of the ischial body forms the ischial tuberosity, the bony prominence that bears the body's weight during sitting.

questions.q: The pubic tubercle, an important landmark in the lower abdominal wall, is located at the:
options: Upper medial part of the pubis
Lower lateral part of the pubis
questions.explain: The pubic tubercle lies at the lower lateral part of the pubic body and is a key surface landmark used to identify the superficial inguinal ring and to differentiate inguinal from femoral hernias.

questions.q: The subpubic (pubic) angle in females is generally:
questions.explain: Females typically have a broader pubic angle, greater than 100 degrees between the pubic bones, compared to the narrower angle in males.

questions.q: True or False: A Colles' fracture is a classic injury sustained after a fall onto an outstretched hand.
questions.explain: Colles' fracture of the distal radius is a very common injury resulting from a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH), particularly in older adults with osteoporotic bone.

questions.q: True or False: Elderly individuals are prone to fracturing the neck of the femur even after only a minor fall.
questions.explain: Due to age-related osteoporosis, elderly individuals are particularly susceptible to femoral neck fractures even from relatively minor falls.

questions.q: A fracture involving the surgical neck of the humerus would most likely affect which nerve?
questions.explain: The axillary nerve winds closely around the surgical neck of the humerus, making it the nerve most at risk in fractures at this site (in contrast to the radial nerve, which is at risk in mid-shaft fractures at the spiral groove).

questions.q: The carpal bones are arranged in two rows of four. Which carpal bone is unusual in having very few articular facets, unlike the rest?
questions.explain: Most carpal bones have several articular facets for neighbouring bones, but the pisiform is an exception, articulating mainly with the triquetrum and acting like a sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.

questions.q: True or False: The gynecoid pelvis shape is considered the type least favorable for vaginal childbirth.
questions.explain: The gynecoid pelvis is the classic rounded shape considered most favorable for vaginal delivery; the android and platypelloid types are generally considered less favorable.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the femur?
options: Lateral condyle, medial condyle and adductor tubercle
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: In females, the sacrum and coccyx show greater curvature, arcing further into the pelvic outlet compared to males.
questions.explain: It is the male sacrum and coccyx that arc more sharply into the pelvic outlet; the female sacrum and coccyx show LESS curvature, helping to enlarge the pelvic outlet for childbirth.

questions.q: Which labelled structure on this clavicle diagram corresponds to the costal tuberosity?
options: There is no costal tuberosity on the clavicle
The structure near the medial/sternal extremity, on the posterior aspect
The structure near the lateral/acromial extremity
The midpoint of the shaft anteriorly
questions.explain: The costal tuberosity sits near the medial (sternal) end on the posterior/inferior aspect of the clavicle and serves as the attachment for the costoclavicular ligament, anchoring the clavicle to the first rib.

questions.q: The lower end of the femur has two spirally curved condyles separated by which structure?
questions.explain: The two distal femoral condyles (medial and lateral) are separated posteriorly by the intercondylar fossa (notch), which provides attachment for the cruciate ligaments of the knee.

questions.q: The side to which a scapula belongs can be determined from the following:
options: The large concave surface is posterior
The acromion and glenoid cavity belong to the lower and lateral part of the scapula
The spine projects from the posterior surface and extends laterally as the acromion
Supraspinous and infraspinous fossae are located on the anterior surface
Coracoid process is located on the posterior surface
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: A pudendal nerve block reliably abolishes the pain of uterine contractions during labour.
questions.explain: Pudendal nerve blocks relieve perineal pain (useful for the second stage of labour and episiotomy) but do NOT relieve the pain of uterine contractions, nor do they completely abolish sensation from the anterior perineum.

questions.q: On this anterior and posterior view of the patella, the pointed inferior tip where the medial and lateral borders converge is the:
questions.explain: The apex of the patella is the pointed distal tip where the medial and lateral borders converge, located opposite the broader superior base.

questions.q: True or False: The upper limb is described as having four segments — the shoulder girdle, arm, forearm, and hand.
questions.explain: The upper limb is classically divided into the shoulder girdle, arm (brachium), forearm (antebrachium), and hand, giving it four functional segments.

questions.q: The oblique groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus, which transmits the radial nerve, is also called the:
questions.explain: The radial groove (spiral groove) runs obliquely across the posterior surface of the humeral shaft and houses the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels.

questions.q: "Stove-in-chest" is another name for which condition?
questions.explain: Flail chest, caused by multiple adjacent rib fractures in more than one place, is also called a stove-in-chest because the loose segment moves paradoxically with breathing.

questions.q: The styloid processes of the radius and ulna are normally separated by approximately how much, a fact used in diagnosing distal radius fractures?
options: They are normally at the exact same level
questions.explain: Normally, the radial and ulnar styloid processes are about 1 cm apart, with the radial styloid more distal; disruption of this relationship helps diagnose fractures of the distal radius.

questions.q: The lateral third of the clavicular shaft is described as flattened, while the medial two-thirds is described as:
questions.explain: The shaft's lateral third is flattened, whereas the medial two-thirds has a rounded, hammer-like cross-sectional shape.

questions.q: True or False: Hammer toe and claw toe both describe abnormalities in the alignment of toe joints, similar in concept to deformities seen in fingers.
questions.explain: Hammer toe and claw toe describe flexion deformities at the interphalangeal joints of the toes, conceptually paralleling deformities like boutonniere or swan-neck seen in the fingers, though the specific joints and mechanisms differ.

questions.q: On the radius, where is the radial tuberosity located relative to the neck?
options: Posterior and distal to the neck
Lateral and proximal to the head
Anterior and medial, distal to the neck
On the posterior border of the shaft
questions.explain: The radial tuberosity lies on the anteromedial aspect of the radius, just distal to the neck, marking the boundary between the upper end and the shaft, and serves as the insertion for biceps brachii.

questions.q: The shaft of the radius has anterior, posterior, and lateral surfaces, along with anterior, posterior, and which other border?
questions.explain: The radial shaft has three borders: anterior, posterior, and an interosseous border, the last of which gives attachment to the interosseous membrane (except near its proximal-most part).

questions.q: True or False: The transverse arch of the foot runs from the heel to the toes, while the longitudinal arches run side to side.
questions.explain: This is reversed: the longitudinal arches (medial and lateral) run from front to back (heel to toes), while the transverse arch runs side to side across the foot.

questions.q: The bones of the hand are grouped into carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges. How many bones are in each group respectively?
questions.explain: The hand has 8 carpal bones (wrist), 5 metacarpals (palm), and 14 phalanges (fingers), totalling 27 bones.

questions.q: Using the mnemonic "So Luke Took Peter To The Church Hall" for the carpal bones from lateral to medial (proximal then distal row), which bone does "Church" represent?
questions.explain: In the mnemonic, the distal row from lateral to medial is Trapezium (To), Trapezoid (The), Capitate (Church), Hamate (Hall) — so "Church" stands for the capitate bone.

questions.q: How many bones make up the entire upper limb (one side), according to the standard count of arm, forearm, and hand bones?
questions.explain: The upper limb has 30 bones: humerus (1), radius and ulna (2), and the hand with carpals (8), metacarpals (5), and phalanges (14) = 1+2+8+5+14 = 30.

questions.q: The bone(s) of the leg which bears no weight is/are
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: On this inferior view of the clavicle, the structure that anchors the trapezoid ligament is the:
questions.explain: The trapezoid line on the inferior surface of the clavicle's shaft is the attachment site for the trapezoid ligament, working alongside the conoid tubercle (for the conoid ligament) to anchor the coracoclavicular ligament complex.

questions.q: A fall onto the shoulder classically fractures the clavicle at which location?
options: The midpoint of the lateral third
The junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third
questions.explain: The clavicle most commonly fractures at the junction between its medial two-thirds and lateral one-third, a relatively weak transition point, after a fall onto the shoulder.

questions.q: In this labelled diagram of the hand, the carpal bone bearing a hook-shaped process (used as a landmark for Guyon's canal) is the:
questions.explain: The hamate, shown with its characteristic hook in the diagram, is the carpal bone whose hook of hamate forms a key landmark for structures passing through Guyon's canal.

questions.q: The scapula articulates with the humerus at which feature?
questions.explain: The glenoid fossa (glenoid cavity), located on the lateral angle of the scapula, is the shallow socket that articulates with the head of the humerus to form the glenohumeral joint.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the femur?
options: Lateral condyle, medial condyle and adductor tubercle
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The inferior angle of the scapula is formed at the junction of the medial and lateral borders.
questions.explain: The inferior angle marks the meeting point of the medial and lateral borders of the scapular body at the lowest point of the bone.

questions.q: True or False: Both the clavicle and the femur can be used to estimate a person's stature because their length correlates with overall body height.
questions.explain: While the femur is most classically used for stature estimation (1/4 to 1/3 of body height), long bone length generally correlates with stature, and forensic methods may also use other long bones including the humerus or, in some methods, account for the clavicle, though the femur remains the gold standard.

questions.q: In this labelled pelvis specimen photo, the prominent bony point inferiorly on which a person bears weight while sitting (marked D) is the:
questions.explain: The bony landmark at the inferior aspect of the ischium that bears weight during sitting is the ischial tuberosity, consistent with its description elsewhere in the material as the structure on which body weight rests when seated.

questions.q: Which of the bones below is the first to ossify in pregnancy?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Inflammation of the bursa covering the ischial tuberosity is termed:
questions.explain: The ischial tuberosity is covered by a bursa that, when inflamed (often from prolonged sitting), causes ischial bursitis.

questions.q: The obturator foramen is bounded by which three structures?
questions.explain: The obturator foramen is bounded by the pubis, the ischium, and their respective rami, and is closed by the obturator membrane except at the obturator groove/canal.

questions.q: On the lower part of the anterior surface of the radial shaft, a roughened oblique line marks the:
questions.explain: The pronator ridge is a rough, obliquely placed line on the lower anterior surface of the radius, providing attachment for part of pronator quadratus.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the tibia:
options: Intercondylar eminence, fibular notch and tibial tuberosity
Medial condyle, lateral condyle and tibial tuberosity
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: At puberty, the three hip bone components are separated by a characteristically shaped cartilage. What shape is this cartilage?
questions.explain: At puberty, a Y-shaped (triradiate) cartilage still separates the ilium, ischium, and pubis at the acetabulum before final fusion occurs.

questions.q: In the same diagram, the oval opening labelled D/E region in the lower part of the hip bone, bounded by pubis and ischium, represents the:
questions.explain: The large oval opening in the lower hip bone, bounded by the pubis and ischium and their rami, is the obturator foramen, normally closed by the obturator membrane.

questions.q: Sexual differences in the human skeleton
options: The mandible is larger and more robust in the female
The sacrum is a long narrow triangle with a less pronounced sacral curvature in the female
Male bones are heavier with prominent bone markings
The male pelvis is broader with a heart-shaped inlet and relatively deep than the female pelvis
The female cranium is about 10% larger on the average
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which scapular angle is formed at the junction of the lateral and superior borders?
questions.explain: The lateral angle is the junction of the lateral and superior borders, and is thickened to form the head of the scapula bearing the glenoid cavity.

questions.q: The pectoral girdle is composed of the
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Where is the articular circumference of the proximal radius widest, and why?
options: It has uniform width all around
Laterally, where it meets the capitulum
Medially, where it articulates with the ulna
questions.explain: The articular circumference of the radial head is widest medially, the side that articulates with the radial notch of the ulna, allowing pronation and supination.

questions.q: Which one of these bones is not found in the pelvis?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: On the posterior view shown, which labelled bony projection of the ulna fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus during full elbow extension?
questions.explain: The olecranon, the prominent posterior projection of the proximal ulna, lodges in the olecranon fossa of the humerus when the elbow is fully extended.

questions.q: The clavicle is the only bony link between which two structures?
options: The scapula and the vertebral column
The axial skeleton and the pectoral appendicular skeleton
The manubrium and the first rib
questions.explain: The clavicle extends from the manubrium of the sternum to the acromion of the scapula, forming the only bony connection between the axial skeleton and the pectoral (shoulder) girdle of the appendicular skeleton.

questions.q: In this anterior/posterior view of the shoulder, the joint formed between the acromion and the clavicle is labelled as the:
questions.explain: The diagram labels the joint between the acromion of the scapula and the lateral end of the clavicle as the acromioclavicular joint, distinct from the glenohumeral joint (shoulder joint proper) and sternoclavicular joint (medial clavicle to sternum).

questions.q: If the distal fragment in a distal radius fracture is displaced anteriorly instead of posteriorly, the injury is termed:
questions.explain: Anterior displacement of the distal fragment, opposite to the classic Colles' pattern, is termed a reverse Colles' fracture, also known as a Smith's fracture.

questions.q: According to the labels in this image, which structure sits directly between the lateral malleolus and medial malleolus distally, marking the ankle joint region?
questions.explain: The talus is shown positioned between the medial malleolus (of the tibia) and lateral malleolus (of the fibula), forming the body of the ankle joint (talocrural joint) mortise.

questions.q: Which of the following bones does not articulate directly with any other bone in the skeleton?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: On this surface anatomy image of the wrist, the small bone palpable on the medial side, embedded in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris, is labelled as the:
questions.explain: The image identifies the pisiform bone (with palmaris brevis) as a palpable landmark on the medial wrist, adjacent to the head of the ulna.

questions.q: Which part of the vertebral column receives the most stress by bearing most of the weight of the body?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The femur:
options: Is the longest and heaviest bone of the body.
In the standing position the femur transmits weight from the hip bone to the tibia
The upper end consists of a head, a neck, greater tubercle and a lesser tubercle
The lower end consists of two condyles and two trochanters
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Based on the labelling shown, the small rounded bones near the base of the thumb (metacarpal I) labelled separately from the carpal row are the:
questions.explain: The diagram identifies small sesamoid bones near the thumb's metacarpophalangeal joint, which are embedded within tendons rather than forming part of the regular carpal row.

questions.q: The superior portion of the sternum is the
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: On the costal (anterior) surface of the scapular body, the shallow concavity is called the:
questions.explain: The costal surface of the scapular body is concave, forming the subscapular fossa, which gives origin to the subscapularis muscle.

questions.q: Proximally, the ulna articulates with the humerus and, more distally, it also relates to which structures?
options: The articular disc below and the radius laterally
The carpals directly and the humerus laterally
Only the radius, with no distal articulation
questions.explain: The ulna articulates with the humerus proximally, and distally relates to an articular disc (of the wrist) below and the radius laterally via the distal radioulnar joint.

questions.q: The anterior fontanelle closes during the second year of life and is then known as the:
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: To correctly orient an isolated hip bone, the obturator foramen should be positioned posteriorly and pointing upward.
questions.explain: To orient a hip bone correctly, the obturator foramen should face anteriorly and is positioned inferiorly (below and in front), not posteriorly or upward.

questions.q: The antebrachium is composed of which of the following two bones?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Joints are classified functionally according to which criterion?
options: The blood supply to the joint
The amount of movement permitted at the joint
The number of bones meeting at the joint
The embryological origin of the bones
questions.explain: The functional classification of joints is based purely on the amount of movement allowed at the joint, giving the categories synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis, and diarthrosis.

questions.q: BIAXIAL JOINT
options: An example is the metacarpophalangeal joint
An example is the wrist joint
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a synarthrotic joint?
questions.explain: Sutures of the skull are classic synarthroses (immovable joints). The pubic symphysis is an amphiarthrosis, the knee is a freely movable diarthrosis, and a syndesmosis is generally classified as amphiarthrotic.

questions.q: A slightly movable joint is functionally termed:
questions.explain: Amphiarthrosis describes a slightly movable joint, with the symphysis and syndesmosis given as examples in the lecture.

questions.q: SYNOVIAL JOINTS possess
options: Hyaline cartilage at the ends of the opposing bones
Hyaline cartilage that absorbs compressive forces
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Structurally, joints are classified based on what feature?
options: The shape of the surrounding muscles
What separates or binds the articulating bones
questions.explain: Structural classification of joints depends on what separates or binds the articulating bones — fibers, cartilage, or a joint cavity — giving fibrous, cartilaginous, and synovial categories.

questions.q: An autoimmune disorder in which joints are affected bilaterally and which involves pannus formation and gradual joint immobilization is
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: All synovial joints have the following structural characteristics
options: The inner layer is the synovial membrane
The outer layer is the fibrous capsule
Articular cartilage covers the surfaces of the bones forming the joint
The joint surfaces are enclosed by a two-layered articular capsule
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A synostosis occurs when:
options: Two bones fuse and the boundary between them disappears
questions.explain: Synostosis is a bony joint where two bones fuse together such that the original boundary between them is lost.

questions.q: Which fibrous joint is found exclusively in the skull, held by short interconnecting fibers with interlocking bone edges?
questions.explain: A suture is held together by very short interconnecting fibers with interlocking bone edges, and it is found only in the skull.

questions.q: Which fibrous joint binds bones using a sheet (interosseous membrane) or bundle (interosseous ligament) of dense connective tissue?
questions.explain: A syndesmosis binds bones via an interosseous membrane or interosseous ligament, as seen between the tibia and fibula.

questions.q: A BALL AND SOCKET JOINT
options: The spherical head of one bone fits into a round socket in another
Permits universal movement in all axes including rotation
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Bones united by hyaline cartilage, such as the epiphyseal plate, describe which type of joint?
questions.explain: Synchondroses are primary cartilaginous joints in which bones are united by hyaline cartilage, with the epiphyseal plate as a key example.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an example of a synchondrosis?
questions.explain: The first sternocostal joint (between the first rib and the sternum) is cited as a synchondrosis, alongside epiphyseal plates and the costochondral joint.

questions.q: Most synchondroses are permanent structures that persist throughout adult life.
questions.explain: False. Most synchondroses are temporary structures that disappear during growth, such as the articulation between the diaphysis and epiphysis.

questions.q: Secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses) are united by which tissue?
questions.explain: Symphyses are secondary cartilaginous joints in which the bones are united by fibrocartilage, e.g., the pubic symphysis and intervertebral joints.

questions.q: Which of the following is a classic example of a symphysis?
questions.explain: The pubic symphysis is the prototypical secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), uniting the two pubic bones via fibrocartilage.

questions.q: In synovial joints, what covers the ends of the opposing bones and acts as a shock absorber?
questions.explain: Articular cartilage covers the ends of opposing bones, decreases in thickness with age, and functions as a shock absorber that also reduces friction.

questions.q: Which layer of the articular capsule is composed of dense irregular connective tissue and strengthens the joint?
questions.explain: The outer fibrous capsule consists of dense irregular connective tissue and provides strength to the joint.

questions.q: Which of the following are responsible for nodding ‘yes’ and for shaking your head ‘no’?
options: Occipital condyles and odontoid process respectively
Odontoid process and occipital condyles respectively
Occipital condyles and odontoid process of atlas respectively
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Synovial fluid contains phagocytes that remove microbes and cellular debris from the joint cavity.
questions.explain: True. Synovial fluid contains phagocytic cells that clear microbes and debris, in addition to lubricating and nourishing the joint.

questions.q: According to the lecture, synovial fluid prevents separation of bone ends much like:
options: A little water between two glass surfaces
questions.explain: The lecture compares synovial fluid's cohesive effect to a little water between two glass surfaces, which resists separation of the surfaces.

questions.q: Which accessory structures are associated with synovial joints?
options: Fat pads, menisci, ligaments, bursae, tendons
questions.explain: Accessory structures of synovial joints include fat pads, menisci, ligaments, bursae, and tendons.

questions.q: An elongated bursa that wraps around a tendon subjected to friction is termed a:
questions.explain: A tendon sheath is an elongated bursa that wraps around tendons of certain muscles, occurring only where tendons are subjected to friction.

questions.q: Synovial joints are classified according to the shape of the articulating surfaces and the type of movement they permit. Which of these is a uniaxial joint type?
questions.explain: Hinge (ginglymus) joints are uniaxial, permitting movement (flexion/extension) in a single plane only, e.g., the elbow and knee.

questions.q: A plane joint, formed when two flat surfaces meet, characteristically allows which type of movement?
questions.explain: Plane joints are formed by two flat articulating surfaces and allow gliding or sliding movements, e.g., intertarsal and intercarpal joints.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a plane joint?
questions.explain: The acromioclavicular joint is listed as a plane joint, alongside intertarsal, intercarpal, and 2nd–7th sternocostal joints.

questions.q: Pivot joint
options: Joint in which the rounded end of one bone fits into a ring formed by another bone
A, B, and C are all correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which joint is formed when a round surface fits into a ring created by a ligament and a depression in another bone?
questions.explain: A pivot (trochoid) joint is formed in exactly this manner; the atlanto-axial joint is a classic example, allowing rotation of the head.

questions.q: Saddle joints, where concave and convex surfaces meet at right angles, allow which category of movement?
questions.explain: Saddle joints are biaxial, permitting flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and circumduction, as seen at the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb.

questions.q: Which joint allows opposition of the thumb?
questions.explain: The first carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is a saddle joint that uniquely allows the movement of opposition.

questions.q: A condyloid (ellipsoid) joint is formed when a convex oval surface fits into an elliptical concavity. Which movement is NOT typically permitted at this joint?
questions.explain: Condyloid joints are biaxial and allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and slight circumduction, but they do not permit axial rotation.

questions.q: NONAXIAL JOINTS
options: Does not involve rotation around any axis
Is found between articular processes of vertebrae and between tarsal bones
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: MULTIAXIAL JOINT
options: Universal movement is allowed in all axes
Rotation is allowed in all axes
An example is the shoulder joint
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of these joint pairs are BOTH classic examples of ball-and-socket joints?
questions.explain: The shoulder (glenohumeral) and hip joints are the two principal ball-and-socket joints highlighted in the lecture.

questions.q: The joint formed at the carpometacarpal joint of the pollex (thumb) is a typical example of which joint type?
questions.explain: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the textbook example of a saddle joint, allowing the unique movement of opposition.

questions.q: UNIAXIAL JOINTS
options: An example is the ankle joint
An example is the Interphalangeal joint
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Rheumatism is best defined as:
options: A type of synovial fluid abnormality
Any painful disorder of supporting structures not caused by infection or injury
A fracture of the epiphyseal plate
questions.explain: Rheumatism is defined as any painful disorder of the body's supporting structures that is NOT due to infection or injury.

questions.q: Which two carpals articulate with the radius to form the wrist joint?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which two types of arthritis are described as the most common?
questions.explain: The lecture identifies rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis as the most common types of arthritis.

questions.q: Which factor does NOT directly influence the stability of a synovial joint, according to the lecture?
questions.explain: Stability depends on articular surface shape, ligament number/position, and muscle tone — blood type has no role in joint stability.

questions.q: Muscle tone, important for maintaining posture, is best defined as:
options: Tension present in a relaxed muscle
The size of a muscle belly
questions.explain: Muscle tone refers to the baseline tension present in a relaxed muscle, which is important for joint stability and posture.

questions.q: A joint injury involving tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule is termed a/an:
questions.explain: A sprain is a joint injury involving tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule, whereas a strain involves muscle or tendon injury.

questions.q: What does the acronym RICE, used in management of soft tissue joint injuries, stand for?
questions.explain: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation — the standard immediate management for soft tissue joint injuries.

questions.q: The stability of a joint depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Tone of muscles around the joint
Synovial membrane and fluid in the joint
Shape and size of articular surfaces
questions.explain: While synovial membrane and fluid lubricate and nourish the joint, the lecture identifies articular surface shape/arrangement, muscle tone, and ligaments as the key determinants of joint stability — not the synovial membrane/fluid.

questions.q: What distinguishes dislocation from subluxation?
options: Dislocation is a complete loss of articular surface contact, while subluxation is a partial loss
questions.explain: A dislocation (luxation) is a complete displacement of articulating bone surfaces from one another, while subluxation is only a partial displacement.

questions.q: The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is best described functionally as:
options: The least movable but most stable joint
questions.explain: The shoulder joint is highly movable but is also the least stable major joint of the body, owing to its shallow socket.

questions.q: Ankylosis means
options: Immobility of a joint due to fusion of the articular surfaces
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The prominent bump on the lateral aspect of the leg at the ankle joint is the
options: A lateral extension of the tibia
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which structure deepens the glenoid cavity to improve shoulder joint stability?
questions.explain: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous ring that deepens the shallow glenoid cavity, improving the fit of the humeral head.

questions.q: Which muscle of the rotator cuff is described as the strongest?
questions.explain: Among the rotator cuff muscles (subscapularis, teres minor, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus), the supraspinatus is described as the strongest.

questions.q: Which structure forms the coracoacromial arch that prevents superior (upward) displacement of the humeral head?
options: Coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament
questions.explain: The coracoacromial arch is formed by the coracoid process, the acromion, and the coracoacromial ligament, and it blocks superior displacement of the humeral head.

questions.q: Shoulder dislocation most commonly displaces the humeral head in which direction relative to the infraglenoid tubercle?
questions.explain: Anterior dislocation accounts for about 95% of shoulder dislocations, making it by far the most common direction, although the overall displacement is described as downward (inferior).

questions.q: Injury to the axillary nerve following shoulder dislocation can cause paralysis of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the 'regimental badge' area.
questions.explain: True. The axillary nerve is vulnerable in shoulder dislocation, and its injury classically produces deltoid paralysis and sensory loss over the regimental badge area of the lateral shoulder.

questions.q: Which nerve can be stretched and damaged by downward displacement of the humerus in shoulder dislocation, in addition to the axillary nerve?
questions.explain: The lecture notes that downward displacement of the humerus can stretch and damage the radial nerve, in addition to the axillary nerve.

questions.q: The elbow joint is composed of how many distinct articulations?
questions.explain: The elbow joint comprises three distinct articulations: humero-ulnar, humeroradial, and superior radio-ulnar.

questions.q: Which articulation of the elbow is classified as a hinge joint?
questions.explain: The humero-ulnar articulation, between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna, is a hinge joint.

questions.q: At the superior radio-ulnar joint, the head of the radius is held in place by which ligament?
questions.explain: The tough annular (orbicular) ligament holds the head of the radius in place at the superior radio-ulnar joint, classified as a pivot joint.

questions.q: Which band of the medial collateral ligament of the elbow is considered the main stabilizer against valgus stress?
questions.explain: The anterior oblique band of the medial collateral ligament is the main stabilizer of the elbow, protecting against excessive valgus forces and internal rotation stress.

questions.q: Within the lateral collateral ligament complex of the elbow, which component is described as the main stabilizer?
questions.explain: The lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) is described as the main stabilizer of the lateral elbow, protecting against varus force.

questions.q: In orthopaedic terminology, when the distal part of a bone deviates more laterally than normal, this angulation is called:
questions.explain: Valgus describes angulation where the distal part is positioned more laterally than it should be.

questions.q: When the distal part of a bone deviates more medially than normal at a joint, this is termed:
questions.explain: Varus describes angulation where the distal part is positioned more medially than it should be.

questions.q: Which bursa of the elbow is implicated in 'student's elbow' or 'miner's elbow'?
questions.explain: The subcutaneous (olecranon) bursa, located between the olecranon and overlying connective tissue, is implicated in olecranon bursitis, also called student's or miner's elbow.

questions.q: Most elbow dislocations occur in which direction, named by the position of the ulna and radius?
questions.explain: Elbow dislocations are mostly posterior, and are named according to the position of the ulna and radius relative to the humerus, not the humerus itself.

questions.q: The carrying angle of the elbow is the acute angle between the median axes of the arm and forearm, measured in which position?
questions.explain: The carrying angle is measured with the elbow in full extension and the forearm supinated, and it allows the forearm to clear the hips during walking.

questions.q: Junctional complexes are located on the:
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A supracondylar fracture of the humerus, typically from a fall onto an outstretched hand, can result in uncontrolled flexion of the hand due to fibrosis of flexor muscles. This complication is called:
questions.explain: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is the complication of uncontrolled hand flexion arising from fibrotic, shortened flexor muscles following a supracondylar fracture with vascular compromise.

questions.q: 'Nursemaid's elbow' refers to which condition?
options: Radial head subluxation pulled out of the annular ligament
questions.explain: Nursemaid's elbow (radial head subluxation) occurs when the radial head is traumatically pulled out of its normal position within the annular ligament, common in young children pulled by the arm.

questions.q: The hip joint articulates between the head of the femur and which structure?
questions.explain: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the hip bone.

questions.q: What fibrocartilaginous structure deepens the acetabulum in the hip joint?
questions.explain: The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous collar that deepens the acetabulum, improving congruency with the femoral head.

questions.q: The ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur) runs from the acetabular fossa to which structure?
questions.explain: The ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres) passes from the acetabular fossa to the fovea on the femoral head, enclosing a branch of the obturator artery.

questions.q: Rupture of the ligament of the head of femur can damage its accompanying artery and lead to which complication?
questions.explain: The ligamentum teres encloses a branch of the obturator artery, and rupture of the ligament can damage this artery, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.q: Which extracapsular ligament of the hip joint is described as the strongest ligament in the body?
questions.explain: The iliofemoral ligament (of Bigelow), which is Y-shaped or an inverted V, is described as the strongest ligament in the body and prevents hyperextension of the hip when standing.

questions.q: Which hip ligament spans from the superior pubic rami to the intertrochanteric line, preventing excessive abduction and extension?
questions.explain: The pubofemoral ligament has a triangular shape and reinforces the capsule anteriorly and inferiorly, preventing excessive abduction and extension.

questions.q: Which extracapsular hip ligament is described as the weakest of the three, reinforcing the capsule posteriorly?
questions.explain: The ischiofemoral ligament, running from the body of the ischium to the greater trochanter, is the weakest of the three main hip ligaments and reinforces the capsule posteriorly.

questions.q: Which nerve, in addition to the sciatic, supplies the hip joint and also the skin of the front and medial sides of the thigh, explaining referred thigh pain in hip disease?
questions.explain: The femoral nerve supplies both the hip joint and the skin of the anterior and medial thigh, which is why hip joint pathology can refer pain to those regions.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, explaining why hip disease can cause referred pain in the knee?
questions.explain: The obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, which explains why hip joint disease sometimes presents with referred pain felt in the knee.

questions.q: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) occurs due to:
options: A shallow acetabulum from failure to develop properly in utero
Premature fusion of the epiphyseal plate
questions.explain: DDH occurs when the acetabulum is shallow as a result of failure to develop properly in utero, leading to instability or dislocation of the hip.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common clinical feature of developmental dysplasia of the hip?
options: Limb length discrepancy with the affected limb shorter
Increased range of abduction at the hip
questions.explain: Common features of DDH include limited abduction, limb length discrepancy (affected limb shorter), and asymmetrical gluteal or thigh skin folds.

questions.q: DDH is typically treated using which device?
questions.explain: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is usually treated with a Pavlik harness, which holds the hips in a flexed and abducted position.

questions.q: Acquired hip dislocation is most commonly seen in which direction, and is associated with risk to which nerve?
questions.explain: Posterior dislocation accounts for about 90% of acquired hip dislocations, since the joint is least stable when flexed and adducted, and this may injure the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: The patella:
options: Is a sesamoid bone that articulates with the femur, tibia and fibula
Has an apex that is directed superiorly and a base that is inferior
Enclosed in the tendon that secures the anterior thigh muscles to the tibia
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The knee joint consists of two articulations enclosed within a single joint cavity. These are the tibiofemoral and:
questions.explain: The knee joint consists of the tibiofemoral (a condylar joint) and patellofemoral (a saddle joint) articulations, both enclosed within a single joint cavity.

questions.q: Clinically, the articular surfaces of the medial and lateral condyles of the tibia are often referred to as:
questions.explain: The medial and lateral condyles of the tibia are clinically referred to as the medial and lateral tibial plateaus.

questions.q: Which collateral ligament of the knee is thicker, stronger, and attached to the medial meniscus, so that injury to it may also injure the meniscus?
questions.explain: The tibial (medial) collateral ligament is thicker and stronger than the fibular collateral, and because it attaches to the medial meniscus, injury to it may involve the meniscus too.

questions.q: The tibial (medial) collateral ligament resists which type of deforming force?
questions.explain: The tibial (medial) collateral ligament limits extension and abduction of the leg, resisting valgus-producing (outward bending) forces.

questions.q: The fibular (lateral) collateral ligament of the knee resists which type of force?
questions.explain: The fibular (lateral) collateral ligament limits extension and adduction of the leg, resisting varus-producing (inward bending) forces.

questions.q: Which cruciate ligament of the knee is described as weaker and more commonly injured?
questions.explain: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is weaker and more commonly injured than the posterior cruciate ligament, and it blends with the medial meniscus.

questions.q: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), being stronger, shorter, and broader than the ACL, primarily limits which movement?
options: Knee hyperflexion and posterior tibial dislocation
questions.explain: The PCL limits knee hyperflexion and prevents posterior dislocation of the tibia relative to the femur.

questions.q: The anterior cruciate ligament primarily functions to:
options: Limit knee hyperextension and prevent anterior tibial dislocation
questions.explain: The ACL limits knee hyperextension and prevents anterior dislocation of the tibia on the femur.

questions.q: The knee menisci primarily function to deepen the articular surface of the tibial condyles and:
options: Increase stability and act as shock absorbers
Replace the need for collateral ligaments
questions.explain: Menisci deepen the articular surface of the tibial condyles, increasing joint stability, and act as shock absorbers by increasing surface area to dissipate forces.

questions.q: Which meniscus of the knee is described as almost a semicircle (C-shaped), relatively immobile, and more likely to be damaged?
options: Neither — menisci are not classified this way
questions.explain: The medial meniscus is C-shaped, broader posteriorly, attached to the medial collateral ligament and joint capsule, making it relatively immobile and more prone to damage.

questions.q: The lateral meniscus of the knee is approximately what fraction of a circle, and how does its mobility compare to the medial meniscus?
options: 4/5 of a circle; smaller and more mobile
questions.explain: The lateral meniscus is about 4/5 of a circle and is smaller and more mobile than the medial meniscus.

questions.q: Prepatellar bursitis is also commonly known as:
questions.explain: Prepatellar bursitis, caused by inflammation and swelling of the prepatellar bursa, is commonly called housemaid's knee.

questions.q: Infrapatellar bursitis (superficial) is commonly known as:
questions.explain: Infrapatellar bursitis is commonly called clergyman's knee, reflecting the kneeling posture historically associated with the condition.

questions.q: A cleaning staff member at the anatomy department developed housemaid's knee due to irritation. Which bursa is most likely involved?
questions.explain: Housemaid's knee specifically involves the prepatellar (subcutaneous) bursa, resulting from prolonged kneeling and friction over the front of the knee.

questions.q: A footballer was kicked on the lateral side of the knee while standing on that leg, and MRI revealed a torn tibial collateral ligament. Which other structure is most likely also injured?
questions.explain: Because the tibial (medial) collateral ligament is attached to the medial meniscus, injury to the MCL from a lateral blow (valgus force) commonly also involves the medial meniscus.

questions.q: At the knee, lateral and medial rotation can only occur when the knee is in which position?
questions.explain: Medial and lateral rotation at the knee can only occur when the knee is flexed; if the knee is extended, such rotation occurs instead at the hip joint.

questions.q: Which structure on the tibia prevents sideways displacement of the femur on the tibia, contributing to knee stability?
questions.explain: The intercondylar eminence of the tibia helps prevent sideways slipping of the femur on the tibia, contributing to overall knee stability.

questions.q: The anterior drawer sign is used to assess injury to which ligament?
questions.explain: The anterior drawer sign tests for ACL tear, where hyperextension with anterior force on the tibia (partly flexed knee) produces excessive anterior tibial translation.

questions.q: The posterior drawer sign, classically caused by a 'dashboard injury,' assesses tearing of which ligament?
questions.explain: The posterior drawer sign tests for PCL tear, occurring when a large force is applied to the shins of a flexed knee, pushing the tibia posteriorly — classically in dashboard injuries.

questions.q: The 'unhappy (terrible) triad' of knee injuries involves the ACL, medial meniscus, and which other structure?
questions.explain: The unhappy triad involves the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial meniscus, and the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, common in contact sports with lateral knee blows.

questions.q: An increased Q-angle is considered a risk factor for several knee disorders. Which group typically has a greater Q-angle, owing to wider pelves?
questions.explain: The Q-angle is greater in adult females than males, owing to females generally having wider pelves.

questions.q: The ankle (talocrural) joint is formed by the articulation of the malleoli, the inferior articular surface of the tibia, and which bone?
questions.explain: The talocrural (ankle) joint is formed by the articulation of the malleoli, the inferior surface of the tibia, and the talus.

questions.q: Movements of inversion and eversion of the foot take place primarily at which joints, NOT at the ankle joint itself?
questions.explain: The lecture specifically notes that inversion and eversion occur at the tarsal joints, not at the ankle (talocrural) joint, which itself permits dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.

questions.q: The ankle joint is most stable in which position and least stable in which other position?
options: Stable in inversion; unstable in eversion
Stable in dorsiflexion; unstable in plantarflexion
Stable in plantarflexion; unstable in dorsiflexion
questions.explain: The ankle joint is stable in dorsiflexion and unstable in plantarflexion, since the wider anterior part of the talus fits snugly into the mortise during dorsiflexion.

questions.q: The prominent bony knobs on each side of the ankle joint are
options: The medial malleolus of the fibula and the lateral malleolus of the tibia
The epicondyles of the tibia and fibula
The styloid processes of the tibia and fibula
The medial malleolus of the tibia and the lateral malleolus of the fibula
The head of the fibula and the tuberosity of the tibia
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The deep and superficial parts of the medial (deltoid) ligament primarily resist which movement of the foot?
questions.explain: The deltoid ligament resists over-eversion of the foot. Because it is the stronger ligament, one is more likely to forcibly invert the ankle (sprain) than evert it.

questions.q: Which ligament of the ankle is weaker than its counterpart and thus more commonly damaged in ankle sprains?
questions.explain: The lateral ligament of the ankle is weaker than the medial (deltoid) ligament, making it more susceptible to damage in ankle sprains, particularly from forced inversion.

questions.q: Which component of the lateral ankle ligament is described as the weakest, making it the most commonly injured?
questions.explain: The anterior talofibular part of the lateral ligament is the weakest component, followed by the calcaneofibular ligament, making it the most frequently injured in ankle sprains.

questions.q: Which test is used clinically to assess ankle ligament integrity by evaluating forced inversion?
questions.explain: The talar tilt test, also called the inversion stress test, evaluates the integrity of the lateral ankle ligaments under forced inversion.

questions.q: Pott's fracture of the ankle, caused by forced eversion of the foot, typically involves which malleoli?
questions.explain: Pott's fracture involves a bimalleolar (medial and lateral malleoli) or trimalleolar (medial and lateral malleoli plus distal tibia) fracture pattern, resulting from forced eversion of the foot.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the 'ankle ring' concept described in the lecture?
options: A ring, when broken, usually breaks in two places
The ankle joint has no ligamentous support
The talus can dislocate without bony injury
The ankle mortise behaves like a flexible band that never fractures
questions.explain: The 'ankle ring' analogy describes how the bony-ligamentous ring of the ankle, like any ring, usually breaks (fractures) in two places when subjected to significant force, as seen in Pott's fracture.

questions.q: The annular ligament of the elbow attaches the radius firmly so it cannot rotate within it during pronation and supination.
questions.explain: False. The annular ligament holds the head of the radius in place against the radial notch of the ulna while still permitting the radial head to rotate within it, enabling pronation and supination.

questions.q: The subscapular bursae communicate with the shoulder joint cavity.
questions.explain: True. The lecture states that the subscapular bursae communicate with the shoulder joint, which has clinical relevance for joint effusions and bursal pathology.

questions.q: The suprapatellar and semimembranosus bursae of the knee can become distended if excess synovial fluid accumulates within the joint, because they communicate with the joint cavity.
questions.explain: True. Both the suprapatellar and semimembranosus bursae communicate with the knee joint and may distend when synovial fluid accumulates excessively.

questions.q: SYNOVIAL JOINTS
options: Have a fibrous capsule of dense irregular connective tissue
Have a synovial membrane of loose connective tissue
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: FIBROUS JOINT
options: The bones are connected by dense regular connective tissue
A, B and C are correct
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The shoulder joint capsule's laxity, combined with the disproportion between the shallow glenoid cavity and the large humeral head, contributes to its wide range of motion but reduced stability.
questions.explain: True. A roughly 1:4 disproportion between the glenoid surface and humeral head, plus capsular laxity, gives the shoulder excellent mobility at the cost of stability.

questions.q: The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperflexion of the hip joint.
questions.explain: False. The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperextension of the hip joint when standing, not hyperflexion.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The shoulder joint is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body.
Reason (R): The shallow glenoid fossa combined with a relatively large humeral head and a lax joint capsule favors mobility over stability.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
questions.explain: Both statements are true, and the anatomical mismatch between the shallow glenoid fossa and the large humeral head, together with capsular laxity, directly explains why the shoulder sacrifices stability for mobility and dislocates so frequently.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): All synovial joints are functionally classified as diarthroses.
Reason (R): Diarthroses are freely movable joints, and synovial joints possess a joint cavity that permits free movement.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
A is true but R is false
questions.explain: Both statements are true. The presence of a synovial (joint) cavity is precisely what allows synovial joints to move freely, which is why they are universally classified as diarthroses.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the tibia:
options: Medial condyle, lateral condyle and tibial tuberosity
Intercondylar eminence, fibular notch and tibial tuberosity
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A suture is classified as an amphiarthrosis.
Reason (R): A suture is found only in the skull and is held by short interconnecting fibers with interlocking bone edges.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
A is true but R is false
questions.explain: The Reason is true (it correctly describes a suture), but the Assertion is false — a suture is classified as a synarthrosis (immovable joint), not an amphiarthrosis.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rupture of the ligament of the head of femur can result in avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Reason (R): The ligamentum teres encloses a branch of the obturator artery that supplies part of the femoral head.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
questions.explain: Both statements are true, and the Reason directly explains the Assertion: damage to the artery enclosed within the ligamentum teres compromises blood supply to the femoral head, leading to avascular necrosis.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The anterior cruciate ligament is more commonly injured than the posterior cruciate ligament.
Reason (R): The ACL is weaker than the PCL.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are true: the lecture states the ACL is weaker and more commonly injured than the stronger, broader PCL, with the relative weakness directly contributing to its higher injury rate.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The ankle is more commonly sprained by forced eversion than by forced inversion.
Reason (R): The lateral ligament of the ankle is weaker than the medial (deltoid) ligament.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
questions.explain: The Reason is true (the lateral ligament is indeed weaker), but the Assertion is false — because the lateral ligament is weaker, the ankle is actually more commonly sprained by forced inversion, not eversion.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Synovial fluid contributes to the nutrition of articular cartilage.
Reason (R): Articular cartilage is avascular and relies on diffusion from synovial fluid for nourishment.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
questions.explain: Both statements are true. Because articular cartilage lacks its own blood supply, it depends on diffusion of nutrients from the surrounding synovial fluid, directly explaining the Assertion.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Hip joint pathology may sometimes present clinically as knee pain.
Reason (R): The obturator nerve supplies sensory branches to both the hip and the knee joints.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are true, and shared innervation by the obturator nerve across both joints directly explains why hip disease can refer pain to the knee.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Posterior dislocation of the hip is far more common than anterior dislocation.
Reason (R): The hip joint is least stable when flexed and adducted, a position commonly assumed during trauma such as a dashboard injury in a road traffic accident.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
questions.explain: Both statements are true and connected: because the hip joint is least stable in the flexed-and-adducted position, it is at greatest risk of posterior dislocation, which is why this accounts for roughly 90% of acquired hip dislocations.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A gomphosis is structurally classified as a synovial joint.
Reason (R): A gomphosis involves a peg-in-socket arrangement, such as a tooth held in its socket by the periodontal ligament.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
questions.explain: The Reason correctly describes a gomphosis, but the Assertion is false — a gomphosis is a fibrous joint, not a synovial joint, since it lacks a joint cavity.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The knee joint requires very little ligamentous and muscular support because its bony surfaces are highly congruent.
Reason (R): Knee stability depends largely on the tone of the quadriceps femoris muscle and the collateral ligaments.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
A is true but R is false
questions.explain: The Reason is true — knee stability does depend largely on the quadriceps tone and collateral ligaments — but the Assertion is false, because this dependence exists precisely because the bony surfaces are NOT highly congruent and need extensive soft-tissue support.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The deltoid (medial) ligament of the ankle is more frequently torn than the lateral ligament.
Reason (R): The deltoid ligament is anatomically larger and stronger than the lateral ligament.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
questions.explain: Both statements are false. The lateral ligament, not the deltoid, is more frequently torn, precisely because the deltoid ligament is the stronger of the two — the opposite of what is asserted.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Damage to the medial circumflex femoral artery can result in avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Reason (R): The medial circumflex femoral artery is a major contributor to the blood supply of the femoral head in adults.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are true. The medial circumflex femoral artery is a principal blood supply to the femoral head, so its damage directly explains the risk of avascular necrosis described in the Assertion.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The anterior talofibular ligament is the most commonly injured ligament in ankle sprains.
Reason (R): It is described as the weakest component of the lateral ligament complex of the ankle.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
questions.explain: Both statements are true and connected: being the weakest part of the lateral ligament complex directly explains why the anterior talofibular ligament fails first and most often in ankle sprains.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joints function as two separate, unconnected joint cavities within the knee.
Reason (R): Both articulations are enclosed within a single, shared joint cavity at the knee.
options: Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: The Reason is true — the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joints do share a single joint cavity — but this directly contradicts and disproves the Assertion, which is therefore false.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Synchondroses are typically permanent joints that persist unchanged throughout life.
Reason (R): The epiphyseal plate, a synchondrosis, eventually ossifies and disappears once skeletal growth is complete.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: The Reason is true — the epiphyseal plate does ossify and disappear after growth — but this fact disproves the Assertion, since it shows synchondroses are typically temporary, not permanent.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The shoulder joint's rotator cuff muscles contribute significantly to its stability.
Reason (R): The rotator cuff is a sheath of tendons from the subscapularis, teres minor, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus that covers and blends with most of the joint capsule.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion: by enveloping and blending with the joint capsule, the rotator cuff musculotendinous sheath provides crucial dynamic stability to an otherwise structurally unstable joint.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A 'sprain' and a 'strain' refer to the exact same type of soft-tissue injury.
Reason (R): A sprain involves tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule, whereas a strain involves injury to muscle or tendon.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
questions.explain: The Reason correctly distinguishes the two terms, which is precisely why the Assertion (claiming they are the same) is false.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bursae located near a joint can sometimes become distended when the joint itself produces excess synovial fluid.
Reason (R): Some bursae, such as the suprapatellar bursa at the knee, directly communicate with the synovial cavity of the adjacent joint.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explain: Both statements are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion: because certain bursae like the suprapatellar bursa communicate directly with the joint cavity, excess synovial fluid in the joint can flow into and distend the bursa.

questions.q: A biopsy shows tissue with cells packed tightly together and almost no space between them for extracellular material. Which basic tissue type does this most likely represent?
questions.explain: Epithelial tissue is defined by cells packed closely with minimal extracellular matrix, the opposite arrangement to connective tissue, which has abundant matrix and sparse cells.

questions.q: A pathologist notes that a sampled epithelium shows no blood vessels running through it at all, yet the cells appear healthy and well-nourished. How is this possible?
options: The sample must have been mishandled, since living epithelium always contains vessels
The cells are actually dead and do not need nutrients
All epithelium secretes its own blood supply
It is avascular and fed by diffusion from below
questions.explain: Epithelial tissue is characteristically avascular; it relies on diffusion of nutrients and oxygen from blood vessels in the adjacent connective tissue across the basement membrane, rather than containing its own vessels.

questions.q: An epithelial cell's apical and basal surfaces differ structurally and functionally from one another. What is this property called?
questions.explain: This apical-versus-basal structural and functional asymmetry is termed polarity, a hallmark feature of epithelial cells.

questions.q: Which cells are commonly found wedged between simple columnar epithelial cells?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A researcher wants to identify the specific junction type responsible for mechanically binding epidermal cells together so the skin can resist friction and stretching without cells tearing apart. Which junction is most directly responsible?
questions.explain: Desmosomes are spot-like junctions that mechanically anchor adjacent cells together, giving epithelium (such as the epidermis) resistance to mechanical stress like friction and stretching.

questions.q: Specializatons of the surface epithelial cells that permit passage of small molecular weight particles through cell membranes of contiguous cells are
options: Are not known to exist in humans
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The type of epithelium which appears to have two or three layers of cells, although all the cells are in contact with the basement membrane is
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location revealed several layers of cells. Only the basal layer of cells was attached to the basement membrane. The basal cells were taller than wide, the intermediate layers contained polyhedral cells and the superficial cell nuclei were flattened in a horizontal plane. The superficial cells were covered with an eosinophilic transluscent band that was anucleated. Parts of the surface also had fibrillar, anucleated, eosinophilic structures. Goblets cells, cilia, microvilli and stereocilia were absent.This epithelium is most likely to be located:
options: Tongue, soft palate, oral surface of lips and anal canal
In the oesophagus, cornea, vagina and tongue
In an internal environment that is subject to abrasion or the external environment

questions.q: In a pseudostratified columnar epithelium, which of the following is characteristic of all cells:
options: Location of nuclei at the same horizontal level
Possession of highly folded basal membranes
Direct contact with the basement membrane
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following types of epithelial tissues is best suited for areas of the body where diffusion or filtration occurs?
