questions.q: The temporary cylinder of microtubules that aids elongation of the spermatid during the acrosomal phase is the:
questions.explain: The manchette is a temporary cylinder of microtubules that aids spermatid elongation during the acrosomal phase.

questions.q: During the maturation phase of spermiogenesis, discarded excess cytoplasm from spermatids is disposed of by:
options: Being expelled directly into the bloodstream
questions.explain: The discarded excess cytoplasm shed during the maturation phase is phagocytosed by Sertoli cells.

questions.q: At the end of the maturation phase, spermatozoa are released into the tubule lumen in which orientation, and in what motility state?
questions.explain: The maturation phase ends with nonmotile spermatozoa released tail first into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule.

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as an intratesticular duct?
questions.explain: The intratesticular ducts are the straight tubules (tubuli recti), the rete testis, and the proximal portion of the efferent ductules.

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as an extratesticular duct?
questions.explain: Extratesticular ducts include the distal portion of the efferent ductules, ductus epididymis, ductus (vas) deferens, ejaculatory ducts, and urethra.

questions.q: In the straight tubules (tubuli recti), the proximal half is lined by which cell type?
questions.explain: The proximal half of the straight tubules is lined by Sertoli cells; the distal half is lined by cuboidal cells.

questions.q: Which structures are devoid of spermatogenic cells and lack smooth muscle in their wall?
options: The ductus deferens and its ampulla
The seminal vesicle and its duct
questions.explain: Both the straight tubules and the rete testis are devoid of spermatogenic cells and have no smooth muscle.

questions.q: The rete testis is located within the:
questions.explain: The rete testis is an irregular, anastomosing network of tubules located within the mediastinum testis.

questions.q: The epithelium of the rete testis is:
questions.explain: The rete testis has a simple cuboidal epithelium with microvilli as well as a single luminal flagellum (cilium).

questions.q: The efferent ductules (ductuli efferentes) have a characteristic luminal margin described as:
questions.explain: Efferent ductules have a saw-toothed luminal margin, produced by alternating tall ciliated columnar and short unciliated cuboidal cells.

questions.q: In the efferent ductules, non-ciliated cuboidal cells function mainly to:
questions.explain: Non-ciliated cells of the efferent ductules reabsorb testicular fluid, while the ciliated cells propel the still-immobile sperm toward the epididymis.

questions.q: The epithelium of the ductus epididymis is best described as:
options: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells
questions.explain: The ductus epididymis has a pseudostratified columnar stereociliated (non-motile) epithelium.

questions.q: Within the ductus epididymis epithelium, which cell type is round and serves as the precursor of principal cells?
questions.explain: Basal cells are round and serve as precursors of the principal cells in the epididymal epithelium.

questions.q: The stereocilia of the ductus epididymis mainly function to:
options: Form part of the blood-testis barrier
Propel sperm along by ciliary beating
questions.explain: Stereocilia (which are non-motile, unlike true cilia) increase the epithelial surface area for reabsorption of about 90% of the luminal fluid.

questions.q: Why is a large volume of fluid secreted by Sertoli cells needed to help move sperm out of the seminiferous tubule?
options: Because sperm are too large to move on their own
Because sperm are initially non-motile as they leave the tubule
Because the tubule lumen is completely blocked otherwise
questions.explain: Sperm are initially non-motile as they leave the seminiferous tubule, so a large secreted fluid volume (from Sertoli cells) helps propel them toward the epididymis.

questions.q: Along the length of the epididymis, which of the following changes occur from head to tail?
options: No structural changes occur along its length
Epithelial height and stereocilia increase; muscularis decreases
questions.explain: Along the epididymis, epithelial cell height and stereocilia height decrease, while the muscularis increases from 1 to 3 layers.

questions.q: Which part of the epididymis serves as the principal reservoir for sperm storage?
questions.explain: The tail of the epididymis is the principal reservoir for sperm storage, while the head and body move sperm via peristaltic contraction.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a listed function of the ductus epididymis?
options: Temporary storage and maturation of sperm
Production of glycoprotein inhibiting premature capacitation
questions.explain: The epididymis stores/matures sperm, absorbs fluid, and secretes an inhibitory glycoprotein — but testosterone synthesis is a function of Leydig cells, not the epididymis.

questions.q: The modification of the sperm head by decapacitation-factor-containing glycoconjugates during epididymal transit is called:
questions.explain: Decapacitation is the process during epididymal maturation in which the sperm head is modified by surface-associated decapacitation-factor glycoconjugates.

questions.q: Stereocilia are present in epithelial linings of the following organs:
options: Trachea, epididymis, penile urethra, membranous urethra
Primary bronchi and gallbladder, vas deferens, penile urethra
Ileum, colon, trachea and respiratory bronchioles, membranous urethra
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The ductus deferens has a muscularis composed of how many smooth muscle layers, and what characteristic lumen shape?
options: 1 layer only; a round, regular lumen
No muscularis at all; irregular lumen
questions.explain: The ductus deferens has a 3-layered muscularis (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal) and a characteristic star-shaped lumen.

questions.q: Compared to the rest of the vas deferens, the ampulla of the ductus deferens is characterized by:
options: A larger lumen with folded mucosa
A smaller lumen and smooth mucosa
questions.explain: The ampulla of the ductus deferens has a larger lumen, highly folded mucosa, and glandular diverticula/crypts, with a comparatively thinner muscle layer.

questions.q: The ejaculatory duct is lined by which epithelium, and what substitutes for its lack of a true muscularis?
options: Stratified squamous epithelium; smooth muscle of the bladder
Simple columnar epithelium; fibromuscular tissue of the prostate
questions.explain: The ejaculatory duct has a simple columnar epithelium and no smooth muscle of its own — the fibromuscular tissue of the prostate substitutes for muscle.

questions.q: In the male embryo, the genital duct system develops from which paired ducts (as opposed to the paramesonephric ducts of the female)?
questions.explain: In the indifferent stage, both sexes have mesonephric (wolffian) and paramesonephric (müllerian) ducts; the male genital duct system develops from the mesonephric (wolffian) ducts.

questions.q: The male urethra serves as the terminal duct for which two systems?
questions.explain: The male urethra serves as the terminal duct for both the urinary and genital systems.

questions.q: The male urethra is approximately how long?
questions.explain: The male urethra is about 20 cm long, considerably longer than the female urethra (3–5 cm).

questions.q: Transitional epithelium is found in all the following EXCEPT
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location, showed 3 layers of cells that were taller than wide. The cells lacked surface specialization. This epithelium is most likely to be located in the:
options: Ureter, spongy urethra and prostatic urethra
Prostatic urethra, membranous urethra and ureter
Membranous urethra and fossa navicularis of the penis
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The membranous urethra is surrounded by skeletal muscle of the deep perineal pouch, forming the:
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle of the deep perineal pouch surrounding the membranous urethra forms the external (voluntary) sphincter of the urethra.

questions.q: The penile (spongy) urethra is surrounded by which erectile body as it passes through the length of the penis?
questions.explain: The penile (spongy) urethra is surrounded by the corpus spongiosum as it passes through the length of the penis.

questions.q: Near its distal end, the penile urethra's epithelium changes to:
questions.explain: At its distal end, the penile urethra is lined with stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the skin of the penis.

questions.q: Which glands' ducts empty into the penile urethra, contributing mucus-secreting glandular openings along its length?
questions.explain: Ducts of the bulbourethral glands and the mucus-secreting urethral glands (glands of Littré) empty into the penile urethra.

questions.q: Compared with the male urethra, the female urethra is:
options: Longer and lined by transitional epithelium throughout
questions.explain: The female urethra is short (3–5 cm), lined primarily by stratified squamous epithelium, with patches of pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

questions.q: The penis contains three masses of erectile tissue: two corpora cavernosa and:
options: The rete testis of the mediastinum
A second pair of corpora cavernosa
The tunica vasculosa of the testis
questions.explain: The penis contains two corpora cavernosa plus a single corpus spongiosum (corpus cavernosum urethrae), through which the penile urethra passes.

questions.q: The vascular spaces of the corpora cavernosa are lined by:
options: A continuous layer of endothelial cells
questions.explain: The corpora cavernosa contain irregular vascular spaces lined by a continuous layer of endothelial cells, separated by CT/smooth muscle trabeculae.

questions.q: Compared with the corpora cavernosa, the corpus spongiosum's trabeculae contain:
options: More elastic fibers and less smooth muscle
More smooth muscle and fewer elastic fibers
questions.explain: Corpus spongiosum trabeculae contain more elastic fibers and less smooth muscle than those of the corpora cavernosa, and its vascular spaces are of uniform size.

questions.q: The dilated distal end of the corpus spongiosum is called the:
questions.explain: The glans penis is the dilated distal end of the corpus spongiosum, covered by the retractable prepuce.

questions.q: The retractable skin covering the glans penis is called the:
questions.explain: The prepuce is the retractable skin covering the glans penis, lined by stratified squamous lightly keratinized epithelium.

questions.q: The thick fibrous CT sheath surrounding both the corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum of the penis is the:
questions.explain: The tunica albuginea is the thick fibrous connective tissue sheath surrounding the paired corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum.

questions.q: During erection, engorgement of the vascular spaces results from which type of nervous impulse?
options: Purely hormonal signals with no nervous input
questions.explain: During erection, vascular spaces become engorged with blood as a result of parasympathetic impulses, which constrict arteriovenous shunts and dilate the helicine arteries.

questions.q: Semen contains fluid and sperm from the testis, along with secretory products from all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Semen contains secretions from the epididymis, ductus deferens, prostate, seminal vesicles, and bulbourethral glands — not the kidneys.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a listed function of semen?
options: Provides DNA identical to body cells
Serves as a transport medium for sperm
questions.explain: Semen transports sperm, neutralizes acidity, liquefies the coagulum, and activates sperm — sperm are haploid, not identical in genetic content to somatic cells.

questions.q: The prostate gland produces a fluid best described as:
questions.explain: The prostate gland produces a clear/watery, slightly alkaline fluid.

questions.q: Which prostatic secretion is specifically responsible for liquefying semen?
questions.explain: Fibrinolysin, secreted by the prostate, liquefies semen.

questions.q: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA), used clinically as a tumor marker, is normally a secretory product of the:
questions.explain: PSA is a normal secretory component of prostatic fluid, though it is used clinically as a marker that can be elevated in prostate disease.

questions.q: Histologically, the prostate gland shows:
options: A honeycomb appearance similar to seminal vesicles
questions.explain: The prostate gland is composed of prostatic acini/glandular alveoli in a fibromuscular connective tissue stroma, and does NOT show the honeycomb appearance seen in seminal vesicles.

questions.q: Prostatic concretions (corpora amylacea) are:
options: Composed purely of calcium with no organic material
questions.explain: Prostatic concretions (corpora amylacea) increase in number with age, forming by precipitation of secretory material around cell fragments, and may become calcified.

questions.q: As the prostate enlarges, which urethral segment is most directly compressed, producing urinary symptoms?
questions.explain: Prostate enlargement narrows the prostatic urethra, which passes directly through the gland, producing obstructive urinary symptoms.

questions.q: Which of the following is a listed urinary symptom of prostate enlargement?
options: Immediate kidney failure in all patients
Complete absence of any urinary symptoms
questions.explain: Prostate enlargement is associated with symptoms including increased night-time frequency, urgency, poor/thin stream, and sense of incomplete emptying, among others.

questions.q: Seminal vesicle secretions contribute approximately what proportion of total semen volume?
questions.explain: Seminal vesicle secretions make up approximately 70% of semen volume.

questions.q: Which of the following is a component of seminal vesicle secretion?
options: Prostatic acid phosphatase and citric acid
questions.explain: Seminal vesicles produce a whitish-yellow viscous fluid containing fructose, fibrinogen, amino acids, ascorbic acid, and prostaglandins.

questions.q: Histologically, the seminal vesicle is distinguished by its:
questions.explain: The seminal vesicle shows a honeycomb appearance, with highly branched folds of mucosa and mucosal crypts.

questions.q: The seminal vesicle epithelium is best described as:
questions.explain: The seminal vesicle has a pseudostratified columnar, low columnar, or cuboidal epithelium, arranged with mucosal crypts.

questions.q: The seminal vesicle wall contains which muscle layers?
options: Three layers identical to the vas deferens
Only a single circular layer of muscle
questions.explain: The seminal vesicle wall has inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers, within 3 coats overall.

questions.q: Bulbourethral (Cowper's) gland secretion is best described as:
options: Identical in composition to prostatic fluid
Composed mainly of fructose and citrate
questions.explain: Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands produce a clear, mucous-like secretion that lubricates the penile urethra just prior to the emission of semen.

questions.q: Which of the following is a listed component of bulbourethral gland secretion?
questions.explain: Bulbourethral gland secretions contain galactose, galactosamine, galacturonic acid, sialic acid, and methylpentose.

questions.q: The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands are histologically composed of:
options: Mucous glands with a fibroelastic capsule
Honeycomb glandular alveoli identical to seminal vesicles
questions.explain: Bulbourethral glands are mucous glands with simple cuboidal or columnar epithelium, surrounded by a fibroelastic capsule containing skeletal muscle, with CT septa.

questions.q: Sperm movement through the female reproductive tract is driven by:
options: Muscular contractions of the uterus/uterine tubes plus their own propulsion
Ciliary beating exclusively, with no sperm motility
questions.explain: Sperm movement is driven by muscular contractions of the uterus and uterine tubes, together with the sperm's own propulsion.

questions.q: The trip of sperm from the cervix to the oviduct requires a minimum of:
questions.explain: The trip from the cervix to the oviduct requires a minimum of 2–7 hours.

questions.q: After reaching the isthmus, sperm:
options: Become less motile and pause their migration
questions.explain: After reaching the isthmus, sperm become less motile and cease their migration until ovulation.

questions.q: At ovulation, sperm become motile again largely due to:
options: Chemoattractants produced by the cumulus cells
questions.explain: At ovulation, sperm regain motility due to chemoattractants produced by the cumulus cells, and swim to the ampulla.

questions.q: Thermotaxis describes how sperm are guided through most of the fallopian tube by:
options: Temperature — the tube with the ovulated oocyte is slightly warmer
questions.explain: Thermotaxis: sperm are guided by temperature through most of the tube, since the tube containing the ovulated oocyte is slightly warmer, before switching to chemical guidance near the egg.

questions.q: Before a spermatozoon is capable of fertilizing, it must undergo which three changes?
options: Capacitation, hyperactivation, and the acrosomal reaction
questions.explain: Pre-fertilization changes required are capacitation, hyperactivation, and the acrosomal reaction.

questions.q: Capacitation occurs in the uterine tubes and lasts approximately:
questions.explain: Capacitation is a period of conditioning in the female reproductive tract, occurring in the uterine tubes and lasting approximately 7 hours.

questions.q: During capacitation, which of the following is removed from the plasma membrane surrounding the acrosomal region?
options: Glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins
questions.explain: Capacitation involves removal of the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the plasma membrane surrounding the acrosomal region of the sperm.

questions.q: Only capacitated sperm can:
options: Pass through the cells of the corona radiata to undergo the acrosomal reaction
questions.explain: Only capacitated sperm can pass through the cells of the corona radiata to undergo the acrosomal reaction.

questions.q: Hyperactivation refers to the sperm's ability to:
options: Swim faster and more vigorously, easing zona pellucida penetration
Fuse with the oocyte membrane directly
questions.explain: Hyperactivation is the ability of the spermatozoon to swim faster and more vigorously, making it easier to penetrate the zona pellucida.

questions.q: The acrosomal reaction is induced by:
questions.explain: The acrosomal reaction occurs after the sperm binds to the zona pellucida and is induced by zona proteins.

questions.q: The acrosomal reaction releases which enzymes needed for zona pellucida penetration?
questions.explain: The acrosomal reaction releases enzymes, including acrosin and trypsin-like enzymes, needed to penetrate the zona pellucida.

questions.q: Fertilization usually takes place within which structure?
options: The isthmus of the uterine tube
questions.explain: Fertilization usually takes place within the ampulla of the oviduct.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of sperm deposited in the vagina enter the cervix?
questions.explain: Only about 1% of the sperm deposited in the vagina enter the cervix.

questions.q: Spermatozoa may remain viable within the female reproductive tract for about:
questions.explain: Spermatozoa may remain viable in the female reproductive tract for approximately 5 days.

questions.q: Fertilization consists of three phases; which is Phase 1?
options: Fusion of oocyte and sperm cell membranes
questions.explain: Phase 1 of fertilization is penetration of the corona radiata.

questions.q: Of the 200–300 million sperm deposited in the vagina, approximately how many reach the ampulla?
questions.explain: Of the 200–300 million sperm deposited in the vagina, only 300 to 500 reach the ampulla.

questions.q: The many sperm that do not fertilize the oocyte serve what role?
options: They aid the fertilizing sperm in penetrating the corona radiata and zona pellucida
They compete to reach the uterus first
They fertilize the polar body instead
questions.explain: The remaining, non-fertilizing spermatozoa aid the fertilizing sperm in penetrating the barriers (corona radiata and zona pellucida) protecting the egg.

questions.q: Which zona pellucida glycoprotein cross-links ZP2 with ZP3, preventing additional sperm from binding?
questions.explain: ZP1 cross-links ZP2 with ZP3, thereby preventing more spermatozoa from binding.

questions.q: Which zona pellucida glycoprotein permits sperm binding and facilitates the acrosome reaction?
questions.explain: ZP3 permits the binding of spermatozoa and facilitates occurrence of the acrosome reaction.

questions.q: Which zona pellucida glycoprotein has an unknown function?
questions.explain: ZP4's function is unknown, unlike ZP1, ZP2, and ZP3.

questions.q: After fertilization, the ovum secretes ovastacin, which:
options: Degrades ZP2, preventing additional sperm binding
questions.explain: After fertilization, the ovum secretes the enzyme ovastacin, which degrades ZP2, preventing binding of additional spermatozoa to the zona pellucida.

questions.q: In Phase 2 of fertilization, release of acrosin allows the sperm to:
options: Penetrate the zona pellucida and contact the oocyte's plasma membrane
questions.explain: Release of acrosin, the acrosomal enzyme, allows the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida, bringing it into contact with the oocyte's plasma membrane.

questions.q: In Phase 3 of fertilization, initial adhesion of sperm to oocyte is partly mediated by:
options: Integrins on the oocyte and disintegrins on the sperm
questions.explain: Initial adhesion is partly mediated by interaction of integrins on the oocyte and their ligands, disintegrins, on the sperm.

questions.q: Cleavage is best defined as:
options: A series of mitotic divisions fractionating the zygote into numerous normal-size cells
A single meiotic division of the oocyte
questions.explain: Cleavage is a series of mitotic divisions by which the large zygote is fractionated into numerous 'normal size' cells.

questions.q: Each daughter cell produced during cleavage is called a:
questions.explain: Each daughter cell of the cleavage process is termed a blastomere.

questions.q: Cleavage begins with the zygote and, via compaction and the morula stage, terminates at the start of the:
questions.explain: Cleavage begins with a zygote, progresses through compaction to a morula stage, and terminates at the start of the blastocyst (blastula) stage.

questions.q: Until the 8-cell stage, blastomeres form:
questions.explain: Until the eight-cell stage, the blastomeres form a loosely arranged clump.

questions.q: After the 3rd cleavage, blastomeres maximize contact with each other, forming a compact ball held together by tight junctions — this process is called:
questions.explain: Compaction is the process by which, after the 3rd cleavage, blastomeres maximize mutual contact, forming a compact ball held by tight junctions.

questions.q: Compaction differentiates blastomeres into which two populations?
options: Inner and outer cells with different fates
questions.explain: The process of compaction differentiates blastomeres into inner and outer cells with different developmental missions.

questions.q: Approximately 3 days after fertilization, the compacted embryo forms a 16-cell structure known as the:
questions.explain: Approximately 3 days after fertilization, cells of the compacted embryo divide again to form a 16-cell morula (named for its resemblance to a mulberry).

questions.q: Inner cells of the morula constitute the:
questions.explain: Inner cells of the morula constitute the inner cell mass, while surrounding cells compose the outer cell mass.

questions.q: The inner cell mass of the morula gives rise to:
questions.explain: The inner cell mass gives rise to tissues of the embryo proper, while the outer cell mass forms the trophoblast, contributing later to the placenta.

questions.q: During cleavage, individual blastomeres:
options: Do not grow — cell size is reduced by almost half at each division
Double in size at each division
questions.explain: Individual blastomeres do not grow during cleavage; the size of the cell is reduced by almost half at each division.

questions.q: The first cleavage division occurs how many days following ovulation?
questions.explain: The first cleavage division occurs 1 to 5 days following ovulation.

questions.q: After the first division, cells divide about once every:
questions.explain: Thereafter, cells divide about once every 12 hours, with up to 8 generations of mitoses occurring without intervening cytoplasmic growth.

questions.q: As fluid from the uterine tube penetrates the zona pellucida into the intercellular spaces of the inner cell mass, these spaces become confluent and form a single cavity called the:
questions.explain: The intercellular spaces gradually become confluent, forming a single cavity — the blastocoel — at which point the embryo is called a blastocyst.

questions.q: In the blastocyst, cells of the outer cell mass (trophoblast) flatten to form:
options: The epithelial wall of the blastocyst
questions.explain: Cells of the outer cell mass (trophoblast) flatten and form the epithelial wall of the blastocyst, while inner cell mass (embryoblast) cells sit at one pole.

questions.q: Disappearance of the zona pellucida in the blastocyst allows:
questions.explain: The zona pellucida disappears, allowing implantation of the blastocyst to begin.

questions.q: Which cell adhesion molecule on trophoblast cells mediates initial attachment of the blastocyst to the uterine epithelium?
questions.explain: L-selectin (CD62L), a cell adhesion molecule on trophoblast cells, and its carbohydrate receptors on the uterine epithelium mediate initial blastocyst attachment.

questions.q: Monozygotic twins arise from:
options: 1 oocyte fertilized by a single spermatozoon
A single oocyte fertilized by 2 sperm
Two separate ovulations in the same cycle, each fertilized separately
questions.explain: Monozygotic (identical) twins arise from 1 oocyte fertilized by a single spermatozoon.

questions.q: Dizygotic twins are always:
options: The same sex, with identical blood groups
Potentially the same or different sex, with separate placentas
questions.explain: Dizygotic twins arise from 2 oocytes and 2 spermatozoa, may be the same or different sex, have different blood groups, and always have separate placentas.

questions.q: Monozygotic twins may share a placenta (monochorionic) or have separate placentas because:
options: They always have separate placentas, like dizygotic twins
Depending on when the single zygote splits, the placenta may or may not be shared
Placenta type depends on maternal blood group
Twin placentation is random and unrelated to zygosity
questions.explain: Depending on the timing of the split, monozygotic twins may share a common placenta (monochorionic) or develop separate placentas (dichorionic).

questions.q: Which factor is associated with a higher likelihood of dizygotic twinning?
questions.explain: A family history of fraternal twins increases the chance of conceiving twins, along with older maternal age, African-American race, obesity, greater height, breastfeeding during conception, and reproductive technologies.

questions.q: In one type of monozygotic twinning, the zygote divides into two separate cells (embryos) at:
questions.explain: One pattern of monozygotic twinning occurs when the zygote divides into two separate cells (embryos) at the first cleavage division.

questions.q: Siamese (conjoined) twins result when:
options: Two inner cell masses form and separate completely
A single inner cell mass forms, divides incompletely
Two separate zygotes fuse at fertilization
The zona pellucida fails to disappear
questions.explain: Conjoined twins result when a single inner cell mass forms and divides incompletely, giving rise to two incompletely separated embryos.

questions.q: By day 8 of development, the trophoblast differentiates into which two layers?
questions.explain: On day 8, the trophoblast differentiates into the cytotrophoblast (inner mononucleated layer) and syncytiotrophoblast (outer multinucleated layer).

questions.q: Mitotic figures are found in which trophoblast layer, but NOT the other?
questions.explain: Mitotic figures are found in the cytotrophoblast but not the syncytiotrophoblast; cytotrophoblast cells divide and migrate into the syncytiotrophoblast, fusing and losing their individual membranes.

questions.q: On day 8, the embryoblast (inner cell mass) differentiates into which two layers?
questions.explain: The embryoblast differentiates into the hypoblast (small cuboidal cells adjacent to the blastocyst cavity) and the epiblast (high columnar cells adjacent to the amniotic cavity).

questions.q: The hypoblast and epiblast, together with the cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, form:
questions.explain: Together, these 4 layers form a flat, bilaminar disc.

questions.q: A small cavity appearing within the epiblast on day 8 enlarges to become the:
questions.explain: A small cavity appears within the epiblast and enlarges to become the amniotic cavity.

questions.q: Epiblast cells adjacent to the cytotrophoblast that line the amniotic cavity are called:
questions.explain: Epiblast cells adjacent to the cytotrophoblast are called amnioblasts, and together with the rest of the epiblast, they line the amniotic cavity.

questions.q: Day 9 of development is known as the lacunar stage because:
options: Lacunae (fused vacuoles) appear in the syncytium at the embryonic pole
The blastocyst first attaches to the endometrium
questions.explain: On day 9, vacuoles appear in the syncytium at the embryonic pole and fuse to form large lacunae — the lacunar stage of trophoblast development.

questions.q: At the abembryonic pole on day 9, flattened hypoblast-derived cells form the:
questions.explain: At the abembryonic pole, flattened cells from the hypoblast form the exocoelomic (Heuser's) membrane, lining the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast.

questions.q: On days 11–12, syncytiotrophoblast cells erode maternal capillaries, which become congested and dilated and are then called:
questions.explain: Eroded maternal capillaries, congested and dilated, are known as sinusoids.

questions.q: When syncytial lacunae become continuous with sinusoids and maternal blood enters the lacunar system, this establishes the:
questions.explain: Continuity between syncytial lacunae and sinusoids allows maternal blood to flow through the trophoblastic system, establishing uteroplacental circulation.

questions.q: Extraembryonic mesoderm, derived from the epiblast, eventually fills the space between the trophoblast and the amnion/exocoelomic membrane, and cavities within it become confluent to form the:
questions.explain: Large cavities in the extraembryonic mesoderm become confluent, forming the extraembryonic coelom, or chorionic cavity.

questions.q: On day 13, cytotrophoblast cells proliferate into the syncytiotrophoblast, forming cellular columns known as:
questions.explain: Cellular columns surrounded by syncytium, formed by cytotrophoblast proliferation into the syncytiotrophoblast, are known as primary villi.

questions.q: The secondary (definitive) yolk sac, formed on day 13 from additional hypoblast cells, is:
options: Larger than the primitive yolk sac
Much smaller than the primitive yolk sac (exocoelomic cavity)
Identical in size to the primitive yolk sac
questions.explain: The secondary yolk sac is much smaller than the original exocoelomic cavity (primitive yolk sac).

questions.q: The extraembryonic mesoderm lining the inside of the cytotrophoblast is known as the:
questions.explain: The extraembryonic mesoderm lining the cytotrophoblast is called the chorionic plate.

questions.q: The connecting stalk, traversed by extraembryonic mesoderm across the chorionic cavity, later develops into the:
questions.explain: With development of blood vessels, the connecting stalk becomes the umbilical cord.

questions.q: By the end of the 2nd week, blood levels of hCG produced by the syncytiotrophoblast are sufficient for:
questions.explain: By the end of week 2, hCG quantities are sufficient to be detected by radioimmunoassays, forming the basis of pregnancy testing.

questions.q: Which unusual MHC class IB molecule helps block maternal immune recognition of the conceptus as foreign?
questions.explain: An unusual MHC class IB molecule, HLA-G, blocks recognition of the conceptus as foreign tissue, alongside immunosuppressive cytokines and proteins.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of ectopic pregnancies occur in the uterine tube?
questions.explain: 95% of ectopic pregnancies occur in the uterine tube, most often in the ampulla.

questions.q: Gastrulation marks the commencement of the embryonic period, which extends from:
questions.explain: Gastrulation marks the commencement of the embryonic period, which extends from week 3 to week 8.

questions.q: Gastrulation transforms the bilaminar embryonic disc into a:
questions.explain: Gastrulation results in transformation of the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar one, comprising ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

questions.q: Gastrulation begins with formation of the:
questions.explain: Gastrulation begins with formation of the primitive (Spemann's) streak on the surface of the epiblast.

questions.q: The cranial end of the primitive streak expands to form the:
questions.explain: The cranial end of the primitive streak is expanded as the primitive (Hensen's) node, containing the primitive pit.

questions.q: Formation of the primitive streak defines which body axes?
options: Cranial-caudal, dorsal-ventral, medial-lateral, and left-right axes
No axes are established by the streak
questions.explain: Formation of the primitive streak defines all major body axes: cranial-caudal, dorsal-ventral, medial-lateral, and left-right.

questions.q: The inward movement of epiblast cells as they detach and slip beneath the epiblast at the primitive streak is called:
questions.explain: This inward movement of epiblast cells is known as invagination.

questions.q: Cell migration and specification during gastrulation is controlled by which growth factor, synthesized by streak cells themselves?
questions.explain: Cell migration and specification during gastrulation are controlled by fibroblast growth factor 8 (FGF8), synthesized by the streak cells themselves.

questions.q: Invaginated epiblast cells that displace the hypoblast create the:
questions.explain: Once cells have invaginated, some displace the hypoblast, creating the embryonic endoderm.

questions.q: Cells that come to lie between the epiblast and the newly created endoderm form the:
questions.explain: Other invaginating cells come to lie between the epiblast and newly created endoderm, forming the mesoderm.

questions.q: Cells remaining in the epiblast (that did not migrate through the streak) become the:
questions.explain: Cells remaining in the epiblast form ectoderm — thus the epiblast is the ultimate source of all three germ layers.

questions.q: Cells migrating through the mid-streak level of the primitive streak become which mesoderm type?
questions.explain: Cells migrating through the mid-streak level become intermediate (intraembryonic) mesoderm, which forms the urogenital system.

questions.q: Cells that ingress through the cranial region of the primitive node become the:
questions.explain: Cells that ingress through the cranial region of the node become the notochord.

questions.q: The prechordal plate is a thickening of which germ layer, at the cranial end of the primitive streak?
questions.explain: The prechordal plate is a thickening of the endoderm at the cranial end of the primitive streak.

questions.q: The prechordal plate later becomes important for:
options: Development of the notochord's blood supply
questions.explain: The prechordal plate later becomes important for induction of the forebrain.

questions.q: The oropharyngeal membrane consists of tightly adherent ectoderm and endoderm and represents the future opening of the:
questions.explain: The oropharyngeal membrane, at the cranial end, represents the future opening of the oral cavity.

questions.q: The intraembryonic mesoderm separates ectoderm from endoderm along the embryo's length except cranially (prechordal plate) and caudally at the:
questions.explain: Caudally, intraembryonic mesoderm is absent at the cloacal membrane, the future site of the anus.

questions.q: By the end of which week does the primitive streak regress and disappear?
questions.explain: The primitive streak regresses and disappears by the end of week 4.

questions.q: The notochordal process fuses transiently with endoderm to form the:
questions.explain: The notochordal process fuses transiently with endoderm to form the notochordal plate.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a listed function of the notochord?
options: Forms a midline axis determining the antero-posterior axis
Induces formation of the neural tube
questions.explain: The notochord forms the midline axis, induces neural tube formation, and persists as the nucleus pulposus — but it does not form the placenta.

questions.q: Remnants of notochordal tissue may give rise to tumors called:
questions.explain: Remnants of notochordal tissue may give rise to tumors called chordomas.

questions.q: Paraxial mesoderm gives rise mainly to:
questions.explain: Paraxial mesoderm undergoes segmentation into somitomeres and somites, giving rise to musculoskeletal structures.

questions.q: The number of somites present in an embryo is a useful indicator of:
questions.explain: There are 42–44 pairs of somites, which do not all appear simultaneously; the number of somites provides a good index of embryonic age.

questions.q: The extraembryonic (fetal) membranes include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Fetal membranes include the chorion, amnion, yolk sac, allantois, and umbilical cord — the notochord is part of the embryo proper, not a fetal membrane.

questions.q: Primary villi consist of a cytotrophoblastic core covered by:
questions.explain: By the beginning of week 3, the trophoblast is characterized by primary villi, consisting of a cytotrophoblastic core covered by a syncytial layer.

questions.q: A villus becomes a secondary villus once:
options: Mesodermal cells penetrate its cytotrophoblastic core
questions.explain: Secondary villi form when mesodermal cells penetrate the core of primary villi and grow toward the decidua.

questions.q: A villus is termed tertiary (definitive placental villus) once mesodermal core cells differentiate into:
options: Blood cells and small blood vessels
questions.explain: By the end of week 3, mesodermal cells in the villus core differentiate into blood cells and small blood vessels, forming the villous capillary system — the tertiary villus stage.

questions.q: Villi that extend from the chorionic plate to the decidua basalis are called:
questions.explain: Villi extending from the chorionic plate to the decidua basalis are called stem or anchoring villi.

questions.q: The fetal component of the placenta develops from the chorionic plate, also called the:
questions.explain: The fetal component of the placenta develops from the chorionic plate, the chorion frondosum, together with extraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.q: The maternal component of the placenta develops from the endometrium, specifically the:
questions.explain: The maternal component of the placenta develops from the decidua basalis, the endometrium to which the chorion frondosum is attached.

questions.q: On the abembryonic side (decidua capsularis), chorionic villi regress, leaving a smooth surface called the:
questions.explain: On the decidua capsularis side, villi regress, leaving a smooth surface known as the chorion laeve (smooth chorion).

questions.q: Erosion of maternal spiral arteries to release blood into the intervillous spaces is accomplished by:
options: Direct action of the syncytiotrophoblast alone
questions.explain: Cytotrophoblast cells undergo endovascular invasion of the spiral arteries, replacing maternal endothelial cells and creating hybrid vessels.

questions.q: Decidual septa divide the placenta into a number of compartments called:
questions.explain: Decidual septa projecting into (but not reaching) the chorionic plate divide the placenta into 15–20 compartments, called cotyledons.

questions.q: The functional unit of the placenta, a villous tree perfused by a single spiral artery, is called the:
questions.explain: The placentome (placental lobe) is the functional unit of the placenta — there are about 50–100 within a full placenta.

questions.q: Before 20 weeks, the layers of the placental membrane, from fetal to maternal side, are (in order):
options: Syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, connective tissue, capillary endothelium
Capillary endothelium, connective tissue, cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast
Cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast, connective tissue, capillary endothelium
Connective tissue, capillary endothelium, syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast
questions.explain: From fetal to maternal side, the placental membrane layers are: capillary endothelium of fetal capillaries, connective tissue of the villus, cytotrophoblast, and syncytiotrophoblast.

questions.q: The placental barrier does NOT exclude which of the following?
questions.explain: The placental barrier does not exclude many potentially dangerous agents such as alcohol, nicotine, viruses, drugs, exogenous hormones, and heavy metals.

questions.q: Placenta previa is defined as:
options: Premature separation of a normally-positioned placenta
Abnormal placentation near or covering the internal cervical os
questions.explain: Placenta previa is abnormal placentation near or covering the internal os of the uterine cervix, typically causing painless vaginal bleeding.
